It is trite law that a person cannot be arrayed as an accused person merely due to association with the accused company in capacity of a director. [Para 20]

■

The petitioners are sought to be implicated on the ground that the petitioners were responsible for the day-to-day affairs of the company. It has been alleged that since the petitioners have annexed numerous internal communications like emails, it only translates to mean that the petitioners were at the helm of the affairs of the accused company, and are responsible for the conduct of the business of the accused company. [Para 24]

■

headnotes.text: Section 138, read with section 141, of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 - Dishonour of cheque for insufficiency of funds etc. - Original complainant had initially filed a suit for dishonor of cheque before Metropolitan Magistrate against appellants (husband and wife) - Accused wife filed a criminal writ petition before High Court for quashing of her liability on grounds that she was neither a signatory to cheque dishonored nor there was a joint bank account - However, High Court refused to quash order - Whether as per section 138, a person who is signatory to cheque and cheque is drawn by that person on an account maintained by him and cheque has been issued for discharge, in whole or in part, of any debt or other liability and said cheque has been returned by bank unpaid, such person can be said to have committed an offence - Held, yes - Whether section 138 does not speak about joint liability and even in case of a joint liability, in case of individual persons, a person other than a person who has drawn cheque on an account maintained by him, cannot be prosecuted for offence under section 138 - Held, yes - Whether further, even section 141 is relating to offence by companies and it cannot be made applicable to individuals - Held, yes - Whether therefore, High Court committed a grave error in not quashing complaint against appellant for offence punishable under section 138 read with section 141 - Held, yes [Paras 7 and 8][In favour of assessee]FEMA, BANKING  INSURANCE : Where person who has not drawn cheque he cannot be prosecuted for offence under section 138 of Negotiable Instruments Act even in case of a joint liability

Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 - Dishonour of cheque for insufficiency, etc., of funds in account - Petitioner was a school teacher while her husband was engaged in business of advertisement - Petitioner’s husband took a loan by giving a blank cheque as security which was dishonoured on presentation - Summon was issued in name of petitioner - Whether words ‘other association of individuals’ as used in Explanation to section 141 pertain to only those individuals who are engaged in same business as a group not likes of petitioner and her husband - Held, yes - Whether fact that petitioner accompanied her husband when he took loan would in no way saddle petitioner with liability of offence under section 138 - Held, yes - Whether, therefore, order summoning petitioner should be recalled - Held, yes

Section 141, read with  section 138, of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 - Dishonour of certain cheques for insufficiency of funds in accounts - Offences by companies - Appellant was an authorized signatory of a company, which had business transactions with respondent - Appellant issued cheques on behalf of company in favour of respondent, which were dishonoured - On a complaint by respondent under section 138 against appellant, trial court took cognizance of offence against her - On writ, High Court refused to quash proceedings against appellant - Whether prosecution of a company is a sine qua non for prosecution of other persons who fall within second and third categories of candidates under section 141 and, therefore, proceedings against appellant must be quashed in absence of company having been joined as an accused - Held, yes [Per S.B. Sinha, J.] - Whether appellant would be liable to be prosecuted even when company had not been joined as an accused - Held, yes [Per V.S. Sirpurkar, J.] [Matter referred to a Larger Bench]

Section 138, read with section 141, of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 - Dishonour of cheque for insufficiency, etc., of funds in account - Accused No. 1, a proprietorship firm represented through accused No. 2 and petitioner, was engaged in distribution and marketing of Indian Made Foreign Liquor (I.M.F.L) - Accused entered into a distributorship agreement with complainant on basis of which it became an authorized distributor - During course of business, it was alleged by complainant that accused No. 1 had an outstanding balance against which it issued cheque but on presentation, said cheque was dishonoured - Resultantly, complaint under section 138 was filed against accused Nos. 1, 2 and petitioner - It was noted that in complaint, complainant itself had pleaded that cheque in question was signed by accused No. 2 as proprietor of accused No. 1 - Further, in complaint, petitioner had been arrayed as accused No. 3 on premise that she was authorized signatory of accused No. 1 and that she signed distributorship agreement between accused No. 1 and complainant along with accused No. 2 - Whether that itself was not sufficient in terms of section 141 to invoke vicarious liability of offence under section 138 on petitioner - Held, yes - Whether in view of above facts and principles of law, complaint against petitioner could not be sustained, and accordingly, same was to be quashed as against petitioner - Held, yes [Paras 12 and 13]FEMA, BANKING  INSURANCE : Where cheque issued by accused firm to discharge its liability had been dishonoured, in view of fact that petitioner had not signed said cheque, mere averments in complaint that petitioner was authorized signatory of accused firm was not sufficient to make him vicariously liable for dishonour of cheque issued by firm

Section 138, read with section 141, of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 - Dishonour of cheque for insufficiency etc., of funds in account -  Whether it is only 'drawer' of cheque who can be made liable for penal action under provisions of Negotiable Instruments Act - Held, yes - Whether under section 138, in case of issuance of cheque from joint accounts, a joint account holder cannot be prosecuted unless cheque has been signed by each and every person who is a joint account holder - Held, yes [Paras 8.1  23]CL: Only drawer of cheque was liable under Negotiable Instrument Act even if cheque was issued from joint account

Section 138, read with section 139, of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 - Dishonour of cheque for insufficiency etc., of funds in account - Whether for initiation of prosecution under section 138, a prior statutory notice is mandatorily required to be given to drawer, to make good payment of amount mentioned in cheque and only when drawer receives a notice and fails to make payment within time provided by Statute, does dishonour become an offence - Held, yes - A complaint was filed against accused under section 138 by complainant on ground that accused had taken friendly loan from complainant and a cheque issued by accused in favour of complainant was dishonoured on presentation - It was noted that subject cheque, copy of which had been placed on record, was signed only by late husband of accused - Although conceded that cheque was issued from a joint account but subject cheque did not bear signature of accused - Whether thus, criminal complaint filed against accused was clearly an abuse of process of law - Held, yes - Whether thus, instant petition by accused filed under section 482 of Cr.P.C seeking quashing of criminal complaint filed under section 138 was to be allowed and consequently, criminal complaint against accused was to be quashed - Held, yes [Paras 7, 8  11]FEMA, BANKING  INSURANCE : Where a complaint under section 138 was filed against accused on ground that cheque issued by her to discharge her loan liability had been dishonoured, in view of fact that said cheque was issued from a account jointly held by accused and her late husband but subject cheque did not bear signature of accused but of her late husband, criminal complaint filed against accused was clearly an abuse of process of law and was to be quashed

Section 141, read with section 138, of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 - Offence by Companies - Petitioner was working partner of a construction Firm JCC - Firm JCC and respondent were working in building contract - Various constructions for Firm JCC were completed by respondent and certain amount was outstanding from Firm JCC - Firm JCC issued cheques which were dishonoured - A criminal complaint under section 138 was filed by respondent and process against petitioner was issued - Petitioner contended that respondent had not invoked provision of section 141 and had accused petitioner in individual capacity while Firm was not made a party to complaint; therefore, petitioner could not be prosecuted - Whether even if firm was not prosecuted, its partner could not escape liability which was created through legal fiction envisaged under section 141 - Held, Yes [para 17]FEMA, BANKING  INSURANCE LAWS : Where a construction firm issued cheques to respondent-contractor which were dishonoured, even if firm could not be prosecuted, its partners could not escape liability; such a liability is created through legal fiction envisaged under section 141

Section 138, read with section 141, of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 - Dishonour of cheque for insufficiency, etc., of funds in account - Complainant supplied graphic designs to accused No. 1 firm - Against supply of same, Rs. 1.41 lakh remained as due - In discharge of same, accused No. 1 issued a cheque - Said cheque, when presented for encashment, was returned dishonoured due to insufficient funds - Resultantly, complaint under section 138 was filed in which it had been stated that accused No. 1 was an unregistered firm wherein accused No. 2 i.e. 'H' and accused No. 3 (petitioner) were authorized signatory/proprietor/partner/deemed and real owner/official of said firm - Trial Court took cognizance of complaint and issued summons against all three accused including petitioner - It was noted that apart from bald averment made in complaint as well as during course of submissions that petitioner was deemed owner of firm, no other evidence had been produced on record to show that petitioner was deemed/real owner or that he was in charge or responsible for business of firm at time of commission of offence - On other hand, petitioner had placed on record a certificate of acknowledgement of registration from Deputy Registrar of Firms - Said document nowhere showed petitioner as a partner in accused No. 1 - Further, said cheque was signed by 'H' and not petitioner - Whether since there was no evidence on record to show that petitioner was a partner of accused firm or that he was signatory of cheque, summoning order as well as complaint against petitioner was to be quashed - Held, yes [Paras 9, 10 and 12]FEMA, BANKING  INSURANCE : Where cheque issued by firm to discharge its liability had been dishonoured, in view of fact that petitioner had not signed said cheque, mere averment in complaint that petitioner was deemed owner of firm would not make him liable for dishonour of cheque issued by firm since certificate issued by Deputy Registrar of Firms, also nowhere showed that he was a partner in accused firm

Section  138,  read with section  141,  of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 - Dishonour of cheque for insufficiency, etc., of funds in the account - Respondent/complainant filed a complaint under section 138 against petitioner/accused - Trial Court took cognizance of complaint - Petitioner filed instant petition seeking to quash proceedings on ground that cheque was issued by a partnership firm and respondent neither impleaded partnership firm and its other partners as accused nor issued statutory notice to them - It was noted that cheque, issued by partnership firm, was signed by partner / authorised signatory; however, respondent did not cause any statutory notice to partnership firm and other partners - Further, in order to attract an offence under section 141, unless partnership firm had committed offence, as principal accused, other accused would not be responsible and convicted as vicariously liable - Whether therefore, complaint itself was not maintainable and entire proceedings initiated under sections 138 and 141 could not be sustained and were liable to be quashed - Held, yes [Para 6]

Section 141, read with section 138, of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 - Offences by companies - Whether an HUF being a person, for an offence punishable under section 138, HUF can be prosecuted and punished, but at same time, since HUF is an artificial person, sentence of imprisonment cannot be imposed on HUF - Held, yes - Whether to constitute an 'association of individuals' in terms of section 141, it is absolutely necessary that combination of individuals must be on their own free will and volition and it is also necessary that such combination of individuals must be with a common purpose - Held, yes - Whether though there may be a common purpose to be carried forward by an HUF, an individual becomes a member of HUF, not on his own free will and volition, but by status and birth and thus, an HUF will not constitute an 'association of individuals' within meaning of section 141 - Held, yes - Whether a HUF is not a legal entity distinct and separate from that of members who constitute it and, therefore, Karta is liable for prosecution in criminal proceedings for dishonour of cheque issued by him - Held, yes [Paras 24, 25, 44  50]NI Act : Though an HUF is not an 'association of individuals' within meaning of section 141, it is an artificial person being a legal entity not distinct from its members and, hence, Karta of HUF is liable to criminal proceeding for dishonour of cheque issued by him

Section 141,  read with section 138, of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 - Dishonour of certain cheques for insufficiency of funds in accounts - Offences by companies - Whether for maintaining prosecution under section 141, arraigning of a company as an accused is imperative - Held, yes - Whether when company can be prosecuted, then only persons mentioned in other categories can be vicariously held liable for offence subject to averments in petition and proof thereof - Held, yes - Whether, thus, an authorized signatory of a company would not be liable for prosecution under section 138 without company being arraigned as an accused - Held, yesCL : An authorized signatory of a company would not be liable for prosecution under section 138 without company being arraigned as an accused

Section 138, read with section 141 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 - Dishonour of cheque for insufficiency of fund etc. - Complainant filed a complaint under section 138 against applicant, alleging that a cheque issued by applicant towards consideration for registered sale deed executed in respect of a shop purchased in name of wife of applicant had been dishonoured due to insufficiency of funds - Trail Court convicted applicant - Applicant relying upon provisions of section 141 filed instant applicant contending that since cheque in question was signed by him as proprietor of 'S' Traders, in absence of said proprietary concern being made a party, complaint was not maintainable - Whether when applicant had not disputed that he had signed cheque, in such a situation, merely because there was rubber stamp of 'S' Traders on cheque in question, would not lead to applicant escaping liability in view of specific admissions given by him - Held, yes - Whether even otherwise, reliance on section 141 was wholly misplaced because it concerned only company, firm or a body corporate or an association of individuals and proprietary concern was not covered under said provision - Held, yes - Whether in view of aforesaid, impugned order passed by Court below did not require any interference - Held, yes [Paras 15 and 16]

Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881, read with section 482, of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 - Dishonour of cheque for insufficiency etc. of funds in account - Accused issued a cheque to complainant on account of lease agreement - Complaint was filed under section 138 against accused on dishonour of said cheque - Trial Court summoned accused - Accused filed instant petition under section 482 of Cr.P.C seeking quashing of complaint as well as summoning order on ground that he was not a signatory to cheque in question, rather said cheque was signed by his mother - It was noted that it was accused who had entered into lease agreement with complainant in pursuance of which cheque in question was handed over to complainant - Further, cheque was issued from an account that was jointly held by accused as well as his mother - All dealings had taken place with accused - Whether thus, accused was rightly summoned by Trial Court for an offence punishable under section 138 and, therefore, instant petition challenging order of Trial Court was to be dismissed - Held, yes [Para 11]FEMA, BANKING  INSURANCE : Where order summoning accused for offence punishable under section 138 was challenged by accused on ground that cheque in question issued to complainant on account of lease agreement was signed by his mother and not by him, in view of fact that it was accused who had entered into lease agreement with complainant in pursuance of which cheque in question was handed over to complainant, further, cheque was issued from an account that was jointly held by accused as well as his mother, accused was rightly summoned by Trial Court for an offence punishable under section 138

Section 138, read with section 141, of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 - Dishonour of cheque for insufficiency etc., of funds in account - Whether persons with authority to take decisions over transaction and having knowledge of transaction are deemed to be incharge of and responsible to company for day-to-day affairs and conduct of company; such persons may or may not be directors of company - Held, yes - Whether persons who are incharge of and responsible for day-to-day affairs of company are targeted to be held vicariously liable and covered within ambit of section 141 - Held, yes - Whether section 141 creates a legal fiction against defaulting company, so as to cover within its ambit all persons who have consented, connived or anyway attributed to commission of offence - Held, yes - Whether where cheque issued by accused company in favour of complainant was issued under signature and directions of petitioners, Metropolitan Magistrate was right in summoning petitioners for offence under section 138 and, therefore, petition filed for quashing of complaint was to be dismissed - Held, yes [Paras 30, 33  36]Negotiable Instruments Act: Section 141 creates a legal fiction against defaulting company, so as to cover within its ambit all persons who have consented, connived or anyway attributed to commission of offence

Section 138, read with section 141, of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 - Dishonour of cheque for insufficiency, etc., of funds in account - Accused No. 1, a proprietorship firm represented through accused No. 2 and petitioner, was engaged in distribution and marketing of Indian Made Foreign Liquor (I.M.F.L) - Accused entered into a distributorship agreement with complainant on basis of which it became an authorized distributor - During course of business, it was alleged by complainant that accused No. 1 had an outstanding balance against which it issued cheque but on presentation, said cheque was dishonoured - Resultantly, complaint under section 138 was filed against accused Nos. 1, 2 and petitioner - It was noted that in complaint, complainant itself had pleaded that cheque in question was signed by accused No. 2 as proprietor of accused No. 1 - Further, in complaint, petitioner had been arrayed as accused No. 3 on premise that she was authorized signatory of accused No. 1 and that she signed distributorship agreement between accused No. 1 and complainant along with accused No. 2 - Whether that itself was not sufficient in terms of section 141 to invoke vicarious liability of offence under section 138 on petitioner - Held, yes - Whether in view of above facts and principles of law, complaint against petitioner could not be sustained, and accordingly, same was to be quashed as against petitioner - Held, yes [Paras 12 and 13]

Section 138, read with section 141, of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 - Dishonour of cheque for insufficiency, etc., of funds -  Complainant supplied graphic designs to accused no. 1 company - Against supply of same Rs. 11 lakh remained as due - In discharge of same, accused firm issued a cheque - Said cheque, when presented for encashment, was returned dishonoured due to insufficient fund - Resultantly, complaint under section 138 was filed - In complaint it had been stated that accused No. 2 i.e. 'H' and accused No. 3 i.e. petitioner were authorized signatory/proprietor/partner/deemed and real owner/official of said accused firm - Trial Court took cognizance of complaint and issued summons against all three accused - It was noted that apart from bald averment made in complaint, no other evidence had been produced/placed by complainant on record to show that petitioner was deemed/real owner or that he was in charge or responsible for business of firm at time of commission of offence - On other hand, petitioner had placed on record a certificate of acknowledgement of registration from Deputy Registrar of Firm - Said document nowhere showed petitioner as a partner in said firm - Further, a perusal of complaint would show that cheque was issued on account of firm and was signed by 'H' and not petitioner - Whether thus, in absence of any such evidence to bring petitioner within fold of section 138, read with section 141 forcing petitioner to stand trial solely on basis of a bald averment that to unsubstantiated, would amount to an abuse of process of law - Held, yes - Whether thus, summoning order as well as complaint against petitioner was to be quashed - Held, yes [Paras 9, 10 and 12]FEMA, BANKING  INSURANCE : Where cheque issued by firm to discharge its liability had been dishonoured, in view of fact that petitioner had not signed said cheque, mere averment in complaint that petitioner was deemed owner of firm would not make him liable for dishonour of cheque issued by firm since certificate issued by Deputy Registrar of Firms, also nowhere showed that he was a partner in accused firm

Section 138, read with section 141, of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 - Dishonour of cheque for insufficiency, etc., of funds in account - Whether a person cannot be arrayed as an accused person merely due to association with accused company in capacity of a Director - Held, yes - Respondent/complainant sanctioned a term loan to accused company - In order to discharge legal liability, accused issued a cheque - Said cheque upon presentation got dishonoured - Complainant filed a complaint under section 138 - Metropolitan Magistrate by impugned order issued summons to accused company being drawer of subject cheque, to signatory of dishonoured cheque, and petitioners along with two other directors being directors of accused company and responsible for managing day-to-day affairs of accused company - Petitioners filed petition seeking quashing of summoning order - Whether since petitioners were not signatory to subject cheque and during series of omission necessary to constitute offence under section 138 read with section 141, petitioners were not in charge of and also responsible for conduct of business of company, proceedings emanating from complaint for offence under section 138 read with section 141 qua petitioners were to be quashed - Held, yes [Paras 20, 28, 29 and 35]

Section 138, read with  section 141 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 - Dishonour of cheque for insufficiency of funds, etc. -  Appellant/complainant was engaged in business of transporting containers and hiring trailer lorries for transporting - Accused-firm issued a cheque in favour of complainant for discharging liability incurred in business but same was dishonoured on presentation for encashment - Accused refused to pay amount and, hence, complaint was filed - Appellant filed case before lower Court against accused Nos. 1 and 2 to prosecute them under section 138 but accused No. 2 was acquitted by impugned order - It was admitted that accused No. 2 was managing director of accused-firm and had signed cheque on behalf of firm - Whether simply because there were no averments in complaint to effect that, managing partner was in charge and responsible he could not escape from responsibility and, therefore, accused No. 2 could not be acquitted - Held, yes - Whether since conviction and sentence imposed on accused-firm became final, accused No. 2, who was actually representing accused-firm could not contend, in an appeal against acquittal of accused No. 2, to effect that, execution of cheque was not proved - Held, yes - Whether thus, accused No. 2 also committed an offence under section 138 and order of acquittal of accused No. 2 was to be set aside - Held, yes [Paras 7, 9, 10, 11  12]FEMA, INSURANCE  BANKING: Where accused No. 2 was Managing Director of accused firm and was signatory of cheque issued to complainant which had dishonoured on presentation, simply because there were no averments in complaint to effect that, Managing Partner was in charge and responsible he could not escape from responsibility and, therefore, accused No. 2 could not be acquitted for offence under section 138

Section  138,  read with section  141,  of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 - Dishonour of cheque for insufficiency, etc., of funds in the account - Appellant was a director of accused company - Company issued three cheques towards payment for supply of iron and steel - Despite company confirming funds availability at time of deposit, cheques were returned unpaid - Statutory legal notices were sent, followed by filing of a complaint under Sections 138 and 142 - Metropolitan Magistrate took cognizance and issued summons to accused, including appellant - Appellant filed a petition under Section 482 of CrPC seeking quashing of proceedings on ground that complaint did not contain specific averments that appellant was in charge of and responsible for conduct of company’s business at relevant time - High Court dismissed petition on ground that appellant was a director and had signed a Board Resolution, which was treated as indicating her involvement in day-to-day management of company - It was noted that substance of establishing appellant's day-to-day involvement in affairs of company was that she had signed Board Resolutions - To say least, same was not inspiring in confidence because a Board Resolution was a document that was signed by members of Board of Directors for decisions taken or conclusions arrived at for matters placed before Board for consideration and decision - This, however, did not in any manner mean that each and every member of Board of Directors was aware of all decisions taken in everyday transactions that were involved in running a business concern - That apart, there was not even as much as a whisper of direct allegation against appellant in complaint made which, as per S.M.S. Pharmaceuticals Ltd. v. Neeta Bhalla (2005) 8 SCC 89 is sine qua non for Section 141 to be attracted - Whether in that view of matter, proceedings against appellant were to be quashed and set aside - Held, yes [Paras 8 and 11]

Section 138, read with section 141, of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 - Dishonour of cheque for insufficiency, etc., of funds in account - Respondent company/complainant, engaged in business of manufacturing men's jeans supplied said goods to accused company from time to time and raised bills, which were duly received and acknowledged by accused company - Subsequently, in order to discharge their liability under bills raised, certain cheques of varied amount (subject cheques) were issued by accused company - Upon presentation, subject cheques were dishonoured and consequently, criminal complaints under section 138 were filed - In said complaints, petitioner being Company Secretary of accused company, was sought to be made vicariously liable for offence owing to assurances advanced by her qua payment of bills raised as well as encashment of subject cheques - It was noted that petitioner was neither authorized signatory of accused company nor had she signed subject cheques - Further, nowhere in complaint, complainant averred that petitioner was in-charge of and responsible for conduct of business of accused company - Further, neither, was there any averment that offence had been committed with consent or connivance on part of petitioner, so as to potentially make her liable under section 141(2) - Whether thus, continuation of proceedings against petitioner would be nothing but an abuse of process of law and consequently, criminal complaint under section 138 was to be quashed qua petitioner - Held, yes [Paras 17 to 19]FEMA, BANKING  INSURANCE : Where petitioner was acting as a Company Secretary of accused company against whom complaint under section 138 of Negotiable Instruments Act had been filed but petitioner had neither signed subject cheques nor she was in-charge of responsible for conduct of business of accused company, petitioner could not be made liable under section 141(2) and, thus, criminal complaint under section 138 was to be quashed qua petitioner

Section 138, read with section 141, of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 - Dishonour of cheque for insufficiency, etc., of funds in account - Whether section 141 is neither intended nor extends vicarious liability on group companies - Held, yes - Whether it is intended to create vicarious liability only on persons and officers who are either in-charge of company, which is main accused, or have connived or are negligent, resulting in accused company committing offence under section 138 - Held, yes - Accused No.1 was an entity with its office in United Arab Emirates (UAE) - It was sales and marketing wing of company 'R' incorporated under Companies Act, 2013 - Respondent Nos.1 and 2, along with others, who had been arrayed as accused Nos. 2 and 3 in complaint, were common Directors of Group, namely, Right Choice Group of Companies, and were responsible for day-to-day affairs of accused No.1 and company ‘R’ - Complainant alleged that respondent Nos.1 and 2, along with accused Nos.2 and 3 approached complainant for investment in accused No.1 assuring him of high rates of return on investments - Complainant invested an amount of Emirati Dirham (AED) 6 lakh in favour accused No.1, by issuing multiple cheques - Accused No.1 issued multiple post-dated cheques to complainant in order to discharge their liability - However, said cheques were dishonoured - Thus, a complaint was filed under section 138 against all accused, respondents and company 'R' - Session Judge by impugned order set aside summons issued against respondents and company 'R' - It was noted that accused No. 1 and company 'R' were separate legal entities; one registered in Dubai and other registered in India - Broucher floated to attract investments itself stated that they were separate companies though part of same group - Therefore, company 'R' could not have been proceeded against only on allegation that it was a group company of accused No.1, which was drawer of cheque in question - As far as respondents were concerned, complainant placed no document on record to show that they were Directors or persons in-charge of accused No. 1 - Complaint was also lacking in basic averments of section 141 against respondents, as had been culled out by Supreme Court in S.P. Mani and Mohan Diary v. Dr. Snehalatha Elangovan [2022] 142 taxmann.com 317/[2023] 175 SCL 242 for fastening liability under section 138 on persons other than company - Therefore, even tested on parameters of section 141, respondents could not be fastened with vicarious liability of dishonour of cheque issued by accused - In light of above, there was no merit in challenge made by complainant in instant petition - Whether thus, appeal against impugned order of Session Judge was to be dismissed - Held, yes [Paras 34, 38, 39, 41, 43, 45  46]FEMA, BANKING  INSURANCE : Where accused company and company 'R' were separate legal entities, one registered in Dubai and other registered in India, company 'R' could not have been proceeded against under section 138 of Negotiable Instruments Act only on allegation that it was a group company of accused company, which was drawer of cheque in question

Section 138, read with section 139, of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 - Dishonour of cheque for insufficiency etc., of funds in account - Whether for initiation of prosecution under section 138, a prior statutory notice is mandatorily required to be given to drawer, to make good payment of amount mentioned in cheque and only when drawer receives a notice and fails to make payment within time provided by Statute, does dishonour become an offence - Held, yes - A complaint was filed against accused under section 138 by complainant on ground that accused had taken friendly loan from complainant and a cheque issued by accused in favour of complainant was dishonoured on presentation - It was noted that subject cheque, copy of which had been placed on record, was signed only by late husband of accused - Although conceded that cheque was issued from a joint account but subject cheque did not bear signature of accused - Whether thus, criminal complaint filed against accused was clearly an abuse of process of law - Held, yes - Whether thus, instant petition by accused filed under section 482 of Cr.P.C seeking quashing of criminal complaint filed under section 138 was to be allowed and consequently, criminal complaint against accused was to be quashed - Held, yes [Paras 7, 8  11]

Section 141, read section 138, of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 - Offence by Companies -  Whether provisions of section 141 impose vicarious liability by deeming fiction, which presupposes and requires commission of offence by company or firm and, therefore, unless company or firm has committed offence as a principal accused, persons mentioned in sub-section (1) or (2) i.e., person in overall control of company or firm or director, manager etc., would not be liable and convicted as vicariously liable - Held, yes - Whether where respondent-bank granted loan to partnership firm and appellant had not issued cheques, which had been dishonoured, in his personal capacity, in absence of any evidence to show that appellant was in charge of and responsible for conduct of affairs of firm, conviction of appellant under section 138 was to be set aside - Held, yes [Paras 11 and 14]FEMA, BANKING  INSURANCE : Provisions of section 141 impose vicarious liability by deeming fiction, which presupposes and requires commission of offence by company or firm and, therefore, unless company or firm has committed offence as a principal accused, persons mentioned in sub-section (1) or (2) would not be liable and convicted as vicariously liable

Section 138, read with section 141, of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 - Dishonour of cheque for insufficiency, etc., of funds in account - Complainant supplied graphic designs to accused No. 1 firm - Against supply of same, Rs. 1.41 lakh remained as due - In discharge of same, accused No. 1 issued a cheque - Said cheque, when presented for encashment, was returned dishonoured due to insufficient funds - Resultantly, complaint under section 138 was filed in which it had been stated that accused No. 1 was an unregistered firm wherein accused No. 2 i.e. 'H' and accused No. 3 (petitioner) were authorized signatory/proprietor/partner/deemed and real owner/official of said firm - Trial Court took cognizance of complaint and issued summons against all three accused including petitioner - It was noted that apart from bald averment made in complaint as well as during course of submissions that petitioner was deemed owner of firm, no other evidence had been produced on record to show that petitioner was deemed/real owner or that he was in charge or responsible for business of firm at time of commission of offence - On other hand, petitioner had placed on record a certificate of acknowledgement of registration from Deputy Registrar of Firms - Said document nowhere showed petitioner as a partner in accused No. 1 - Further, said cheque was signed by 'H' and not petitioner - Whether since there was no evidence on record to show that petitioner was a partner of accused firm or that he was signatory of cheque, summoning order as well as complaint against petitioner was to be quashed - Held, yes [Paras 9, 10 and 12]

Section 138, read with section 141, of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 - Dishonour of cheque for insufficiency, etc., of funds in account - Respondent company/complainant, engaged in business of manufacturing men's jeans supplied said goods to accused company from time to time and raised bills, which were duly received and acknowledged by accused company - Subsequently, in order to discharge their liability under bills raised, certain cheques of varied amount (subject cheques) were issued by accused company - Upon presentation, subject cheques were dishonoured and consequently, criminal complaints under section 138 were filed - In said complaints, petitioner being Company Secretary of accused company, was sought to be made vicariously liable for offence owing to assurances advanced by her qua payment of bills raised as well as encashment of subject cheques - It was noted that petitioner was neither authorized signatory of accused company nor had she signed subject cheques - Further, nowhere in complaint, complainant averred that petitioner was in-charge of and responsible for conduct of business of accused company - Further, neither, was there any averment that offence had been committed with consent or connivance on part of petitioner, so as to potentially make her liable under section 141(2) - Whether thus, continuation of proceedings against petitioner would be nothing but an abuse of process of law and consequently, criminal complaint under section 138 was to be quashed qua petitioner - Held, yes [Paras 17 to 19]

Section 141,  read with section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 Penalties in case of dishonour of certain cheques for insufficiency of funds in accounts - Offences by companies -  Whether by virtue of section 141, criminal liability for commission of offence under section 138 by a company is on those who, at time of commission of offence, are incharge of and are responsible to company for conduct of its business - Held, yes - Whether for purpose of section 141, a firm comes within ambit of a company - Held, yes - Whether where complainant filed a complaint under section 138 alleging that appellants were partners of firm, whose cheque dishonoured, but filed no document showing that appellants were actively participated in business, complaint filed against appellants would not be maintainable - Held, yes

Section 138, read with section 141, of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 - Dishonour of cheque for insufficiency, etc., of funds in account - Whether section 141 is neither intended nor extends vicarious liability on group companies - Held, yes - Whether it is intended to create vicarious liability only on persons and officers who are either in-charge of company, which is main accused, or have connived or are negligent, resulting in accused company committing offence under section 138 - Held, yes - Accused No.1 was an entity with its office in United Arab Emirates (UAE) - It was sales and marketing wing of company 'R' incorporated under Companies Act, 2013 - Respondent Nos.1 and 2, along with others, who had been arrayed as accused Nos. 2 and 3 in complaint, were common Directors of Group, namely, Right Choice Group of Companies, and were responsible for day-to-day affairs of accused No.1 and company ‘R’ - Complainant alleged that respondent Nos.1 and 2, along with accused Nos.2 and 3 approached complainant for investment in accused No.1 assuring him of high rates of return on investments - Complainant invested an amount of Emirati Dirham (AED) 6 lakh in favour accused No.1, by issuing multiple cheques - Accused No.1 issued multiple post-dated cheques to complainant in order to discharge their liability - However, said cheques were dishonoured - Thus, a complaint was filed under section 138 against all accused, respondents and company 'R' - Session Judge by impugned order set aside summons issued against respondents and company 'R' - It was noted that accused No. 1 and company 'R' were separate legal entities; one registered in Dubai and other registered in India - Broucher floated to attract investments itself stated that they were separate companies though part of same group - Therefore, company 'R' could not have been proceeded against only on allegation that it was a group company of accused No.1, which was drawer of cheque in question - As far as respondents were concerned, complainant placed no document on record to show that they were Directors or persons in-charge of accused No. 1 - Complaint was also lacking in basic averments of section 141 against respondents, as had been culled out by Supreme Court in S.P. Mani and Mohan Diary v. Dr. Snehalatha Elangovan [2022] 142 taxmann.com 317/[2023] 175 SCL 242 for fastening liability under section 138 on persons other than company - Therefore, even tested on parameters of section 141, respondents could not be fastened with vicarious liability of dishonour of cheque issued by accused - In light of above, there was no merit in challenge made by complainant in instant petition - Whether thus, appeal against impugned order of Session Judge was to be dismissed - Held, yes [Paras 34, 38, 39, 41, 43, 45  46]

Section 141, read with  section 138, of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 - Offences by companies -  Certain amount was due to complainant financing company from petitioners (A1 to A5) - Petitioners had issued cheques in favour of complainant finance company but cheques were dishonoured - Except for A-4 whose role was not clear in commission of offence, others had a role in working of accused firm - Whether except for A-4 all other petitioners would be liable for prosecution - Held, yes

Section 141, read with section 138, of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 and section 482, of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 - Offences by Companies - Whether a vicarious liability will be attracted only when ingredients of section 141(1) are satisfied - Held, yes - Whether merely because somebody is managing affairs of company, per se, he would not become in charge of conduct of business of company - Held, yes - Accused-firm had purchased goods from complainant on credit basis - Accused issued a cheque in favour of complainant for discharging liability but same was dishonoured on presentation - Hence, a complaint was filed against accused-firm and its partners including appellant - High Court declined to quash complaint qua appellant in exercise of power under section 482 of Code of Criminal Procedure - It was noted that nowhere in complaint it was averred that appellant was in charge of conduct of business of company at relevant time when offence was committed - What was stated in complaint was only that appellant being partner was responsible for day-to-day conducts and business of company - An overall reading of complaint had not disclosed any clear and specific role of appellant - Whether since averments in complaint were insufficient to attract provisions of section 141(1) to create vicarious liability upon appellant, he was entitled to succeed in instant appeal - Held, yes - Whether thus, impugned order passed by High Court was to be set aside - Held, yes [Paras 12, 16 and 17]FEMA, BANKING  INSURANCE : Where cheque issued by firm to discharge its liability had been dishonoured, in view of fact that appellant-partner of firm had not signed said cheque, mere averment in complaint that appellant was 'managing affairs of firm' was not sufficient to make him vicariously liable for dishonour of cheque issued by firm

Section  138,  read with section  141,  of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 – Dishonour of cheque for insufficiency, etc., of funds in account – Whether expression 'month' under section 3(35) of General Clauses Act means month reckoned according to British calendar and, therefore, period of three months under section 138 cannot be computed as 90 days, first day being excluded and period ending on corresponding date of third month – Held, yes – Whether where cheques were presented within prescribed period but were returned for reason 'instrument out dated/stale' by banker, for which accused were in no way responsible, no cause of action arose under section 138 – Held, yes – Whether where fourth accused was neither partner of first accused-firm nor signatory to cheques, he was not vicariously liable under section 141 – Held, yes – Whether consequently entire criminal proceedings were liable to be quashed – Held, yes [Paras 8, 10, 12 and 13]

Section 141, read with section 138, of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 - Offence by Companies - Appellants were non-executive directors of accused company-An inter corporate deposit was executed between accused company and respondent to avail a financial facility- Accused company issued cheques towards repayment of ICD but same were dishonoured- Complaints under section 138 were filed against appellants - High Court by impugned order dismissed appellants’ petition under Section 482 of CrPC seeking quashing of proceedings - It was noted that appellants were neither signatories to dishonoured cheques nor had any role in their execution - Their involvement in company’s affairs was purely non-executive, confined to governance oversight, and did not extend to financial decision-making or operational management - Whether appellant(s) could not be held vicariously liable under section 141 and thus impugned order of High Court was to be set aside- Held, yes [Paras 17, 18, 19 and 20]

Section  141,  read with section  138,  of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 -  Offence by companies  - Whether in event there are no averments at all in complaint filed under section 138 for invoking vicarious liability, director cannot be held vicariously liable on ground that reply to notice is not given by director - Held, yes - Whether for taking cognizance of complaint against Director, Magistrate has to apply mind whether there are requisite averments in complaint - Held, yes - Accused-company issued a cheque in favour of complainant towards legally outstanding debts but same was dishonoured on presentation-Complainant filed complaint under section 138 - Magistrate issued process against accused-company and its directors including petitioner - Whether since petitioner was not signatory to dishonoured cheque, petitioner could not be held vicariously liable and prosecuted by invoking section 141 - Held, yes - Whether since there were no sufficient averments to invoke vicarious liability against petitioner, proceedings against petitioner were to be quashed and set aside - Held, yes [Paras 30,31 and 33]

Section 138, read with section 141, of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 - Dishonour of cheque for insufficiency etc., of funds in account -  Petitioner was one of directors of company 'B' and her husband was other director of said company - 'B' entered into a Distributorship Agreement with complainant on basis of which they became an authorized distributor on non-exclusive basis - During course of business, it was alleged by complainant company that 'B' had an outstanding balance against which it issued a cheque but on presentation, said cheque was returned unpaid due to reason 'payment stopped by drawer' - Complainant company issued a legal notice to 'B' as well as its directors, i.e., petitioner and her husband - Petitioner had been summoned by impugned order for offence punishable under section 138 by Trial Court - Whether since petitioner neither signed cheque in question nor signed nor witnessed Distributorship Agreement, necessary ingredients required to constitute offence under section 141 qua petitioner were not satisfied - Held, yes - Whether, therefore, impugned order only to extent of summoning petitioner for offence punishable under section 138 was to be quashed - Held, yes [Paras 17, 18 and 20]FEMA, BANKING  INSURANCE : Where petitioner-director neither signed dishonoured cheque nor signed distribution agreement between company 'B' and complainant, order summoning petitioner for offence punishable under section 138 was to be quashed

Section 138, read with section 141, of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 - Dishonour of cheque for insufficiency, etc., of funds -  Complainant supplied graphic designs to accused no. 1 company - Against supply of same Rs. 11 lakh remained as due - In discharge of same, accused firm issued a cheque - Said cheque, when presented for encashment, was returned dishonoured due to insufficient fund - Resultantly, complaint under section 138 was filed - In complaint it had been stated that accused No. 2 i.e. 'H' and accused No. 3 i.e. petitioner were authorized signatory/proprietor/partner/deemed and real owner/official of said accused firm - Trial Court took cognizance of complaint and issued summons against all three accused - It was noted that apart from bald averment made in complaint, no other evidence had been produced/placed by complainant on record to show that petitioner was deemed/real owner or that he was in charge or responsible for business of firm at time of commission of offence - On other hand, petitioner had placed on record a certificate of acknowledgement of registration from Deputy Registrar of Firm - Said document nowhere showed petitioner as a partner in said firm - Further, a perusal of complaint would show that cheque was issued on account of firm and was signed by 'H' and not petitioner - Whether thus, in absence of any such evidence to bring petitioner within fold of section 138, read with section 141 forcing petitioner to stand trial solely on basis of a bald averment that to unsubstantiated, would amount to an abuse of process of law - Held, yes - Whether thus, summoning order as well as complaint against petitioner was to be quashed - Held, yes [Paras 9, 10 and 12]

Section 141 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 - Offence by Companies -  Petitioners were directors of company 'A' which issued cheques to respondents - Cheques so issued were dishonoured and proceedings were initiated under section 138 - Metropolition Magistrate summoned petitioners herein as accused, invoking their vicarious criminal liability under section 141 - Petitioners filed instant petition contending that on account of being 'non-executive directors', they were not responsible for day-to-day affairs or conduct of business of company and, therefore, proceedings initiated against them deserved to be quashed - Whether, on facts, petitioners concededly being non-executive directors, in absence of any further averments as to their role in company at time of commission of offences, presumption under section 141 could not be raised against them - Held, yes - Whether, therefore, instant petition was to be allowed - Held, yes [Paras 10 and 11]FEMA  BANKING: Where proceedings under section 141 were initiated against petitioners i.e. directors of company 'A', for issuing cheques which got dishonoured, in view of fact that petitioners were non-executive directors not responsible for day to day affairs of company 'A', proceedings initiated against than deserved to be quashed

Section 141, read with section 138, of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 - Offence by companies - Whether mere designation as a director cannot import vicarious liability for a dishonoured cheque; there should be specific averment that particular accused was in charge of day-to-day affairs of company at time of commission of offence - Held, yes - Whether phraseology used in section 141 of being in charge and responsible to company for conduct of business of company is a reference to an 'executive activity' which imports an element of running day-to-day affairs of company and would not be extended to a role which is essentially supervisory, policy oriented, of oversight or regulatory, i.e., non-executive in character - Held, yes - Whether where petitioner was an independent and non-executive director of accused company who was not managing day-to-day affairs of company and he was not signatory to dishonoured cheque, complaint and proceedings under section 138 would be quashed qua petitioner - Held, yes [Paras 25 and 26]

Section 138, read with section 141 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 - Dishonour of cheque for insufficiency of fund etc. - Respondent filed a complaint under section 138 against petitioners, partners of firm, alleging that cheque issued by petitioners towards discharge of retirement dues had been dishonoured due to insufficiency of funds - Petitioners sought to quash proceedings primarily on ground that cheque in question was drawn in favour of respondent only on behalf of partnership firm and therefore, complaint could not be maintained without issuing statutory notice to partnership firm and making partnership firm as an accused in complaint - Respondent however submitted that partnership firm was not registered and therefore could not be made an accused - Whether registration or non-registration of partnership firm will have no bearing insofar section 141 is concerned - Held, yes - Whether in a cheque dishonour case involving a partnership firm, complaint cannot be maintained against partners of firm without making partnership firm as an accused in complaint - Held, yes - Whether therefore, where cheque was given in name of partnership firm and after cheque was dishonoured, no statutory notice was issued to partnership firm, and partnership firm was not made as accused in complaint, such a complaint was not in consonance with section 141 and hence would be not be sustainable - Held, yes [Paras 19 and 20]FEMA, BANKING  INSURANCE: In a cheque dishonour case involving a partnership firm, complaint cannot be maintained against partners of firm without making partnership firm as an accused in complaint

Section 138, read with section 141, of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 - Dishonour of cheque - Dishonoured cheques were issued by accused petitioner on company’s account and not on account maintained by him in his personal capacity - Whether requirement of section 138 that cheque should have been issued by accused on account maintained by him for payment of any money to another person from out of that account for discharging legally enforceable liability was satisfied in instant case - Held, no

Section 138, read with section 141 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 - Dishonour of cheque for insufficiency etc., of funds in account - Whether a complaint can be filed for offence under section 138 not only against partnership firm on whose behalf cheque was issued but also against an individual partner or person who, at time of commission of offence, was in charge of affairs of firm or responsible to it for conduct of its business - Held, yes - Whether a partnership firm is a separate legal entity in terms of Indian Partnership Act, 1932 and it is answerable in law in that capacity - Held, yes - Whether prosecution launched against only one of partners of partnership firm, without joining partnership firm, would not be maintainable as arraigning of a partnership firm is imperative for prosecution against partners under section 141 - Held, yes [Paras 19, 20  34]Negotiable Instruments Act: Prosecution launched against only one of partners of partnership firm, without joining partnership firm, would not be maintainable as arraigning of a partnership firm is imperative for prosecution against partners under section 141

Section 141, read with  section 138, of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 - Offence by Companies - Whether every person who is sought to be roped in by virtue of section 141(1) must be a person who at time when offence was committed was in charge of and was responsible to company for conduct of business of company - Held, yes - Whether words 'was in charge of' and 'was responsible to company for conduct of business of company' cannot be read disjunctively and same ought to be read conjunctively in view of use of word 'and' in between - Held, yes - Whether thus, merely because somebody is managing affairs of company, per se, he does not become in charge of conduct of business of company or person responsible for company for conduct of business of company - Held, yes - Accused company was alleged to have issued an account payee cheque in favour of complainant towards discharge of its liability, which had been dishonoured - Since, appellant was director of accused company at a relevant time, a criminal complaint under section 138 was filed against appellant - It was noted that cheques in question were not signed by appellant - Further, appellant was only incharge of company at relevant time and, thus, by no stretch of imagination, it could not be concluded that appellant was also responsible to company for conduct of business - Whether therefore, impugned order passed by High Court dismissing a petition filed by appellant for quashing complaint filed under section 138 was to be set aside - Held, yes [Paras 19 and 20]FEMA, BANKING  INSURANCE : Every person who is sought to be roped in by virtue of section 141(1) of Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 must be a person who at time when offence was committed was in charge of and was responsible to company for conduct of business of company; merely because somebody is managing affairs of company, per se, he does not become in charge of conduct of business of company or person responsible for company for conduct of business of company

Section 138, read with section 141, of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 - Dishonour of cheque for insufficiency, etc., of funds in account - Complainant company was engaged in business of providing telecommunication services, under a license issued by Government of India, in various telecom circles in India - Complainant had agreed to provide required services to accused company, whereupon parties entered into a Service Agreement, vide which accused had to pay Rs. 14 lakh as fixed monthly recurring charges to complainant - Accused owed a sum of Rs. 2.55 crore to complainant - In discharge of same, accused issued a cheque - Said cheque, when presented for encashment, was returned dishonoured due to 'payment stopped by drawer' - Resultantly, complaint under section 138 was filed against accused company in which one 'M' and appellant being directors of accused were arrayed as co-accused - High Court by impugned order dismissed appellant's application for quashing of complaint on file of Metropolitan Magistrate - It was noted that it was only 'M' who was authorized signatory of cheque in question and was in-charge of and responsible for day-to-day affairs of accused company and it was also not case of complainant that appellant was either Managing Director or Joint Managing Director of accused Company or that appellant was in-charge of and responsible for day-to-day affairs of accused company - Whether thus, instant appeal against impugned order of High Court was to be allowed - Held, yes [Paras 19 and 22]FEMA, BANKING  INSURANCE : Cheque bounce case against director of accused company quashed by Supreme Court as she was neither incharge/responsible for day-to-day affairs of company nor was a signatory of cheque

Section  138, read with section  141, of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 -  Dishonour of cheque for insufficiency, etc., of funds in account - Appellant-complainant had advanced loan to respondents for business purposes - In order to discharge debt, respondent No.1-accused issued a cheque in favour of appellant-complainant from partnership firm account maintained at bank - However, upon presentation of said cheque, it was returned as dishonoured - Appellant-complainant issued a statutory notice to respondents demanding discharge of legally enforceable debt - Subsequently, appellant-complainant filed a complaint under section 138 against respondents - High Court quashed complaint on ground that while cheque was issued on behalf of partnership firm, no notice was issued to partnership firm and it was also not arraigned as an accused in complaint - Whether partners of firm who had issued cheque in name of firm for discharging debt were jointly and severally liable along with firm for offence under section 138 - Held, yes - Whether notice issued to partners of firm was to be construed as notice issued to partnership firm also - Held, yes - Whether even in absence of partnership firm being proceeded against by complainant by issuance of legal notice or being made an accused specifically in complaint filed under section 200 of CrPC, complaint under section 138 was maintainable - Held, yes - Whether High Court was not right in dismissing complaint for reason that partnership firm was not named as an accused and no notice had been issued to it under section 138 - Held, yes - Whether notice issued to partners of firm was to be construed as a notice issued to partnership hence, permission was to be granted to arraign partnership firm as an accused in complaint - Held, yes [Paras 9.7, 9.9, 10 and 11]

Section 141, read with section 138, of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 - Offence by companies - Whether mere designation as a director cannot import vicarious liability for a dishonoured cheque; there should be specific averment that particular accused was in charge of day-to-day affairs of company at time of commission of offence - Held, yes - Whether phraseology used in section 141 of being in charge and responsible to company for conduct of business of company is a reference to an 'executive activity' which imports an element of running day-to-day affairs of company and would not be extended to a role which is essentially supervisory, policy oriented, of oversight or regulatory, i.e., non-executive in character - Held, yes - Whether where petitioner was an independent and non-executive director of accused company who was not managing day-to-day affairs of company and he was not signatory to dishonoured cheque, complaint and proceedings under section 138 would be quashed qua petitioner - Held, yes [Paras 25 and 26]FEMA, BANKING  INSURANCE : Phraseology used in section 141 of being in charge and responsible to company for conduct of business of company is a reference to an 'executive activity' which imports an element of running day-to-day affairs of company and would not be extended to a role which is essentially supervisory, policy oriented, of oversight or regulatory, i.e., non-executive in character

Section 141, read with section 138, of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 - Dishonour of cheque - Offences by companies - Whether where no allegation is made against an accused specifically averring that at time when offence was committed accused was incharge and was responsible for conduct of business of company, no complaint under Act would be maintainable against such accused - Held, yes

Section  138,  read with section  141,  of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 and section  149  of the Companies Act, 2013 -  Dishonour of cheque for insufficiency, etc., of funds in account  - Petitioner was non-executive director of accused company which had taken loan from respondent-finance company - Respondent filed complaint under section 138 against accused company for dishonour of cheques issued by accused company towards repayment of loan - Respondent also sought to attach a liability on petitioner by asserting that dishonoured cheques were handed over by him - Petitioner filed instant petition for quashing of complaint - It was noted that petitioner was non-executive director and neither cheques nor any documents pertaining to said transaction, had been signed by him - Further, complaint did not spell out as to how and in what manner petitioner was in-charge of or was responsible to accused company for conduct of its business - Whether therefore, petitioner could not be held liable for any act or offence of accused company and instant petition was to be allowed - Held, yes [Paras 50 and 53]

Section  138,  read with section  141,  of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 -  Offence  -  Dishonour of cheque  (Liability of Managing Director) - Company, represented by its Managing Director (accused no. 2) and Director (accused no. 3), issued three cheques towards payment of red chillies supplied by complainant - Cheques were presented for payment after writing dates on them but were dishonoured - Complainant filed a complaint against accused for offence under section 138 - Accused no. 2 submitted that cheques were given towards security and were presented for realisation after expiry of validity period of 3 months, thus, impugned proceedings could not be sustained - It was noted that signatures on cheques were not in dispute - Further, in legal notice, it was specifically mentioned about issuance of cheques by accused and on receipt of aforesaid legal notice, part payment had been made by accused to complainant which showed that they had not only admitted transaction, but also issuance of aforesaid three disputed cheques in question - Whether thus, in view of Supreme Court decision in K.K. Ahuja v. V.K. Vora [2009] 94 SCL 140 (SC)/(2009) 10 SCC 48, accused no. 2 being Managing Director and signatory of cheques, would be liable to be prosecuted for offence punishable under section 138 - Held, yes - Whether however, so far as accused no. 3 was concerned, except a bald averment that she was also actively taking part in day to day affairs of company, there was no other material to show her participation in day to day administrative affairs of company, thus, in absence of necessary particulars, mandatory requirements of section 141(1) could not be satisfied to prosecute accused no. 3 for alleged offence - Held, yes [Paras 15 and 20]

Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 - Dishonour of cheque for insufficiency etc. of funds in account - Whether if cheque had been issued by firm which was subsequently dishonoured, a partner of firm would not be liable for prosecution under section 138 without firm being arraigned as an accused - Held, yes [Paras 33 and 34]FEMA  BANKING : If cheque had been issued by firm which was subsequently dishonoured, a partner of firm would not be liable for prosecution under section 138 without firm being arraigned as an accused

Section 138, read with section 141, of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 - Dishonour of cheque - Appellant was director of a company that issued two cheques which were dishonoured - Whether a person other than company can be proceeded against under provisions of section 141(1) only if that person was in charge of and was responsible to the company for conduct of its business - Held, yes - Whether since allegations made in complaint against appellant, in instant case, did not either in express words or with reference to allegations contained therein, make out a case that at time of commission of offence appellant was in charge of and was responsible to company for conduct of its business, High Court misdirected itself in holding that requirements of section 141 were prima facie satisfied insofar as appellant was concerned - Held, yes

Section 138, read with section 141, of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 and section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 - Dishonour of cheque for insufficiency etc., of funds in account - Whether section 141 of Negotiable Instruments Act has envisaged vicarious liability on part of Directors or other persons, mentioned therein, of company who were in charge of and responsible for conduct of affairs of company at time of commission of offence - Held, yes - Whether a person would be vicariously liable for commission of offence under section 138 by company only in event, conditions laid down in section 141 are satisfied - Held, yes - Whether, where on date offence under section 138, petitioners were not Directors of company, they could not be held responsible for conduct of its affairs and for that matter for issuance and dishonour of cheques under reference - Held, yes - [Paras 12, 26 and 27]FEMA, BANKING  INSURANCE: Where on date of offence under section 138, petitioners were not Directors of company, they could not be held responsible for issuance and dishonour of cheques

Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881, read with section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973/section 528 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 - Dishonour of cheque for insufficiency etc., of funds in account - Respondent-company had sold its property to complainant and issued a cheque for refund of sale consideration - However, said cheque was dishonoured on presentation - Complainant filed complaint under section 138 against company and its directors including petitioner - Petitioner filed instant petition seeking quashing of complaint and summoning order on ground that petitioner was not involved in day-to-day activities and affairs of company - It was noted that petitioner was one of promoters and director of company and was responsible for day-to-day discharge of functions of respondent company - It was observed that petitioner had knowledge of issuance of cheque in question to complainant and had been involved in sale transaction of subject property since initial stages - Whether not being an authorised signatory would not absolve petitioner from liability of commission of offence as long as requisites under Section 138 and 141 were met - Held, yes - Whether therefore, summons were rightly issued against petitioner as a prima facie case was made out under Section 138 - Held, yes - Whether thus, instant petition was to be dismissed - Held, yes [Paras 30, 31, 34, 37 and 39]FEMA, BANKING  INSURANCE : Where petitioner was director of company and was responsible for day-to-day discharge of functions of company and had knowledge of issuance of cheque in question to complainant, petitioner could not be absolved from liability of commission of offence under section 138 of Negotiable Instruments Act on dishonour of said cheque

facts.text: The appellant, an authorized signatory of a company, issued a cheque in favour of the respondent company which was dishonoured as a consequence of which the said respondent initiated criminal action by filing a complaint before the concerned Judicial Magistrate under section 138. In the complaint petition, the company was not arrayed as an accused. However, the Magistrate took cognizance of the offence against the accused appellant. Being aggrieved by the said order, she invoked the jurisdiction of the High Court under section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure for quashing of the criminal proceeding and the High Court, considering the scope of sections 138 and 139 and various other factors, refused to quash proceeding holding that the ground urged would be in the sphere of defence of the accused and would not strengthen the edifice for quashing of the proceeding. While assailing the said order before the two-Judge Bench of the Supreme Court, the substratum of argument was that as the company was not arrayed as an accused, the legal fiction created by the Legislature in section 141 would not get attracted. One of the Judges, of the two Bench Judge, S.B. Sinha, J. held that prosecution of a company is a sine qua non for prosecution of other persons who fall within second and third categories of candidates under section 141 and, therefore, proceedings against appellant must be quashed in absence of company having joined as an accused. The other Judge V.S. Sirpurkar, J. held that appellant would be liable to be prosecuted even when the company had not joined as an accused. Due to difference in opinion of the two Judges, the matter was referred to a Larger Bench.

The petitioner sought for quashing of complaints filed against her under section 138 regarding bouncing of cheques issued by the company on the ground that she was not a director of the company and was implicated in the case only because she happened to be the wife of the managing director of the company and also that she was of indifferent health. The complainant-company alleged that the petitioner and other directors were in charge of the day-to-day affairs of the company and were running the business and had issued the cheque with an intention to evade payment on some pretext or the other, being fully aware of the consequences of dishonour and that the petitioner had not produced even a scrap of paper to show that she was not a director of the company.

On writ :

by the drawer alone, to include other persons who are made vicariously liable, particularly when the principal offender is a company. The word 'drawer' is used in singular and plural; therefore, it is restricted to the principal offender only and not persons who fall within the dragnet of being vicariously liable either under section 141(1) or 141(2). There is no provision analogous to section 141 of the Act found in section 143A to rope in individuals. In the case of the company, the notice under proviso (b) of section 138 had to be issued to the drawer of the cheque, i.e. company and not to the authorised signatory of a cheque as it was the company who was liable to make payment under the cheque. Accused also submitted that the liability of the signatory of the cheque or the managing directors or joint managing director would only be under section 141(2) Act which is in relation to section 138, provided he had done overt the act on behalf of the company.

Accused also he submitted that the criminal liability on account of dishonour of cheque primarily falls on the drawer. If the drawer is a company, then dragnet is extended to its officers under section 141.

According to accused sections 143A and 148 need to be interpreted in plain language; whereas complainant/respondent submitted that both provisions need to be interpreted by applying the rule of purposive construction.

For appreciating submissions on interpretation of statute, well-settled rule of interpretation of a statute needs to be borne in mind that when a language of a provision was plain and unambiguous and capable of only one meaning, there was no question of the construction of a statute, as the provision speaks for itself. The natural and ordinary meaning of words should only be departed from if it was shown that the legal context in which the words were used requires a different meaning. In that case, it would not be open to the courts to adopt any other hypothetical construction on the ground that such construction was more consistent with the alleged object and policy of the act. When the provision's plain meaning produces injustice, absurdity or contradiction of the statutory object, the language would be interpreted to avoid such disadvantage. When the legislature chooses appropriate words to express its intention, such intention must be employed so long as this did not result in absurdity.
