Supreme Court’s Verdict on Vicarious Criminal liability of Directors for Dishonour of Company’s Cheques

S. VENUGOPALAN

THE AUTHOR IS A COMPANY SECRETARY.

Dishonour of cheque is a criminal offence under section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881. The offence is to be tried by a First Class Magistrate on a complaint by the payee of the dishonoured cheque. Section 141 of the said Act makes the company and directors, managers or secretary and other officers in charge of and responsible for conduct of business of the company as well as the company, liable for prosecution under section 138 of the Act. Vicarious criminal liability of certain directors for dishonour of company’s cheque for insufficiency of funds in the bank account of the company is explained in this article by making reference to the Apex Court’s decision in S.M.S. Pharmaceuticals Ltd. v. Neeta Bhalla and the author opines that this decision will be helpful in interpreting the standard penal provisions.

Vicarious liability of directors

1. The expression ‘vicarious liability’ denotes a legal liability imposed on one person for torts (civil wrong) or crimes committed by another. In the law of torts, it is the responsibility of the master for the acts of the servant or agent done in the course of or during his employment.

A ‘company’ is an artificial person created by law, and is capable of acting only through human agency occupying the position of directors; it is but natural that directors are prosecuted for an offence committed by the company. Directors are the agents of the company. They are, therefore, liable for the offences committed, in law, by the company.

Courts equate the mind of these human persons with that of the legal person, i.e., the company, so as to hold the latter responsible for the company’s offences. It has been held by the courts that it cannot be said that a company cannot have a guilty mind inasmuch as the company’s mind is the mind of the persons controlling the company. In one case, Lord Denning observed:

"Company may in many ways be likened to a human body. It has a brain and nerve centre which controls what it does. It also has hands which hold the tools and act in accordance with directions from the centre. Some of the people in the company are mere servants and agents who are nothing more than hands to do work and cannot be said to represent the mind or will. Others are directors and managers who represent the directing mind and will of the company, and control what it does. The state of mind of these managers is the state of mind of the company and is treated by the law as such."

It cannot be said that a company cannot have a guilty mind. The company’s mind is the mind of the persons controlling the company. If the persons controlling the company have acted fraudulently on behalf of the company, it is the company which would be indicted for the fraud committed by the persons controlling it. Even though mens rea is one of the elements of the offence which is the subject-matter of the criminal complaint against a company, the company can be held guilty of the offence if the persons controlling the company had acted on its behalf in committing the offence. [Taken from "Role of independent directors’ powers, duties and liabilities" by Ramadevi R. Iyer]

In India more than 156 enactments contain Standard Penal Provisions. ‘Offences by Companies’ is an identical provision regarding vicarious liability of directors and other company officers for company’s offences under the various enactments. "Offences by companies.— (1) Where an offence under this Act has been committed by a company, every person who, at the time the offence was committed, was in charge of, and was responsible to, the company for the conduct of the business of the company, as well as the company, shall be deemed to be guilty of the offence and shall be liable to be proceeded against and punished accordingly :

Provided that nothing contained in this sub-section shall render any such person liable to any punishment provided in this Act if he proves that the offence was committed without his knowledge or that he exercised all due diligence to prevent the commission of such offence.

Penalty v. Prosecution – Section 142

4. Out of the above provisions, the important provision in section 142 dealing with Penalty and prosecution for defaults in compliance of the provisions of section 138. The important ingredient to complete an offence under section 138 of the Act is the failure of the accused to make payment within 15 days after service of notice. If payment is made within the said notice period then no offence is committed but in case of failure the offence gets completed. Even if the payment is made on the 16th day, the same is not sufficient to come out of the rigours of section 138 of the Act. In Criminal Law, commission of an offence is one thing and prosecution is quite another thing. Commission of an offence is governed by section 138 of the Act. The appellant's contentions were accepted by the Gujarat High Court which quashed 40 different complaints under section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 filed by the appellant against the respondents. Relying upon the decision of the Supreme Court in the case of Vinod Tanna v. Zaher Siddiqui [2002] 7 SCC 541, the High Court took the view that dishonour of a cheque on the ground that the signatures of the drawer of the cheque did not match with the specimen signatures available with the bank, would not attract the penal provisions of section 138 of the NIA. According to the High Court, the provisions of section 138 would be attracted only in cases where a cheque was dishonoured either because the amount of money standing to the credit to the account maintained by the drawer was insufficient to pay the cheque amount or the cheque amount exceeded the amount arranged to be paid from account maintained by the drawer by an agreement made with the bank. Dishonour of a cheque on the ground that the signature of the drawer did not match with the specimen signature available with the bank would not, according to the High Court, fall in either of these two contingencies, thereby rendering the prosecution of the respondents legally impermissible. The relevant observations of the High Court were as under:

"In the instant case, there is no dispute about the endorsement that "drawers signature differs from the specimen supplied" and/or "no image found-signature" and/or "incomplete signature/illegible" and for return/dishonour of cheque on the above endorsement will not attract ingredients of section 138 of the Act and insufficient fund as a ground for dishonouring cheque cannot be extended so as to cover the endorsement "signature differed from the specimen supplied" or likewise. If the cheque is returned/bounced/dishonoured on the endorsement of "drawers signature differs from the specimen supplied" and/or "no image found-signature" and/or "incomplete signature/illegible", the complaint filed under section 138 of the Act is not maintainable. Introduction

1. Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 provides criminal liability for the dishonour of cheques. Section 139 incorporates a rule of presumption that the holder of the cheque has received the cheque for discharge of whole or part of debt or liability. This presumption can be rebutted by the accused by proving to the contrary. Recently, on 19th February, 2020 the Supreme Court held that the rebuttal of presumption under section 139 of the Act can only be done after adducing evidence and not at the stage of taking cognizance by the Court. The author in this article shall be analyzing the relevant provisions of the Negotiable Instruments Act, the judicial precedents and the judgment of the court in case of Shiv Kumar alias Jawahar Saraf v. Ramavtar Agarwal.1

2. Relevant Provisions of Negotiable Instruments Act :

2.1 Dishonour of cheque for insufficency of funds etc. - Section 138 of the Act lays down punishment for dishonour of cheque for insufficiency etc. of funds in the account. It provides that where any cheque drawn by any person for the discharge of any liability is returned by the bank unpaid for the reason of the insufficiency of the amount of money standing to the credit of the account on which the cheque was drawn or for the reason that it exceeds the arrangements made by the drawer of the cheque with the bankers for that account, the drawer of such cheque shall be deemed to have committed an offence. The object of the section is to infuse credibility to negotiable instruments including cheques and to encourage and promote the use of negotiable instruments including cheques in financial transactions. The penal provision of Section 138 is intended to be a deterrent to callous issuance of negotiable instruments such as cheques without serious intention to honour the promise implicit in the issuance of the same.

Ingredients of section 138 - To constitute an offence under section 138, the following ingredients must be satisfied:

The drawer must have drawn a cheque on an account maintained by him for payment of a certain amount of money to another person from out of that account;

The cheque must have been issued by the drawer for the discharge of some debt or other liability. The debt or liability may be discharged in whole or in part;

The cheque must be presented to the bank within a period of six months from the date on which it is drawn or within the period of its validity, whichever is earlier.

The cheque presented to the bank must be returned by the bank as unpaid (dishonoured). The cheque must have been dishonoured either because the amount of money standing in the account of drawer is insufficient to honour the cheque or it exceeds the amount arranged to be paid from that account by an agreement made by the drawer with the bank.

When the cheque has been returned by the bank as unpaid, the payee or the holder in due course of the cheque shall make a demand for the payment of the said amount of money by giving a notice in writing to the drawer of the cheque. This notice has to be issued within a period of 30 days from the date of receipt of information from the bank regarding the dishonor of cheque.

The drawer of the cheque fails to make payment of the cheque amount to the payee or the holder of the cheque in due course within 15 days of the receipt of the demand notice.

Concatenation of all the above acts is sine qua non for completion of offence under section 138. Being cumulative, it is only when all the aforementioned ingredients are satisfied that the person who had drawn the cheque can be deemed to have committed an offence under Section 138 of the Act.

Punishment for dishonour of cheques - In case of dishonor of cheque, the maximum punishment that can be awarded under section 138 is imprisonment for a term which may extend to two years or fine which may extend to twice the amount of the cheque or both.

2.2 Presumption in favour of the holder - Section 139 raises a presumption in favour of holder. Section 139 provides that unless the contrary is proved, the Court shall presume that the holder of a cheque received the cheque for the discharge (in whole or in part) of any debt or other liability.

4. Legal Framework of the Dishonour of Cheque

(a) The Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 - Sections 138 to 147 - To ensure promptitude and remedy against defaulters and to make sure credibility of the holders of the negotiable instrument, a criminal remedy of penalty was inserted in the Act, in form of the Banking, Public Financial Institutions and Negotiable Instruments Laws (Amendment) Act, 1988 that inserted sections 138 to 147 in the Act, which were further modified by the Negotiable Instruments (Amendment and Miscellaneous Provisions) Act, 2002.

The issue of dishonour of cheque is dealt with under sections 138 to 147 that provide for remedies and various forms of punishment in case of dishonour of cheque. Section 138 deals with the dishonour of cheque for insufficiency, etc., of funds in the account. It provides that a person shall be punishable for two years imprisonment or with fine, if the cheque issued by drawers is returned by the bank unpaid. The cheque must be issued in discharge of whole or part, of any debt or other liability.

Object of Chapter XVII

3. If the cheque is dishonored for insufficiency of funds or because it exceeds the amount arranged to be paid from that account, the drawer is to be punished with imprisonment for a term which may extend to two years or with fine which may extend to twice the amount of the cheque or with both.

A striking feature of the present discussion is the similarity between Section 141 of the N.I. Act and Section 137 of the CGST Act. Both provisions employ nearly identical language in attributing liability to persons in charge of and responsible for the conduct of business, while also recognising defences based on lack of knowledge and due diligence. 5. Discussion & Findings of the Supreme Court

5.1 On the Law Relating to Prosecution of Directors

The Court reiterated that the law governing prosecutions under Section 138 read with Section 141 of the N.I. Act is well settled. It emphasised that a complaint must contain specific averments demonstrating that the accused was in charge of and responsible for the conduct of the business of the company at the time of the offence. Absent such foundational pleadings, the prosecution cannot be sustained.

5.2 Regarding No Deeming Liability on Account of Being a Director

A crucial clarification made by the Court is that merely holding the position of a director does not automatically attract liability. There is no deemed liability in law solely on account of designation. The requirement of Section 141 is substantive and must be satisfied through clear and specific allegations establishing active responsibility.

5.3 Regarding Signing of Board Resolution and Day-to-Day Affairs

The Court decisively rejected the reasoning that signing a Board Resolution ipso facto establishes involvement in day-to-day management. It observed that Board Resolutions pertain to policy-level decisions and cannot be equated with operational control. In the absence of specific allegations indicating direct participation in the conduct of business, such a basis is insufficient to attract criminal liability.

6. Application of Principles to the Present Case

Applying the above principles, the Supreme Court found that there was no material to show that the appellant was in charge of and responsible for the conduct of the business of the company. The complaint lacked the necessary averments, and the reliance placed solely on the signing of a Board Resolution was misplaced.

The Court noted that criminal liability, particularly vicarious liability, cannot be imposed in a mechanical or casual manner. In the absence of specific allegations and supporting material, the continuation of proceedings would amount to an abuse of process. Accordingly, the proceedings against the appellant were quashed, reinforcing the principle that liability must be founded on role and responsibility, not merely on designation.

7. Conclusion

The judgment marks an important reaffirmation of the limits of vicarious liability in corporate jurisprudence. It preserves the delicate balance between ensuring accountability of those who are genuinely responsible for corporate conduct and protecting individuals from unwarranted prosecution merely due to their formal association with a company.

Equally, the ruling serves as a reminder that criminal law cannot be stretched to compensate for deficiencies in pleadings or evidence. The insistence on specific averments and demonstrable involvement ensures that prosecutions remain grounded in legal principle rather than assumption. In doing so, the Court has strengthened the integrity of both corporate law and criminal jurisprudence.

8. Lessons from the Judgment

The decision underscores that liability of directors is not a matter of presumption but of proof. It highlights the necessity of carefully drafted complaints, clearly identifying the role of each accused. For companies and their boards, the judgment provides reassurance that participation in governance, without involvement in day-to-day operations, does not automatically expose directors to liability.

At the same time, it reinforces that those who are actively in control cannot evade responsibility behind the corporate veil. Importantly, the ruling assumes even greater significance in the context of independent directors. It implies, in principle, that independent and non-executive directors—whose role is largely supervisory and advisory—cannot be routinely implicated in proceedings in the absence of specific material demonstrating their involvement in the conduct of business or their consent, connivance, or negligence. Mere presence on the Board, participation in meetings, or approval of resolutions in a governance capacity cannot, by itself, trigger liability. This serves as a crucial safeguard to ensure that independent and non-executive directors are not deterred from discharging their oversight functions due to the risk of unwarranted prosecution, while still preserving accountability in cases where there is demonstrable complicity or failure of due diligence.

An Overview of Section 138 under N.I. Act

Negotiable Instruments have long been used in the business world as one of the simplest ways to move capital. Until 1988, there was no effective legislative mechanism to prevent individuals from issuing checks without adequate funds in their account, nor was there any severe penalty for doing so. For instance, a legal responsibility arose from the non-payment of checks. To secure the check's drawee, it was decided that cheque dishonour should be considered a criminal offence. Banking, Public Financial Institutions, and Negotiable Instruments Laws (Amendment) Act, 1988 added Sec.138 to 142 for that reason. This was accomplished by having the drawer responsible for fines if the check bounced due to a lack of funds, with sufficient protections in place to deter abuse of the truthful drawer. However, it was later discovered that the courts were unwilling to resolve the proceedings in a timely and efficient fashion. The loopholes were filled in by the amendment of 2002, which resulted in the passage of the Negotiable Instruments (Amendment and Miscellaneous Provisions) Act, 2002. The provisions of sections 143 to 147 were included, and the provisions of sections 138, 141, and 142 were changed.

This amendment act aimed to control the growing business, exchange, commerce, and industrial activities and encourage greater financial vigilance. Also, to protect creditors' trust in the cheque box. The Hon'ble SC in the matter of Modi Cements Ltd. v. Kuchil Kumar Nandi held that "The object of Chapter XVII, containing Sections 138 to 142, is to promote the efficacy of banking operations and to ensure credibility in transacting business through cheques."1

Under Sections 118 and 139 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, there are presumptions in favour of the receiver of the cheque that it was drawn to discharge debts or liabilities. It is, however, rebuttable, and the victim will refute it by cross-examination without having to reach the witness box. The complainant is also responsible for proving that the check was given for a properly enforceable debt or liability. The burden on the accused in such a situation will be heavier than in proceedings under section 114 of the Evidence Act. The operation of notification is deemed to have been effected until notice is submitted by registered mail to the proper addressee of the cheque, as stated in Section 27 of the General Clauses Act, 1897, and Section 114 of the Evidence Act, 1872. The drawer, on the other hand, is free to refute this assumption as per N. Paraeswaran Unni v. G. Kannan2. Section 139 provides a requirement that the holder of a cheque collects the cheque in discharge, in full or in part, of any debt or other obligation until the execution of the cheque is admitted, It was held in Basalingappa v. Mudibasappa3. Cheques with no date or post-dated cheques are often given. In Bir Singh v. Mukesh Kumar4, the Supreme Court held that if a signed blank cheque is willingly handed over to a payee for any payment, the payee is free to fill in the balance and other information. This will not invalidate the check on its own.

In the case of Kusum Ingots and Alloys Ltd v. Pennar Peterson Securities Ltd5, the Supreme Court found out the basic ingredients of the crime as contemplated under Sec.138 of the act that, "an individual must have drawn a check on a bank account that he maintains for transfer of a certain sum of money to another person from that account for the discharge of some debt or other liability; the cheque was issued to the bank within six months of the date on which it was drawn, or within the validity limit of the cheque, whichever comes first; According to RBI guidelines, the validity duration of Cheques, Demand Drafts, Pay Orders, and Banker's Cheques has been shortened from six to three months as of April 1, 2012, from the date of the instrument. The bank returns the check as outstanding. either because the sum of money in the account is inadequate to honour the cheque or because it reaches the amount arranged to be charged by the account under a bank agreement; within 30 days of receiving details from the bank about the return of the cheque as outstanding, the payee or issuer of the cheque makes a case for reimbursement of the said sum of money by sending a note in writing to the drawer of the cheque; within 15 days of receiving the said note, the drawer of the cheque fails to allow delivery of the said sum of money to the payee or the holder of the cheque in the proper course of the cheque."

Vicarious liability

Vicarious mean acting or done for another. A person is vicariously liable for the act done by another.

Since a legal person is a fiction of the law and does not exist in actuality, the issue of vicarious liability of the office bearers through whom a company, or a partnership or association of persons must necessarily act, comes to the fore. Many modern statutes incorporates stringent principle of strict vicarious criminal liability of persons who are responsible to the company or firm or association of persons for the conduct of its business or are its responsible office bearers like the director, manager, secretary in particular or the member of association. Strict vicarious liability is somewhat an exception to the general rule of direct personal culpability and is a modern development through statutory provisions. That there can be such vicarious criminal liability by legislative mandate is no longer in dispute. Nevertheless steeped as we are in the basic principle of criminal jurisprudence that mens rea must be an ingredient of an offence and both the act and intent must concur to constitute a crime, it requires some effort to accept wholeheartedly the legislative mandate of vicarious criminality even in the absence of either the aforesaid ingredients.

Vicarious liability "is a necessary doctrine for the proper enforcement of much modern legislation - but is not one to be extended" [Gardner v. Akeroyd (1952) 2 QB 743]. The normal rule against vicarious liability in cases involving criminal liability that no one is to be held criminally liable for an act of another, is subject to exception on account of specific provision being made in statutes extending liability to others [S.M.S Pharmaceuticals Ltd. v. Neeta Bhalla [2005] 127 Comp. Cas. 563 (SC)]. The Supreme Court in that case observed that section 141 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881, is an instance to a specific provision which in case an offence under section 138 of the Act is committed by a company, extends criminal liability for dishonour of a cheque to officers of the company and that since the provision creates criminal liability, the conditions which have to be satisfied before the liability can be extended to officers of a company have to be strictly complied with. The conditions are intended to ensure that a person who is sought to be made vicariously liable for an office of which the principal accused is the company, had a role to play in relation to the incriminating act and further that such a person should know what is attributed to him to make him liable. In other words, persons who had nothing to do with the matter need not be roped in.

Whether one person will be held responsible for the acts of another is a matter of construction in each case. Regard must be had to the object of the statute, the words used, the nature of the duty laid down, the person upon whom it is imposed, the person by whom it would in ordinary circumstances be performed and the person upon whom the penalty is imposed [Mousell Bros. Ltd. v. L.M.W. Rly. Co. (1917) 2 KB 836]

If the doctrine of vicarious liability is held to apply, a person subject to a statutory duty to which a penal sanction is attached who chooses to delegate the performance of that duty to another person (usually but not necessarily an employee), will nevertheless be himself liable for breaches of that duty by his delegate. In many cases his delegate’s ‘knowledge’ will be imputed to him [see Vane v. Vianmopoullos (1965) AC 486 and Gifford v. Police (1965) NZLR 484]

(Para 5): "Criminal liability on account of dishonour of cheque primarily falls on the drawer company and is extended to officers of the company. The normal rule in the cases involving criminal liability is against vicarious liability, that is, no one is to be held criminally liable for an act of another. This normal rule is subject to exception on account of specific provision being made in the statutes extending liability to others. ….A company being a juristic person, all its deeds and functions are result of acts of others. It makes every person who, at the time the offence was committed, was in- charge of and was responsible to the company for the conduct of business of the company as well as the company, liable for the offence. The proviso to the sub-section contains an escape route for persons who are able to prove that the offence was committed without their knowledge or that they had exercised all due diligence to prevent commission of the offence".

(Para 6) "….a complaint must contain material to enable the Magistrate to make up his mind for issuing process. It is settled law that at the time of issuing of the process, the Magistrate is required to see only the allegations in the complaint and where the allegations in the complaint or the charge sheet do not constitute an offence against a person, the complaint is liable to be dismissed".

(Para 9) "A perusal of sections 291 to 293 of the Companies Act shows that a board of directors is empowered to do in relation to a particular company depends upon the role and functions assigned to directors as per the memorandum and articles of association of the company. There is nothing which suggests that simply by being a director in a company, one is supposed to discharge particular functions on behalf of the company. It happens that a person may be a director in a company but he may not know anything about day-to-day functioning of the company. As a director he may be attending meetings of the board of directors of the company where usually they decide policy matters and guide the course of business of a company. It may be that a board of directors may appoint sub-committees consisting of one or two directors out of the board of the company who may be made responsible for day-to-day functions of the company. These are matters which form part of resolutions of board of directors of a company. Nothing is oral. What emerges from this is that the role of a director in a company is a question of fact depending upon the particular facts in each case. There is no universal rule that a director of a company is in charge of its everyday affairs. There is no magic as such in a particular word, be it director, manager or secretary. It all depends upon respective roles assigned to the officers in a company. …Not every person connected with a company is made liable under section 141."

(Para 10): "The position of a Managing Director or a Joint Managing Director in a company may be different. These persons, as the designation of their office suggests, are in-charge of a company and are responsible for the conduct of the business of the company. In order to escape liability such persons may have to bring their case within the proviso to section 141(1), that is, they will have to prove that when the offence was committed they had no knowledge of the offence or that they exercised all due diligence to prevent the commission of the offence".

The Department is of the view that this judgment has correctly interpreted the provisions of section 5 as amended in 1988. It may, therefore, please be ensured that where the penal provisions provide for punishment of ‘officers in default’, prosecutions be filed against the managing director(s), whole-time director(s) and Manager, apart from the Secretary, if any, and the company, and only in those cases where there is no such managerial personnel (i.e., managing director, whole-time director/Manager), prosecutions be filed against all ordinary directors, apart from the Secretary, if any, and the company". The Act gives scope to company Boards to name who from amongst the Board of Directors or any other person to be responsible for what to comply under the Act with the person so named duly consenting to be so responsible, whereupon a return in Form 1AB of the Companies (Central Government’s) General Rules & Forms, 1956 may be filed with the Registrar within 30 days of the Board charging such a director or other person, making it easy for the Regulators to trace the ‘in-charge’ of the company’s functions complained against being the company itself. Only when nothing of the sort is done by the Board, which unfortunately it is the general choice of almost all company Boards, all the occupants of the offices named in section 5 of the Act are liable to be proceeded against as ‘officers in default’. It is the same in all cases of Board managed companies, that is, all of the directors being liable to be proceeded against, as if uniting them in criminal liability for defaults and offences of a company.

Offences under other laws

11.10-7 It would appear that it is no different in other Acts intended to serve various purposes of the country’s economy in the attribution of the offences to a company. While sparing the whole lot of officers of the company unlike under section 5 of the Act, particularly the ordinary directors, those Acts short-list only those of them likely to be connected with the offences in the charging section itself or otherwise as ‘principal officer’ or ‘person in-charge’, the procedure being what it is provided under the Act itself, (the Acts are usually silent on this), or failing that, according to the general principles of criminal law requiring proof beyond reasonable doubt. Under the labour related laws, for example the Factories Act, it is the ‘owner’ or ‘occupier’ or ‘manager’ defined in that Act and under the other Acts like the Essential Commodities Act, 1955 or Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1957, it is generally the person in-charge of and responsible to the company for conduct of its business. Excepting under the labour laws, under other Acts the company is hardly made a party to the proceeding due to the difficulties of attribution of the liability to it, it being an abstract person. An exception to this is found under the Negotiable Instruments Act in respect of dishonour of cheques where the authorized signatory is a director who signed the cheque in his representative capacity for the company. It is he who is proceeded against without impleading the company, but it is the company that is ultimately caught, O.N. Phadnish v. Radhakrishnan [2001] 105 Comp. Cas. 210 (Mad.).

The modern concept of penal laws with reference to public, social welfare legislations or economic laws, contradicts the traditional penal theory which insists upon identifiable mens rea identifiable conduct, identifiable victim, identifiable harm.

Sherras v. De Rutzen [1895] 1 QB 918 Wright, J., found that there are three classes of cases where the Legislature normally enacts absolute prohibition : (1) One is a class of acts which, in the language of Lush J. in Davis v. Harvey (Law Rep. 9 QB 433) are not criminal in any real sense, but are acts which in the public interest are prohibited under a penalty. Several such instances are to be found in the decisions on the Revenue Statutes, Adulteration Acts, Games Acts etc.;

(2) Another class comprehends some, and perhaps all, public nuisances : Reg v. Stephens (Law Rep 1 QB 702) where the employer was held liable on the indictment for a nuisance caused by workmen without his knowledge and contrary to his orders;

(3) Lastly, there may be cases in which, although the proceeding is criminal in form, it is really a summary mode of enforcing a civil right : see per Williams and Willes JJ. in Modern v. Porter [7 C.B (N.S.) 641; 29 LJ (M.C. 213], as to the unintentional trespass in pursuit of game; Lee v. Simpson (3 C.B. 871) as to unconscious dramatic piracy and Hargreaves v. Diddams (Law Rep. 10 QB 582), as to a bona fide belief in a legally impossible right to fish.

The Bombay High Court, after quoting Sherras v. De Rutzen, observed as follows in Mayuri Pulse Mills v. Union of India [1996] 86 Comp. 121 (Bom.) :

“Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881, can be said to be falling either in the class of acts which are not criminal in a real sense, but are acts which in the public interest are prohibited under the penalty or those where although the proceedings may be criminal in form, they are really only a summary mode of enforcing a civil right.”

INSTRUMENT OF TRANSFER OF SECURITY

A company shall not register transfer unless proper instrument of transfer duly stamped and executed by transferor and transferee specifying name, address and occupation of transferee is delivered to company along with original share/debenture certificate or letter of allotment of shares/debentures. These requirements are mandatory and transfer cannot be registered if transfer deed does not fulfil these requirements. Hence, a company (public or private) can decline transfer in following situations.

The share transfer deed should be in prescribed form. If it is not in prescribed form, the transfer cannot be said to be as per law. The transfer deed must be lodged within its validity period.

Execution of transfer deed by transferor and transferee - The transfer deed should be duly executed by transferor and transferee or by a person authorised on their behalf. Name, occupation and address of transferee should be specified. If the deed is not properly executed, transfer can be declined. In case of joint holding, all joint holders must sign and their signatures should be witnessed. If signatures are not witnessed, transfer can be declined.

Original share certificates to be enclosed - Shares cannot be transferred unless the original share certificates are attached to the share transfer deed. If company has not issued share certificate, original letter of allotment should be attached. This is the specific requirement.

If share certificate has been lost, first duplicate will have to be obtained.

11.9-1 Witnessing of signature of transferor/s.

The signature of transferor/s has to be witnessed. Otherwise, transfer is required to be rejected. Note that attestation is not compulsory, but 'witness' is essential.

11.9-2 Transfer of security where signature of transferor does not tally

Normally, share transfer should be declined if signature of share transferor/s does not tally with the specimen signature available with the company. This is because, if the signature of transferor does not tally, the instrument of transfer cannot be said to be properly executed by or on behalf of transferor.

Attestation of signature - There is a provision in share transfer form that in case of signature difference, the signature of transferor can be attested by * Magistrate * Notary Public * manager of transferor's bank * member of a stock exchange.

If the signature does not tally and the variation is major, transfer can be declined even if signature is attested, on the ground that transfer deed is not properly executed. This is because transfer cannot be recorded unless 'duly executed' document is submitted to the company. If the signature of transferor does not tally, the document cannot be termed as 'duly executed'.

If the signature is attested, and company records the transfer even if signature does not tally, there is no legal protection to the company, if it later turns out that the signature was forged. It may be noted that forgery is nullity at law and forged document can never pass on a good title.

Normally, if the signature is attested, minor variations may be ignored. However, if the variation is major, the company is indeed in a difficult position, if the signature is attested. This is because there is no provision in law that the company will be indemnified if company registers the transfer based on the basis of attested signatures. Some unscrupulous transferors deliberately make wrong signatures, so that transfer is delayed and they can enjoy benefit of shares like dividend, bonus, rights etc. even after they sell the shares and get the money.

If signature is attested by notary under his seal and required stamps has been affixed, there is a legal presumption that the official acts are properly done. Hence, company may act upon such attestation. However, the legal presumption is rebuttable.

Protection to company if it acts in good faith - In Bhuwaneshwar Nath Nigam v. Hindustan Lever (2002) 38 SCL 124 = 111 Comp Cas 590 (CLB), company issued a warning to transferor in respect of 200 shares as there was minor signature difference. Since company did not receive any objection, the shares were transferred. In respect of some shares, there was no signature difference and signature was attested by Bank and hence company effected the transfer. Later, shareholder filed petition that his signature was forged and attestation was fraudulent. It was held that the transfers made by company were valid and company is not liable. It was also held that all persons to whom shares were subsequently transferred should have been impleaded.

Company can apply for rectification of register if signature does not tally - In difficulty, Company can apply for rectification of register in case of difference in signature under section 53 of the 2011 Act.

Provisions relating to evidence

GST Law makes specific provisions relating to evidence in various cases.

50.1 Relevancy of statements under certain circumstances

Section 136 of CGST Act provides as follows -

A statement made and signed by a person on appearance in response to any summons issued under section 70 during the course of any inquiry or proceedings under this Act shall be relevant, for the purpose of proving, in any prosecution for an offence under this Act, the truth of the facts which it contains -

(a)

when the person who made the statement is dead or cannot be found, or is incapable of giving evidence, or is kept out of the way by the adverse party, or whose presence cannot be obtained without an amount of delay or expense which, under the circumstances of the case, the Court considers unreasonable; or

(b)

when the person who made the statement is examined as a witness in the case before the Court and the Court is of the opinion that, having regard to the circumstances of the case, the statement should be admitted in evidence in the interests of justice.

Interestingly, this section states that the statement is relevant only in prosecution of offence. Thus, the statement is not a relevant evidence before Appellate Authority and Appellate Tribunal also.

Validity of similar provision in excise and customs [section 9D of Central Excise Act and section 138B of Customs Act] has been upheld in J&K Cigarettes v. CCE (2009) 242 ELT 189 (Del HC DB) [The challenge was provision for admitting evidence even without cross examination of witness].

CCE 2001(131) ELT 568 (CEGAT), it was held that statements of witness who are not cross examined cannot be relied upon and demand on basis of such statement without any corroboration is not sustainable. - same view in Nu-Trend Business Machines v. CCE 2002(141) ELT 119 (CEGAT) * Metro (India) Wood Crafts v. CCE (2016) 333 ELT 418 (CESTAT) * Jindal Drugs v. UOI (2016) 340 ELT 67 (P&H HC DB) * CCE v. Statement not signed by officer who took the statement has no value - In State v. Voting by joint holders - Regulation 52 of Model Articles of Association Table-F of Companies Act, 2013 provides that in the case of joint holders, the vote of the senior who tenders a vote, whether in person or by proxy, shall be accepted to the exclusion of the votes of the other joint holders. - - For this purpose, seniority shall be determined by the order in which the names stand in the register of members. Other joint holders can attend the meeting as they are members, but cannot vote.

Nomination form or share transfer forms prescribed also envisage shares in joint names.

In case of joint shareholders, the cheque or warrant of dividend should be sent to the holder first named in the register of members. However, if joint holders direct in writing, the cheque or dividend can be sent to another person as directed by the joint shareholders [Regulation 85(i) of Model Articles of company limited by shares as contained in Table-F of Schedule I of Companies Act, 2013].

Any one of the joint shareholders can give effective receipt of any dividend, bonuses or other monies payable in respect of such shares [Regulation 86 of Model Articles of company limited by shares as contained in Table-F of Schedule I of Companies Act, 2013].

Upto 3 names are generally permitted by the company as per listing agreement with stock exchange. Notice of meeting should be sent to first named person. Bonus shares and rights are, however, issued in the name of all joint holders.

Proxy should be signed by all joint holders ? - Regulation 52 of Table F of Companies Act, 2013 makes it clear that in case of joint holders, vote of senior who tenders a vote, whether in person or by proxy, shall be accepted to the exclusion of votes of other joint holders. Thus, senior member (seniority as per names listed in register of members) can appoint a proxy all by himself. Another view is that a proxy is in nature of instrument appointing an agent. It creates a contractual relationship which can be effective only when all principals jointly execute it or when it is executed by one of them acting under authority of all. Hence, in case of proxy, all joint holders must act jointly in appointing a proxy. In my opinion, in view of provisions of Regulation 52 of Table F, proxy signed by senior member will be enough.

33.3

Who can be punished

Any person who commits an offence as prescribed is punishable.

Offences in case of company or firm - In case of Company or partnership firm, every person who was in-charge of or was responsible to affairs of the Company/firm is deemed to be guilty. Normally, a Managing Director (partner in case of firm) or other person specially authorised is deemed to be in-charge. However, such person can prove that offence was committed without his knowledge or he had taken due care to prevent the offence [section 140(1) of Customs Act].

In addition, if it is proved that the offence in relation to Company is committed with consent or connivance of, or due to neglect on part of any director, manager or Secretary or other officer of Company or partnership firm, such person shall be deemed to be guilty [section 140(2) of Customs Act].

Difference between provisions of section 140(1) and section 140(2) of Customs Act is that in former case, the person in charge is deemed to be guilty and burden of proof is on him to prove that he had no knowledge; while in later case, burden of proof is on prosecution to prove that offence was committed with knowledge or connivance of the director, manager, secretary or other officer.

A director/partner as well as the Company/firm can be prosecuted. JOINT OWNERSHIP

Jointly owned property is any property held in the names of two or more parties. The PBPT Act, 1988 does not cover all types of joint ownership as exception to benami transaction. The section 2(9)(A)(iv) refers to specified transactions between two or more parties as exception to benami transaction. There is a rider in section 2(9)(A)(iv) to claim exclusion from benami transaction. This is only in respect of property jointly held by a person in the names of his brother, sister or lineal ascendant and lineal descendants. In order to come out of the ambit of benami transaction, the individual must be a joint owner in the document evidencing the transaction of the property along with others specified persons mentioned in this section and the consideration must flow out of the known sources of the individual. If the property is not in joint ownership as specified in the Benami Act, then it would fall within the definition of benami Transaction and all consequences would follow. Joint ownership must be evidenced by a document. Mere oral claim would not suffice.

Fixed deposit - Joint account

A fixed deposit in the joint names of two persons is nothing but a joint account which, as the name itself suggests, is payable on the expiration of the agreed period. The fixed deposit receipt is merely a written acknowledgement by the bank that it holds a certain sum to the use of its customers. The bank is thus a debtor to the account holders in respect of the amount deposited a debt which is repayable by the bank to the account holder with interest on the expiry of an agreed period. [Anumati v. Punjab National Bank [2005] 126 Comp. Cas. 322 (SC)]

The debt in the form of fixed deposit receipt is that of the bank to the joint account holders and the bank cannot set off a debt due from one of the joint account holders against such a joint debt (Nath Bank Ltd. v. Sisir Kumar Sarkar AIR 1954 Cal. 303). In Hirschorn v. Evans (Barclays Bank Ltd., Garnishee) (1938) 2 KB 801 (L), it was held that inasmuch as the debt which the bank owed was not a debt due to the husband alone, but to him jointly with his wife, it could not be attached to answer the judgment against the husband.

This Chapter was introduced in the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 with a view to enhance the acceptability of cheques in settlement of liabilities by making the drawer liable for penalties in case of bouncing of cheques due to insufficiency of the funds in the account or for the reason that it exceeds the arrangement made by the drawer with adequate safeguards to prevent harassment of honest drawers. Law is settled that payment of any amount by cheque would be on date of presentation of cheque, if it is not dishonoured . It only says that the declarant shall pay the amount within a period of 30 days. If rule 80 of the Treasury Rules is applied, the date of presentation of the cheque should be treated as the date of payment. Though rule 81 provides for imposition of any condition as to the realisation of the cheques if presented, such conditions were not imposed in section 90(2) of the Finance (No. 2) Act. In the absence of any such condition imposed in the Act, it was not open to the respondents to contend that the date of realisation should be treated as the date of payment and if so treated, the payment made by the petitioner was beyond the period of 30 days. 35.5

Evidence by documents

Provisions regarding documentary evidence are as follows.

Presumption regarding Documents seized from a person - Any document seized from a person shall be presumed to be true about the contents therein. Signature and other part of hand written document on such seized document, purporting to have been of a person or reasonably assumed to be of that person shall be presumed to be of that person. If such person claims that the document is not true or not signed by him, the burden of proof is on him [section 139(i) of Customs Act].

Presumption regarding documents received from place outside India - If any document is received from a place out of India in the course of investigation, it will be presumed that signature and other part of hand written document on such seized document, purporting to have been of a person or reasonably assumed to be of that person shall be presumed to be of that person. However, in case of such documents, there is no presumption that the contents are true. In other words, in case of documents obtained from abroad, prosecution has to prove that the contents are true, though they don't have to prove that the signature or hand-writing is of that person only, who is purported to have signed it or written it [section 139(ii) & (c) of Customs Act].

Meaning of 'document' for section 139 of Customs Act - Section 139 of Customs Act provides for presumptions of documents in certain cases. For purposes of section 139, 'document' includes inventories, photographs and lists certified by Magistrate under section 110(1C) or by Commissioner (Appeals) under section 110(1D) of Customs Act - Explanation to section 139 of Customs Act [The words in italics inserted w.e.f. 28-3-2021].

Other documents admissible - (a) A document which is required by law to be stamped, will be admissible as evidence even if it is not duly stamped. [Section 139(b) of Customs Act] (b) Micro film or Photostat/Xerox copy of document or reproduction of image is admissible, without further proof of original [Section 138C(1) of Customs Act].

In Kirpal Castings v. CCE 1999(108) ELT 552 (CEGAT), it was held that once photostat copies are made available to appellant, giving of original is not required.

Charge of under-valuation on basis of unsigned Xerox copies of documents is not sustainable - CC v. Bussa Overseas (2007) 216 ELT 659 (SC).

Fax letters are deemed to be 'documents' without proof of evidence, particularly when genuineness is acknowledged and corroborated by other evidence - Dungarmal Pruthviraj v. CC (2011) 272 ELT 606 (CESTAT).

Computer printouts - Statement printed by Computer is admissible if (a) Computer printout was produced during the period when the computer was used for storing and processing the information (b) the information contained in the statement was regularly supplied to computer during the period (c) computer was operating properly during the period or breakdowns were not significant to affect accuracy of documents (d) the print out is reproduced in ordinary course of activities. [Section 138C(2) of Customs Act].

The computer print outs will be allowed as evidence even if multiple computers or different computers or different combinations of computers were used. A statement or a certificate given by a responsible person to the best of his knowledge and belief identifying the statement or describing its contents or giving particulars of computers used in production of documents shall be evidence of any matter contained in the certificate.

4.19-8 Other interesting cases In the case which arose before the Madhya Pradesh High Court in CIT v. H.H. Maharani Manekaraje Pawar [1996] 86 Taxman 449 (MP) the facts were as under-

In pursuance of a consent decree to live apart obtained from competent court, the assessee gave some equity shares to his wife along with cash and other properties. The Assessing Officer held that the assessee transferred the shares and other assets and he added the capital gain to the income of the assessee. The assessee filed an appeal claiming that there was no transfer of capital asset and no capital gain assessable under the Act accrued to it. As the claims were rejected by the Commissioner of Income-tax (Appeals), the assessee filed an appeal before the Tribunal. The Tribunal held that there was transfer of shares by the assessee to his wife but no gain accrued which could be added in the income of the assessee as capital gain under section 45 of the Act.

The Indore Bench of the Tribunal-the order which gave rise to the appeal filed by the Revenue as seen above- categorically observed that "the question of a family settlement comes in when there is a dispute between admitted co-sharers or persons claiming a share in the properties although their rights may be disputed by the other co-sharers. In the present case, the wife was not claiming any right of sharing the assessee's properties as a co-sharer. Her claim was for maintenance and it was in lieu of maintenance that the properties in question were transferred by the assessee to her. The right of a wife for maintenance is an incident of the status or estate of matrimony and a Hindu is under a legal obligation to maintain his wife. The obligation to maintain the wife is personal in character and arises from the very existence of the relations between two parties. Therefore, when certain property is transferred to the wife in settlement of a claim for maintenance, it cannot, amount to a family settlement because there is no dispute between the co-shares and the other persons are not interested in the dispute."- refer H.H. Maharani Manekaraje Pawar v. ITO [1986] 15 ITD 545 (Indore)

The High Court endorsed the views of the Tribunal and held as under-

"The property was given to wife in connection with an agreement to live apart. Such an act is permissible under section 64(1)(iv) of the Act. The giving of property was not as a consideration but was in connection with an agreement to live apart.

According to section 125(4) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898, the wife is disentitled to receive any allowance from her husband if 'they are living separately by mutual consent' (in this case living apart is through court decree). The assessee in the instant case gave the property in connection with an agreement to live apart and thus created a case of living separately by mutual consent. There was no question of any capital gain in terms of section 45 of the Act. Therefore, the Tribunal was right in law in holding that no capital gain arose to the assessee under section 45 of the Act.

As to whether, the transaction amounted to transfer, it was found that the assessee extinguished his right on the above said property and as such the act was covered by section 2(47) of the Act and was clearly transfer in terms of the provisions of the Act. The spouse became the owner of the property given to her in connection with the agreement to live apart. It was clearly a case of transfer of capital asset in favour of the wife, though in pursuance of the consent decree and in connection with the agreement to live apart in terms of section 45 of the Act.

Therefore, the Tribunal was right in holding that there was a transfer of shares by the assessee but no capital gain arose to the assessee within the meaning of section 45 of the Act.".

NAME IN WHICH BONDS SHOULD BE PURCHASED

A question arises as to whether deduction under section 54EC be available where assessee invests in REC/NHAI bonds is-sued under section 54EC and name of spouse/son appears as co-holder? The answer appears to be "Yes" in view of ITAT's decision in ITO v. Smt. Sarawsati Ramanathan [2009] 116 ITD 234 (Delhi) (SMC) wherein it was held that the word 'invested' in section 54EC cannot be interpreted to mean 'invested in the assessee's name' as such an interpretation adds words into the section and also ignores the purpose which the section is intended to serve. There is no requirement in section 54EC that the investment should be in the name of the assessee. The requirement, having regard to the object of the section to exempt capital gains if the sale proceeds find their way into certain specified assets, is that the sale proceeds of the capital asset must be invested in certain specified assets such as bonds of the NABARD, the National Highways Authority of India; the Rural Electrification Corporation Ltd.; National Housing Bank, etc. These are corporations established by the Government of India for development of infrastructure in the country and to muster funds for the purpose an incentive to invest in these corporations carrying out infrastructure development activities was given in the form of exemption from capital gains tax if the sale proceeds were invested in the bonds issued by these corporations. If development of infrastructure is the object, it would hardly matter whether the investment is made in the name of the assessee exclusively or in the joint names of the assessee and somebody else. The only condition is that the funds used for the investment must be traceable to the sale proceeds of the capital asset.

The requirement of section 54EC is that "the assessee has, at any time within the period of six months after the date of such transfer, invested the whole or any part of capital gains in the long-term specified asset.....". So what is relevant for claiming exemption under section 54EC is that the whole or any part of the capital gain should be invested in the long-term specified assets. If the amount of capital gain is invested by the assessee, the requirement of the section is fulfilled. It is wholly extraneous that the name of another person is also introduced as co-holder- Dr. (Mrs.) Sudha S.Trivedi v. ITO [2009] 31 SOT 38 (Mum. - Trib.).

Deduction will be available where assessee is a co-holder even though name of the spouse appears first in the REC bonds -Asstt. CIT v. Vijay S. Shirodkar [2011] 14 taxmann.com 70/48 SOT 8 (Mum. - Trib.)

The Chartered Accountants Act,1949 as amended by the Amendment Act, 2011 recognises sole proprietorship firm of CA registered with ICAI as a 'firm'. The following points are noteworthy:

Section 139A of the Act provides that persons specified therein, who is not allotted permanent account number (PAN), should apply to Assessing Officer for allotment thereof.

In the Memorandum, reasons for amendment are explained as follows:

"In order to use PAN as Unique Entity Number (UEN) for non-individual entities, it is proposed that every person, not being an individual, which enters into a financial transaction of an amount aggregating to two lakh and fifty thousand rupees or more in a financial year shall be required to apply to the Assessing Officer for allotment of PAN.

In order to link the financial transactions with the natural persons, it is also proposed that the managing director, director, partner, trustee, author, founder, karta, chief executive officer, principal officer or office bearer or any person competent to act on behalf of such entities shall also apply to the Assessing Officer for allotment of PAN".

FEMA, BANKING & INSURANCE : Where appellant non-executive directors of accused company were neither signatories to dishonoured cheques nor had any role in their execution and their involvement in company’s affairs was purely non-executive confined to governance oversight, they could not be held vicariously liable under section 141.
CL : An authorized signatory of a company would not be liable for prosecution under section 138 without company being arraigned as an accused

FEMA, BANKING & INSURANCE : Where cheque issued by firm to discharge its liability had been dishonoured, in view of fact that appellant-partner of firm had not signed said cheque, mere averment in complaint that appellant was 'managing affairs of firm' was not sufficient to make him vicariously liable for dishonour of cheque issued by firm

FEMA, BANKING & INSURANCE: Where cheques issued towards repayment of loan taken for partnership firm’s business were presented within prescribed period but were dishonoured as 'instrument out dated/stale' due to banker’s wrongful return, petitioners could not be held liable under section 138; and since fourth accused was neither partner of firm nor signatory to cheques, no offence was made out against him, and entire proceedings were liable to be quashed

FEMA, BANKING & INSURANCE : Where accused no. 1 and accused no 6 were separate legal entities; one registered in Dubai and other registered in India, and thus, accused no 6 could not have been proceeded against under section 138 only on allegation that it was a group company of accused no. 1, which was drawer of cheque in question

FEMA, BANKING & INSURANCE : Where cheque issued by firm to discharge its liability had been dishonoured, in view of fact that petitioner had not signed said cheque, mere averment in complaint that petitioner was deemed owner of firm would not make him liable for dishonour of cheque issued by firm since certificate issued by Deputy Registrar of Firms, also nowhere showed that he was a partner in accused firm

FEMA, BANKING & INSURANCE : Where cheque issued by firm to discharge its liability had been dishonoured, in view of fact that petitioner had not signed said cheque, mere averment in complaint that petitioner was deemed owner of firm would not make him liable for dishonour of cheque issued by firm since certificate issued by Deputy Registrar of Firms, also nowhere showed that he was a partner in accused firm

FEMA, BANKING & INSURANCE : Notice issued to partners of a firm is deemed notice to partnership firm also; Where partnership firm issued cheque for discharging debt which was dishonoured, partners of firm were jointly and severally liable along with firm for offence under section 138

FEMA BANKING AND INSURANCE : Where petitioner-managing director of company had not issued cheques which were dishonoured on presentation and in complaint filed under section 138 there was no averment against said director as to how he was responsible for conduct of company, bald assertion against such director did not satisfy requirements of section 141, and order passed by CJM taking cognizance against said director was to be set aside
Petitioner-MD of Co. who didn’t issue the cheque wasn’t vicariously liable for its dishonour u/s 141: HC

FEMA, BANKING INSURANCE : Where Trial Court acquitted appellant from charge of committing an offence under sec. 138 on ground that dishonored cheque was issued from account of a firm and said account was in name of 'V' and not in name of appellant, in view of fact that appellant had not disputed his signature on cheque presented for clearance and that there was nothing on record to show that said firm was maintained by 'V', High Court was justified in setting aside Trial Court's order and passing conviction order against appellant
Non-executive directors weren't liable u/s 141 since they neither signed nor played a role in executing dishonoured cheques: SC

FEMA AND BANKING : Signatory of cheque, authorized by company, is not a drawer in terms of section 143A of Negotiable Instruments Act and cannot be directed to pay interim compensation under section 143A; in an appeal under section 148 filed by persons other than drawer against conviction under section 138, a deposit of 20 per cent of fine or compensation is not necessary
Petitioner couldn't be held vicariously liable u/s 141 of NI Act as he was not a signatory & had no financial role: HC

FEMA, BANKING & INSURANCE : Where in complaint for dishonour of cheque issued by accused-Limited Liability Partnership (LLP), no specific role of petitioner-designated partner of accused-LLP was ascribed in alleged offence and petitioner had specifically denied his liability, averments in complaint were not sufficient to attract rigour of section 141 of Negotiable Instruments Act to create vicarious liability upon petitioner and, therefore, criminal complaint in relation to petitioner

FEMA, BANKING & INSURANCE: Where a cheque was issued by a partnership firm and complainant neither issued statutory notice to firm and other partners nor impleaded them as accused, prosecution under sections 138 and 141 of Negotiable Instruments Act was not maintainable and entire proceedings were liable to be quashed as there was non-compliance with mandatory statutory requirements.
CL: Section 141 makes directors in charge and responsible to company 'for conduct of business of company' within mischief of section 138 and not particular business for which cheque was issued

FEMA & BANKING : If cheque had been issued by firm which was subsequently dishonoured, a partner of firm would not be liable for prosecution under section 138 without firm being arraigned as an accused

FEMA & BANKING: Where proceedings under section 141 were initiated against petitioners i.e. directors of company 'A', for issuing cheques which got dishonoured, in view of fact that petitioners were non-executive directors not responsible for day to day affairs of company 'A', proceedings initiated against than deserved to be quashed

Negotiable Instrument Act: Where a cheque was issued by the accused son from the account belonging to his father, accused-son couldn't held liable for prosecution under section 138 of Negotiable Instruments Act as one of the ingredients form holding one guilty that cheque must have been issued from an account maintained by accused was not satisfied

FEMA, BANKING AND INSURANCE : Where proceedings under section 138 of NI Act have commenced against company and during pendency of proceedings, resolution plan of company is approved or company gets dissolved, signatories/directors cannot escape from their liability by citing its dissolution; what is dissolved, is only company, not personal liability of accused covered under section 141 of NI Act
