A striking feature of the present discussion is the similarity between Section 141 of the N.I. Act and Section 137 of the CGST Act. Both provisions employ nearly identical language in attributing liability to persons in charge of and responsible for the conduct of business, while also recognising defences based on lack of knowledge and due diligence. 5. Discussion & Findings of the Supreme Court

5.1 On the Law Relating to Prosecution of Directors

The Court reiterated that the law governing prosecutions under Section 138 read with Section 141 of the N.I. Act is well settled. It emphasised that a complaint must contain specific averments demonstrating that the accused was in charge of and responsible for the conduct of the business of the company at the time of the offence. Absent such foundational pleadings, the prosecution cannot be sustained.

5.2 Regarding No Deeming Liability on Account of Being a Director

A crucial clarification made by the Court is that merely holding the position of a director does not automatically attract liability. There is no deemed liability in law solely on account of designation. The requirement of Section 141 is substantive and must be satisfied through clear and specific allegations establishing active responsibility.

5.3 Regarding Signing of Board Resolution and Day-to-Day Affairs

The Court decisively rejected the reasoning that signing a Board Resolution ipso facto establishes involvement in day-to-day management. It observed that Board Resolutions pertain to policy-level decisions and cannot be equated with operational control. In the absence of specific allegations indicating direct participation in the conduct of business, such a basis is insufficient to attract criminal liability.

6. Application of Principles to the Present Case

Applying the above principles, the Supreme Court found that there was no material to show that the appellant was in charge of and responsible for the conduct of the business of the company. The complaint lacked the necessary averments, and the reliance placed solely on the signing of a Board Resolution was misplaced.

The Court noted that criminal liability, particularly vicarious liability, cannot be imposed in a mechanical or casual manner. In the absence of specific allegations and supporting material, the continuation of proceedings would amount to an abuse of process. Accordingly, the proceedings against the appellant were quashed, reinforcing the principle that liability must be founded on role and responsibility, not merely on designation.

7. Conclusion

The judgment marks an important reaffirmation of the limits of vicarious liability in corporate jurisprudence. It preserves the delicate balance between ensuring accountability of those who are genuinely responsible for corporate conduct and protecting individuals from unwarranted prosecution merely due to their formal association with a company.

Equally, the ruling serves as a reminder that criminal law cannot be stretched to compensate for deficiencies in pleadings or evidence. The insistence on specific averments and demonstrable involvement ensures that prosecutions remain grounded in legal principle rather than assumption. In doing so, the Court has strengthened the integrity of both corporate law and criminal jurisprudence.

8. Lessons from the Judgment

The decision underscores that liability of directors is not a matter of presumption but of proof. It highlights the necessity of carefully drafted complaints, clearly identifying the role of each accused. For companies and their boards, the judgment provides reassurance that participation in governance, without involvement in day-to-day operations, does not automatically expose directors to liability.

At the same time, it reinforces that those who are actively in control cannot evade responsibility behind the corporate veil. Importantly, the ruling assumes even greater significance in the context of independent directors. It implies, in principle, that independent and non-executive directors—whose role is largely supervisory and advisory—cannot be routinely implicated in proceedings in the absence of specific material demonstrating their involvement in the conduct of business or their consent, connivance, or negligence. Mere presence on the Board, participation in meetings, or approval of resolutions in a governance capacity cannot, by itself, trigger liability. This serves as a crucial safeguard to ensure that independent and non-executive directors are not deterred from discharging their oversight functions due to the risk of unwarranted prosecution, while still preserving accountability in cases where there is demonstrable complicity or failure of due diligence.

9. Applicability under GST Law

The relevance of this judgment in the GST context is both immediate and substantial. Section 137 of the CGST Act mirrors the language of Section 141 of the N.I. Act, and therefore the interpretative principles laid down by the Supreme Court would squarely apply. Authorities seeking to fasten liability on directors must demonstrate, through clear allegations and evidence, that such persons were in charge of and responsible for the conduct of business at the relevant time.

An Overview of Section 138 under N.I. Act

Negotiable Instruments have long been used in the business world as one of the simplest ways to move capital. Until 1988, there was no effective legislative mechanism to prevent individuals from issuing checks without adequate funds in their account, nor was there any severe penalty for doing so. For instance, a legal responsibility arose from the non-payment of checks. To secure the check's drawee, it was decided that cheque dishonour should be considered a criminal offence. Banking, Public Financial Institutions, and Negotiable Instruments Laws (Amendment) Act, 1988 added Sec.138 to 142 for that reason. This was accomplished by having the drawer responsible for fines if the check bounced due to a lack of funds, with sufficient protections in place to deter abuse of the truthful drawer. However, it was later discovered that the courts were unwilling to resolve the proceedings in a timely and efficient fashion. The loopholes were filled in by the amendment of 2002, which resulted in the passage of the Negotiable Instruments (Amendment and Miscellaneous Provisions) Act, 2002. The provisions of sections 143 to 147 were included, and the provisions of sections 138, 141, and 142 were changed.

This amendment act aimed to control the growing business, exchange, commerce, and industrial activities and encourage greater financial vigilance. Also, to protect creditors' trust in the cheque box. The Hon'ble SC in the matter of Modi Cements Ltd. v. Kuchil Kumar Nandi held that "The object of Chapter XVII, containing Sections 138 to 142, is to promote the efficacy of banking operations and to ensure credibility in transacting business through cheques."1

Under Sections 118 and 139 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, there are presumptions in favour of the receiver of the cheque that it was drawn to discharge debts or liabilities. It is, however, rebuttable, and the victim will refute it by cross-examination without having to reach the witness box. The complainant is also responsible for proving that the check was given for a properly enforceable debt or liability. The burden on the accused in such a situation will be heavier than in proceedings under section 114 of the Evidence Act. The operation of notification is deemed to have been effected until notice is submitted by registered mail to the proper addressee of the cheque, as stated in Section 27 of the General Clauses Act, 1897, and Section 114 of the Evidence Act, 1872. The drawer, on the other hand, is free to refute this assumption as per N. Paraeswaran Unni v. G. Kannan2. Section 139 provides a requirement that the holder of a cheque collects the cheque in discharge, in full or in part, of any debt or other obligation until the execution of the cheque is admitted, It was held in Basalingappa v. Mudibasappa3. Cheques with no date or post-dated cheques are often given. In Bir Singh v. Mukesh Kumar4, the Supreme Court held that if a signed blank cheque is willingly handed over to a payee for any payment, the payee is free to fill in the balance and other information. This will not invalidate the check on its own.

In the case of Kusum Ingots and Alloys Ltd v. Pennar Peterson Securities Ltd5, the Supreme Court found out the basic ingredients of the crime as contemplated under Sec.138 of the act that, "an individual must have drawn a check on a bank account that he maintains for transfer of a certain sum of money to another person from that account for the discharge of some debt or other liability; the cheque was issued to the bank within six months of the date on which it was drawn, or within the validity limit of the cheque, whichever comes first; According to RBI guidelines, the validity duration of Cheques, Demand Drafts, Pay Orders, and Banker's Cheques has been shortened from six to three months as of April 1, 2012, from the date of the instrument. The bank returns the check as outstanding. either because the sum of money in the account is inadequate to honour the cheque or because it reaches the amount arranged to be charged by the account under a bank agreement; within 30 days of receiving details from the bank about the return of the cheque as outstanding, the payee or issuer of the cheque makes a case for reimbursement of the said sum of money by sending a note in writing to the drawer of the cheque; within 15 days of receiving the said note, the drawer of the cheque fails to allow delivery of the said sum of money to the payee or the holder of the cheque in the proper course of the cheque."

5.22D-7h MENS REA AND VICARIOUS AND STRICT LIABILITY - It is well-settled that the strict criminal liability of companies, partnership firms, or legal persons is in a class by itself and poses problems peculiar to them. Since a legal person is a fiction of the law and does not exist in actuality, the issue of vicarious liability of the office bearers through whom a company or a partnership firm or association of persons must necessarily act, comes to the fore.1 Strict vicarious liability is somewhat an exception to the general rule of direct personal culpability and is a modern development through statutory provisions. That there can be such vicarious criminal liability by legislative mandate is no longer in dispute. Nevertheless steeped as we are in the basic principles of criminal jurisprudence that mens rea must be an ingredient of an offence and both the act and intent must concur to constitute a crime, it requires some effort to accept whole-heartedly the legislative mandate of vicarious criminality even in the absence of either of the aforesaid ingredients.

Vicarious liability ‘is a necessary doctrine for the proper enforcement of much modern legislation—but it is not one to be extended.1 Whether one person will be held responsible for the acts of another is a matter of construction in each case. Regard must be had to the object of the statute, the words used, the nature of the duty laid down, the person upon whom it is imposed, the person by whom it would in ordinary circumstances be performed and the person upon whom the penalty is imposed.2

If the doctrine of vicarious liability is held to apply, a person subject to a statutory duty to which a penal sanction is attached who chooses to delegate the performance of that duty to another person (usually but not necessarily an employee), will nevertheless be himself liable for breaches of that duty by his delegate. In many cases his delegate’s ‘knowledge’ will be imputed to him.3

5.22D-7i MASTER IS VICARIOUSLY LIABLE FOR THE ACTS OF HIS SERVANT - A master is vicariously liable for the acts of his servant in the course of his employment, for the master’s liability to arise, the act should be authorised by the master or a wrongful and unauthorised mode of doing some act be also authorised by the master. The driver of a car taking the car on the masters’ business makes him vicariously liable if he commits an accident. But it is equally well-settled that if the servant, at the time of the accident, is not acting within the course of his employment, but is doing something for himself, the master is not liable. There is a presumption that a vehicle is driven on the master’s business and by his authorised agent or servant but presumption can be met.4

Central Bureau of Investigation (2015) 4 SCC 609 (SC 3 member bench), it has been held that director can be held vicariously liable only if (a) there is sufficient incriminating evidence against him coupled with criminal intent or (b) statutory regime attracts doctrine of vicarious liability. In Mahendra Pratap Singh v. N K Metals (1998) 31 CLA 325 (Del HC), it was held that a mere director cannot be prosecuted unless there is averment or allegation in the complaint and pre-summoning evidence he is in charge of and responsible to the company for its day to day business, or offence was committed with his consent or connivance - similar views in Secunderabad Health Care Ltd. v. Secunderabad Hospitals (1999) 96 Comp Cas 106 (AP) - contrary view in N Doraisamy v. Archana Enterprises (1995) 2 CCC 378 (Mad HC), where it was held that such specific averment is not necessary in the complaint.

Director can be relieved from personal liability of a civil nature by High Court under section 463 of Companies Act, 2013 [parallel section 633 of the 1956 Act].

A director can be prosecuted also. Aspects regarding prosecution of director and relief from civil liability are discussed in a subsequent chapter under 'Offences and Penalties'.

Person should be both in charge and responsible for business of company - In K K Ahuja v. V K Vora (2009) 10 SCC 48 = 94 SCL 140 (SC), it was held that Deputy General Manager of a company cannot be prosecuted, unless there is averment in complaint as to how and in what manner accused is guilty of consent and connivance or negligence. Mere mechanical reproduction of requirements of section 141(1) of Negotiable Instruments Act would not be sufficient. It was held that he should be responsible to the company for conduct of business of company and in addition is also in charge of business of the company. There may be directors and secretaries who are not in charge of business of the company at all. The words 'person in charge of business of the company' refer to a person who is in overall control of the day-to-day business of the company - relying on Katta Sujatha v. Fertiliser and Chemicals Travancore (2002) 7 SCC 655 - same view in State of NCT of Delhi v. Rajiv Khurana (2010) 104 SCL 671 (SC).

Ex-director cannot be punished, if he was not director at relevant time - Ex-director cannot be held liable if cheque was issued and dishonoured after he ceased to be director - Harshendra Kumar D v. Rebatilata Koley (2011) 3 SCC 351.

18.17-4 Vicarious liability only if statute makes special provision

Unless there is specific provision in Statute, a director of company or employee cannot be held to be vicariously liable for any offense committed by the company itself - S K Alagh v. State of UP (2008) 5 SCC 662 = 142 Comp Cas 228 (SC) - quoted with approval in Maharashtra State Electricity Board v. Datar Switchgear Ltd. 11.1-4 Blank transfer deed Practice of dating of stamp by ROC was introduced to stop problems created due to blank transfer deeds.

Validity of blank transfers has been upheld in Howrah Trading Co. Ltd. v. CIT (1959) 29 Comp Cas 282 (SC) = (1959) Supp 2 SCR 448 = AIR 1959 SC 775 and relying on Vasudev Ramchandra Shelat v. Companies Act, 2013 does not contain any provision relating to dating of share transfer form. There is no provision in Rules also.

Probable reason is that after wide spread use of demat shares on stock exchange, the provision has lost its usefulness.

11.1-5 Time limit for submission of transfer deed is not mandatory

Share certificate with transfer deed should be lodged within 60 days as per section 56 of Companies Act, 2013.

In Dove Investments v. Gujarat Industrial Inv. Corpn (2006) 66 SCL 89 = 129 Comp Cas 929 (SC 2 member bench), it was held that time limit for submission of transfer deed, specified in section 108 of the 1956 Act is directory. The company cannot refuse transfer even if application for transfer is submitted late, unless the company shows that prejudice is caused to it (due to late submission).

In Gujarat Industrial Investment Corpn v. Sterling Holiday Resorts (2005) 57 SCL 88 = 124 Comp Cas 390 (CLB), it has been held that the two month limit prescribed in section 108(1C) of the 1956 Act are directory and not mandatory. Transfer is required to be registered even if documents are lodged beyond a period of two months. In this case, actually, the transfer deeds were date stamped by authority as prescribed under section 108(1A) of the 1956 Act. Even then, it was held that section 108(1A) of the 1956 Act does not apply to transfer deeds lodged with bank/Financial Institution and transfer is required to be registered even if transfer deed is filed beyond two months - view confirmed in Dove Investments v. Corpn (2006) 66 SCL 89 = 129 Comp Cas 929 (SC 2 member bench).

11.1-6 Signing of transfer deed for shares

The transfer deed should be signed by the transferor.

Signature in case of joint holding - In case of joint holding, all joint holders must sign the transfer deed. - Hemalata Saha v. Stadmed P Ltd. AIR 1965 Cal 436.

If transfer deed is signed by only three out of four joint holders, transfer cannot be registered - Smt Claude-Lila Parulekar v. Sakal Papers P Ltd. (2005) 11 SCC 73 = 59 SCL 414 (SC).

Signature by power of attorney holder - Transfer deed can be signed by holder of power of attorney on behalf of transferor/s. Such power of attorney should be registered with company beforehand or certified copy should be furnished along with the transfer deed. If power of attorney was already registered with company by submitting certified copy, its registration number and date of registration with the company shall be given on reverse of transfer deed. However, a power of attorney holder cannot appoint a nominee. Similarly, a power of attorney holder cannot be appointed as a nominee.

Signature by holder of probate or letter of administration - Transfer by legal representative of deceased member is specifically permitted under section 56(5) of Companies Act, 2013 [parallel section 109 of the 1956 Act]

Employees of Government or FI who are nominee directors are not liable for dishonour of cheques - A person who is nominated as director of a company by virtue of his holding any office or employment in the Central Government or State Government or a financial corporation owned or controlled by the Central Government or State Government shall not be liable for prosecution for dishonour of cheques under section 138 of Negotiable Instruments Act. It may be noted that the exemption is only to those who are employees of Central/State Government or Financial institutions controlled by Government. Thus, other nominee directors of Government/FI who are not employees of Government/FI are not exempted. It may be noted that Financial institutions/Government can and in fact do nominate persons as directors on companies even when they are not employees of Government/FI. [In many cases, ex-employees are nominated as one way of providing them some retirement benefit at the cost of the company]. Such nominee directors do not get protection under this section.

15.10-5 No disqualification under section 164(2) of Companies Act, 2013 of directors of Government companies

Provisions relating to disqualification of directors under section 164(2) of Companies Act, 2013 for five years [for non-filing of financial statements or annual returns, non-payment of public deposits] are not applicable to Government companies - MCA Notification dated 5-6-2015 issued under section 462 of Companies Act, 2013.

[Question is whether the exemption is only in case of companies in which the persons are nominated as directors or even in other companies where they are directors on their own and not nominated. Really intention seems to be that it should not apply to director of such Government company, even when he is director in some other company, but that intention does not get reflected in this provision].

Earlier, vide DCA circular No. 8/2002 dated 22-3-2002, it was clarified that directors nominated by (a) Public Financial Institutions like IDBI, LIC, UTI, IIBI who have statutory powers to nominate directors with non obstante provisions in their respective statutes (b) Other Public Financial Institutions as defines under section 4A of Companies Act (c) Central or State Government and (d) Banking companies are exempt from provisions of section 274(1)(g) of the 1956 Act [parallel section 164(3) of Companies Act, 2013].

Validity of this circular under new Act is doubtful.

15.10-6 Protection to public servants who is a nominee

As per section 197 of CrPC, a person who is a 'public servant' cannot be prosecuted without sanction of Government. In APSECC Ltd. v. ROC (2002) 38 SCL 1016 (AP HC), it was held that director who is a 'public servant' cannot be prosecuted without obtaining prior sanction of Government, as per section 197 of Code of criminal Procedure. However, prosecution against company can continue.

Employees of LIC are public servants. - Sam Chand v. Vibhuti Bhushan AIR 1965 SC 588. Employees of nationalised banks are 'public servants'. - State of Maharashtra v. L D Kanchan 1989 SLR(58) 707. Employees of LIC and GIC are public servants. - State v. O P Dogra (1985) 4 SCC 319 = AIR 1986 SC 312.

It seems that nominee directors of these institutions will be entitled to protection from criminal prosecution under these provisions. However, so far there seems to be no case law on this issue, may be because such stand was not specifically taken in any of the cases.

11.9

INSTRUMENT OF TRANSFER OF SECURITY

A company shall not register transfer unless proper instrument of transfer duly stamped and executed by transferor and transferee specifying name, address and occupation of transferee is delivered to company along with original share/debenture certificate or letter of allotment of shares/debentures. These requirements are mandatory and transfer cannot be registered if transfer deed does not fulfil these requirements. Hence, a company (public or private) can decline transfer in following situations.

The share transfer deed should be in prescribed form. If it is not in prescribed form, the transfer cannot be said to be as per law. The transfer deed must be lodged within its validity period.

Execution of transfer deed by transferor and transferee - The transfer deed should be duly executed by transferor and transferee or by a person authorised on their behalf. Name, occupation and address of transferee should be specified. If the deed is not properly executed, transfer can be declined. In case of joint holding, all joint holders must sign and their signatures should be witnessed. If signatures are not witnessed, transfer can be declined.

Original share certificates to be enclosed - Shares cannot be transferred unless the original share certificates are attached to the share transfer deed. If company has not issued share certificate, original letter of allotment should be attached. This is the specific requirement.

If share certificate has been lost, first duplicate will have to be obtained.

11.9-1 Witnessing of signature of transferor/s.

The signature of transferor/s has to be witnessed. Otherwise, transfer is required to be rejected. Note that attestation is not compulsory, but 'witness' is essential.

11.9-2 Transfer of security where signature of transferor does not tally

Normally, share transfer should be declined if signature of share transferor/s does not tally with the specimen signature available with the company. This is because, if the signature of transferor does not tally, the instrument of transfer cannot be said to be properly executed by or on behalf of transferor.

Attestation of signature - There is a provision in share transfer form that in case of signature difference, the signature of transferor can be attested by * Magistrate * Notary Public * manager of transferor's bank * member of a stock exchange.

If the signature does not tally and the variation is major, transfer can be declined even if signature is attested, on the ground that transfer deed is not properly executed. This is because transfer cannot be recorded unless 'duly executed' document is submitted to the company. If the signature of transferor does not tally, the document cannot be termed as 'duly executed'.

If the signature is attested, and company records the transfer even if signature does not tally, there is no legal protection to the company, if it later turns out that the signature was forged. It may be noted that forgery is nullity at law and forged document can never pass on a good title.

Normally, if the signature is attested, minor variations may be ignored. However, if the variation is major, the company is indeed in a difficult position, if the signature is attested. This is because there is no provision in law that the company will be indemnified if company registers the transfer based on the basis of attested signatures. Some unscrupulous transferors deliberately make wrong signatures, so that transfer is delayed and they can enjoy benefit of shares like dividend, bonus, rights etc. even after they sell the shares and get the money.

If signature is attested by notary under his seal and required stamps has been affixed, there is a legal presumption that the official acts are properly done. Hence, company may act upon such attestation. However, the legal presumption is rebuttable.

Protection to company if it acts in good faith - In Bhuwaneshwar Nath Nigam v. Hindustan Lever (2002) 38 SCL 124 = 111 Comp Cas 590 (CLB), company issued a warning to transferor in respect of 200 shares as there was minor signature difference. Since company did not receive any objection, the shares were transferred. In respect of some shares, there was no signature difference and signature was attested by Bank and hence company effected the transfer. Later, shareholder filed petition that his signature was forged and attestation was fraudulent. It was held that the transfers made by company were valid and company is not liable. It was also held that all persons to whom shares were subsequently transferred should have been impleaded.

Company can apply for rectification of register if signature does not tally - In difficulty, Company can apply for rectification of register in case of difference in signature under section 53 of the 2011 Act.

Provisions relating to evidence

GST Law makes specific provisions relating to evidence in various cases.

50.1 Relevancy of statements under certain circumstances

Section 136 of CGST Act provides as follows -

A statement made and signed by a person on appearance in response to any summons issued under section 70 during the course of any inquiry or proceedings under this Act shall be relevant, for the purpose of proving, in any prosecution for an offence under this Act, the truth of the facts which it contains -

(a)

when the person who made the statement is dead or cannot be found, or is incapable of giving evidence, or is kept out of the way by the adverse party, or whose presence cannot be obtained without an amount of delay or expense which, under the circumstances of the case, the Court considers unreasonable; or

(b)

when the person who made the statement is examined as a witness in the case before the Court and the Court is of the opinion that, having regard to the circumstances of the case, the statement should be admitted in evidence in the interests of justice.

Interestingly, this section states that the statement is relevant only in prosecution of offence. Thus, the statement is not a relevant evidence before Appellate Authority and Appellate Tribunal also.

Validity of similar provision in excise and customs [section 9D of Central Excise Act and section 138B of Customs Act] has been upheld in J&K Cigarettes v. CCE (2009) 242 ELT 189 (Del HC DB) [The challenge was provision for admitting evidence even without cross examination of witness].

In Takshila Spinners v. CCE 2001(131) ELT 568 (CEGAT), it was held that statements of witness who are not cross examined cannot be relied upon and demand on basis of such statement without any corroboration is not sustainable. - same view in Nu-Trend Business Machines v. Statement not signed by officer who took the statement has no value - In State v. 10.4-3 Punishment for personation as a member

If a person deceitfully personates as owner of share or interest in the company or attempts to receive money due to owner, he is punishable with imprisonment which is minimum one year but can extend upto three years. It creates a contractual relationship which can be effective only when all principals jointly execute it or when it is executed by one of them acting under authority of all. Hence, in case of proxy, all joint holders must act jointly in appointing a proxy. In my opinion, in view of provisions of Regulation 52 of Table F, proxy signed by senior member will be enough. Joint holder is also a member - Every person who agrees in writing to become a member of company and whose name is entered in register of members is a member of the company. Thus, all joint holders are 'members'. In case of joint holding, all members attending will be counted for quorum (This is because all joint holders are members) - Jarnail Singh v. Bakshi Singh AIR 1960 Punjab 455 = (1960) 30 Comp Cas 192 (Punj HC DB).

Thus, a joint holder is also a member. He has his own rights as a member - e.g. he can inspect register of members, attend general meeting, sign for a requisition meeting, apply for winding up, apply to NCLT for oppression and mismanagement. A joint holder is jointly and severally liable for calls. [Regulation 15 of Table F]. Any one of joint holder can give effectual receipt of dividend, bonus or other moneys payable in respect of share. [Regulation 86 of Table F].

Joint holder can be considered for purpose of quorum - As per section 103(1) of Companies Act, 2013 [Corresponding to section 174 of the 1956 Act], quorum at general meeting consists of members personally present. Since joint holder is a 'member' as explained above, he will be considered for purpose of quorum, as he is also a 'member' in his own right.

Thus, if first named member as well as joint holder attends the meeting, both are members and hence can be considered for purpose of quorum.

When joint holder counted as single member - Joint holders are treated as single member in following cases - (a) for counting number of members of a private company - section 2(68) of Companies Act, 2013 [parallel proviso to section 3(1)(iii) of the 1956 Act]. (b) In case of application to NCLT in respect of oppression and mismanagement, any one joint holder can sign the application. However, for counting number of members required to sign the application, joint shareholders will be counted as 'one member' - section 244(1) of Companies Act, 2013 [Corresponding to section 399(2) of the 1956 Act].

This is a legal fiction and cannot be extended beyond its limited scope. The sections 2(68) and 244(1) themselves state that this is only for the purpose of those sections.

Joint holders must sign jointly on transfer deed - If the shares are in joint names, the transfer form must be jointly signed.

If transfer deed is signed by only three out of four joint holders, transfer cannot be registered - Smt Claude-Lila Parulekar v. Sakal Papers P. Ltd. (2005) 11 SCC 73 = 59 SCL 414 (SC).

Fixed deposit in joint name cannot be pledged by one of depositor - Fixed deposit with Bank in joint name is a tripartite agreement between joint holders inter se and Bank. An 'either or survivor' clause means, on maturity, Bank can make payment to either of them. This tripartite agreement cannot be bilaterally modified. One of the depositor cannot pledge the deposit receipt without authority or concurrence of other deposit holder - Anumati v. Punjab National Bank AIR 2005 SC 29 = 2004 AIR SCW 6215.

10.8-1 Transposition of name of joint holders

If all members are alive, transposition of names i.e. changing the sequence of the name of joint holders is permissible, with consent of all joint holders for the entire holdings. This is not a transfer and company should not insist on a transfer deed - . - Exposure Draft - Secretarial Standard 1 (CS July 1998).

In department letter No. F1/24/- SEBI PMD circular No. I (2000-01) dated 9-5-2001/80 dated 5.9.1980, it has been clarified that transposition of joint names, i.e. changing sequence (like A, B, C to B, C, A) is not a share transfer and share transfer deed is not required. However, if some name is to be added or deleted, share transfer deed will be required.

10.8-2 Effect on ownership of shares when one of the joint holder dies

As per Regulation 23(i) of Model Articles of company limited by shares as contained in Table-F of Schedule I of Companies Act, 2013, on the death of a member, the survivor/s i.e. joint member/s, and his legal representative if deceased was a sole holder, shall be the only persons recognised by the company as having title to his interest in the shares.

10.8

JOINT HOLDING OF SHARES

Though the 2013 Act makes no specific provision allowing shares in joint names, the Companies Act has recognised issue of shares in joint names - e.g.

Section 2(68) of Companies Act, 2013, which is in respect of private company [Corresponding to section 3(1)(iii) of the 1956 Act] - When share are held in joint names, they shall be treated as 'single member' to decide number of members of a private company (limit is 200) -confirmed in Durtus Rutton Kavasmaneck v. Ghardia Chemicals Ltd. (2017) 143 SCL 372 = 84 taxmann.com 87 (Bom HC).

Nomination is required to be signed by all joint holders - section 72(2) of Companies Act, 2013.

Explanation to section 244(1) of Companies Act, 2013 [Corresponding to section 399(2) of the 1956 Act] - Application to NCLT in respect of oppression or mismanagement - in case of joint share-holding, application will be counted as signed by one member.

In respect of shares jointly held by several persons, delivery of certificate to one of several joint holders shall be sufficient delivery to all such shareholders - Regulation 2(iii) of Model Articles of Association Table-F of Companies Act, 2013.

Joint holders of a share shall be jointly and severally liable to pay all calls made on shares [Regulation 15 of Model Articles of company limited by shares as contained in Table-F of Schedule I of Companies Act, 2013].

Regulation 23(ii) of Model Articles of Association Table-F of Companies Act, 2013 specifically provides that transmission in the name of joint holder shall not release the estate of a deceased joint holder from any liability in respect of any share which had been jointly held by the deceased - - This provision applies only to liability of deceased shareholder and not to rights of the successors of the deceased.

Voting by joint holders - Regulation 52 of Model Articles of Association Table-F of Companies Act, 2013 provides that in the case of joint holders, the vote of the senior who tenders a vote, whether in person or by proxy, shall be accepted to the exclusion of the votes of the other joint holders. - - For this purpose, seniority shall be determined by the order in which the names stand in the register of members. Other joint holders can attend the meeting as they are members, but cannot vote.

Nomination form or share transfer forms prescribed also envisage shares in joint names.

In case of joint shareholders, the cheque or warrant of dividend should be sent to the holder first named in the register of members. However, if joint holders direct in writing, the cheque or dividend can be sent to another person as directed by the joint shareholders [Regulation 85(i) of Model Articles of company limited by shares as contained in Table-F of Schedule I of Companies Act, 2013].

Any one of the joint shareholders can give effective receipt of any dividend, bonuses or other monies payable in respect of such shares [Regulation 86 of Model Articles of company limited by shares as contained in Table-F of Schedule I of Companies Act, 2013].

Upto 3 names are generally permitted by the company as per listing agreement with stock exchange. Notice of meeting should be sent to first named person. Bonus shares and rights are, however, issued in the name of all joint holders.

Proxy should be signed by all joint holders ? - Regulation 52 of Table F of Companies Act, 2013 makes it clear that in case of joint holders, vote of senior who tenders a vote, whether in person or by proxy, shall be accepted to the exclusion of votes of other joint holders. Thus, senior member (seniority as per names listed in register of members) can appoint a proxy all by himself. Another view is that a proxy is in nature of instrument appointing an agent. It creates a contractual relationship which can be effective only when all principals jointly execute it or when it is executed by one of them acting under authority of all. Hence, in case of proxy, all joint holders must act jointly in appointing a proxy. In my opinion, in view of provisions of Regulation 52 of Table F, proxy signed by senior member will be enough.

Who can be punished

Any person who commits an offence as prescribed is punishable.

Offences in case of company or firm - In case of Company or partnership firm, every person who was in-charge of or was responsible to affairs of the Company/firm is deemed to be guilty. Normally, a Managing Director (partner in case of firm) or other person specially authorised is deemed to be in-charge. However, such person can prove that offence was committed without his knowledge or he had taken due care to prevent the offence [section 140(1) of Customs Act].

In addition, if it is proved that the offence in relation to Company is committed with consent or connivance of, or due to neglect on part of any director, manager or Secretary or other officer of Company or partnership firm, such person shall be deemed to be guilty [section 140(2) of Customs Act].

Difference between provisions of section 140(1) and section 140(2) of Customs Act is that in former case, the person in charge is deemed to be guilty and burden of proof is on him to prove that he had no knowledge; while in later case, burden of proof is on prosecution to prove that offence was committed with knowledge or connivance of the director, manager, secretary or other officer.

In Sunil Bharti Mittal v. Central Bureau of Investigation (2015) 4 SCC 609 (SC 3 member bench), it has been held that director can be held vicariously liable only if (a) there is sufficient incriminating evidence against him coupled with criminal intent or (b) statutory regime attracts doctrine of vicarious liability.

In Girdhari Lal Gupta v. D N Mehta AIR 1972 SC 2162, it was held that the first part of definition is applicable to the one who is in overall control of the company. In Municipal Corporation of Delhi v. Ram Kishan Rohtagi AIR 1983 SC 67, it was held that there should be averment that director was responsible to the conduct of business of the company. Otherwise, he cannot be prosecuted. If there is no evidence that they were responsible for conduct of business of the company, they cannot be prosecuted - followed in D K Jhaver v. State of Punjab (1997) 24 CLA 133 (P&H).

A director/partner as well as the Company/firm can be prosecuted. Of course, Company/firm can only be fined, while the guilty officers/partners can be imprisoned and personal fine also can be imposed. In some cases, it has been held that a director can be prosecuted even if company itself is not prosecuted.

Company includes firm and AOP - As per Explanation to section 140(2) of Customs Act, 'company' means any body corporate and includes a firm or other association of individuals, and 'director' in relation to firm means a partner of the firm.

JOINT OWNERSHIP

Jointly owned property is any property held in the names of two or more parties. The PBPT Act, 1988 does not cover all types of joint ownership as exception to benami transaction. The section 2(9)(A)(iv) refers to specified transactions between two or more parties as exception to benami transaction. There is a rider in section 2(9)(A)(iv) to claim exclusion from benami transaction. This is only in respect of property jointly held by a person in the names of his brother, sister or lineal ascendant and lineal descendants. In order to come out of the ambit of benami transaction, the individual must be a joint owner in the document evidencing the transaction of the property along with others specified persons mentioned in this section and the consideration must flow out of the known sources of the individual. If the property is not in joint ownership as specified in the Benami Act, then it would fall within the definition of benami Transaction and all consequences would follow. Joint ownership must be evidenced by a document. Mere oral claim would not suffice.

Fixed deposit - Joint account

A fixed deposit in the joint names of two persons is nothing but a joint account which, as the name itself suggests, is payable on the expiration of the agreed period. The fixed deposit receipt is merely a written acknowledgement by the bank that it holds a certain sum to the use of its customers. The bank is thus a debtor to the account holders in respect of the amount deposited a debt which is repayable by the bank to the account holder with interest on the expiry of an agreed period. [Anumati v. Punjab National Bank [2005] 126 Comp. Cas. 322 (SC)]

The debt in the form of fixed deposit receipt is that of the bank to the joint account holders and the bank cannot set off a debt due from one of the joint account holders against such a joint debt (Nath Bank Ltd. v. Sisir Kumar Sarkar AIR 1954 Cal. 303). In Hirschorn v. Evans (Barclays Bank Ltd., Garnishee) (1938) 2 KB 801 (L), it was held that inasmuch as the debt which the bank owed was not a debt due to the husband alone, but to him jointly with his wife, it could not be attached to answer the judgment against the husband.

Payment on the cheque being honoured and encashed relates back to the date of the receipt of the cheque, and in law the date of payment is the date of delivery of the cheque. [K. Saraswathy v. P.S.S. Somasundaram Chettiar [1989] 4 SCC 527] In Commissioner of Income Tax, Bombay South, Bombay v. Messrs Ogale Glass Works Ltd. Ogale Wadi, A.I.R. 1954 S.C. 429 it was the Supreme Court held that payment by cheque realised subsequently on the cheque being honoured and encashed relates back to the date of the receipt of the cheque, and in law the date of payment is the date of delivery of the cheque. Payment by cheque is an ordinary incident of present-day life, whether commercial or private, and unless it is specifically mentioned that payment must be in cash there is no reason why payment by cheque should not be taken to be due payment if the cheque is subsequently encashed in the ordinary course.

The Supreme Court, in the case of K. Saraswathy (supra) while considering the provisions of sections 10 and 82 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881, held that the payment by cheque should be taken to be due payment if the cheque is subsequently encashed in the ordinary course. Therefore, the Parliament, in its wisdom, enacted the Negotiable Instruments Act to regulate and manage the transactions through cheques. Further, section 138 of the said Act was amended by the Banking, Public Financial Institutions and Negotiable Instruments Laws (Amendment) Act, 1988 by inserting Chapter XVII comprising of sections 138 to 142 with effect from 1-4-1989. This Chapter was introduced in the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 with a view to enhance the acceptability of cheques in settlement of liabilities by making the drawer liable for penalties in case of bouncing of cheques due to insufficiency of the funds in the account or for the reason that it exceeds the arrangement made by the drawer with adequate safeguards to prevent harassment of honest drawers. Therefore, the intention of the Legislature is to encourage the citizens to settle their liabilities through cheque or draft. [P.L. Haulwel Trailers Ltd. v. Deputy Commissioner of Income-tax, Special Range V. [2006] 100 ITD 485 (Chennai)]

Law is settled that payment of any amount by cheque would be on date of presentation of cheque, if it is not dishonoured . It was not open to department to deny benefit of Kar Vivad Samadhan Scheme to petitioner on ground that cheque was realised after prescribed period of 30 days. The provision in section 90(2) of the Finance (No. 2) Act, 1998 which refers to the payment within 30 days does not refer to the mode of payment. It only says that the declarant shall pay the amount within a period of 30 days. If rule 80 of the Treasury Rules is applied, the date of presentation of the cheque should be treated as the date of payment. Though rule 81 provides for imposition of any condition as to the realisation of the cheques if presented, such conditions were not imposed in section 90(2) of the Finance (No. 2) Act. In the absence of any such condition imposed in the Act, it was not open to the respondents to contend that the date of realisation should be treated as the date of payment and if so treated, the payment made by the petitioner was beyond the period of 30 days. It is settled law that payment of any amount by a cheque would be the date of the presentation of the cheque, if it is not dishonoured. as per the judgment of the Supreme Court in the case of CIT v. Ogale Glass Works Ltd. [1954] 25 ITR 529 as well as the judgment of the Gujarat High Court in Kangold (India) Ltd. v. CIT [1999] 239 ITR 842, the date of presentation of the cheque, if honoured, would amount to payment on that date and, therefore, the presentation of the cheque on 27-3-1999 should be treated as payment. It was not the case of the department that the cheque presented by the petitioner was dishonoured. But their claim was only that the cheque was realized after the prescribed period of 30 days. It was not open to the department to deny the benefit to the petitioner on that ground, in view of the above settled position. [K. Venkata Reddy v. CIT [2001] 117 Taxman 141 (Andhra Pradesh)]

35.5

Evidence by documents

Provisions regarding documentary evidence are as follows.

Presumption regarding Documents seized from a person - Any document seized from a person shall be presumed to be true about the contents therein. Signature and other part of hand written document on such seized document, purporting to have been of a person or reasonably assumed to be of that person shall be presumed to be of that person. If such person claims that the document is not true or not signed by him, the burden of proof is on him [section 139(i) of Customs Act].

Presumption regarding documents received from place outside India - If any document is received from a place out of India in the course of investigation, it will be presumed that signature and other part of hand written document on such seized document, purporting to have been of a person or reasonably assumed to be of that person shall be presumed to be of that person. However, in case of such documents, there is no presumption that the contents are true. In other words, in case of documents obtained from abroad, prosecution has to prove that the contents are true, though they don't have to prove that the signature or hand-writing is of that person only, who is purported to have signed it or written it [section 139(ii) & (c) of Customs Act].

Meaning of 'document' for section 139 of Customs Act - Section 139 of Customs Act provides for presumptions of documents in certain cases. For purposes of section 139, 'document' includes inventories, photographs and lists certified by Magistrate under section 110(1C) or by Commissioner (Appeals) under section 110(1D) of Customs Act - Explanation to section 139 of Customs Act [The words in italics inserted w.e.f. 28-3-2021].

Other documents admissible - (a) A document which is required by law to be stamped, will be admissible as evidence even if it is not duly stamped. [Section 139(b) of Customs Act] (b) Micro film or Photostat/Xerox copy of document or reproduction of image is admissible, without further proof of original [Section 138C(1) of Customs Act].

In Kirpal Castings v. CCE 1999(108) ELT 552 (CEGAT), it was held that once photostat copies are made available to appellant, giving of original is not required.

Charge of under-valuation on basis of unsigned Xerox copies of documents is not sustainable - CC v. Bussa Overseas (2007) 216 ELT 659 (SC).

Fax letters are deemed to be 'documents' without proof of evidence, particularly when genuineness is acknowledged and corroborated by other evidence - Dungarmal Pruthviraj v. CC (2011) 272 ELT 606 (CESTAT).

Computer printouts - Statement printed by Computer is admissible if (a) Computer printout was produced during the period when the computer was used for storing and processing the information (b) the information contained in the statement was regularly supplied to computer during the period (c) computer was operating properly during the period or breakdowns were not significant to affect accuracy of documents (d) the print out is reproduced in ordinary course of activities. [Section 138C(2) of Customs Act].

The computer print outs will be allowed as evidence even if multiple computers or different computers or different combinations of computers were used. A statement or a certificate given by a responsible person to the best of his knowledge and belief identifying the statement or describing its contents or giving particulars of computers used in production of documents shall be evidence of any matter contained in the certificate.

18.17-3 Directors etc. liable only if offense committed with their connivance or due to their negligence

As per clause (2) of the section (as contained in many of the Acts), in case of other directors, manager and Secretary, they are held guilty only when it is proved that the offence was committed with their consent/connivance or is attributable to their negligence, i.e. the burden of proof is on prosecution (complainant) to allege and prove that the offence was committed with their consent/connivance or negligence.

In SMS Pharmaceuticals Ltd. v. Neeta Bhalla (2005) 8 SCC 89 = 148 Taxman 128 = 63 SCL 93 (SC 3 member bench), it has been held that simply being a director in a company, one is not supposed to be in-charge of affairs of the company. A director may not know anything about day-to-day functioning of a company. As a director, he may be attending meetings of Board where usually they decide policy matters and guide the course of business of a company. One or two directors may be made responsible for day-to-day functions of the company by a resolution. - - However, in case of MD or JMD, by virtue of the office they hold as Managing Director or Joint Managing Director, these persons are in charge of and responsible for the conduct of business of the company. In order to escape liability, they have to prove that when the offense was committed, they had no knowledge of the offense or that they exercised all due diligence to prevent commission of the offense [decision in case of bouncing of cheque under Negotiable Instruments Act, but principle should apply in all cases].

It is trite law that wherever a legal fiction of the principle of vicarious liability is attracted, and a person otherwise not personally involved in the commission of an offense is made liable for the same, it has to be specifically provided in the statute concerned - Maharashtra State Electricity Board v. 4.19-8 Other interesting cases In the case which arose before the Madhya Pradesh High Court in CIT v. H.H. Maharani Manekaraje Pawar [1996] 86 Taxman 449 (MP) the facts were as under-

In pursuance of a consent decree to live apart obtained from competent court, the assessee gave some equity shares to his wife along with cash and other properties. The Assessing Officer held that the assessee transferred the shares and other assets and he added the capital gain to the income of the assessee. The assessee filed an appeal claiming that there was no transfer of capital asset and no capital gain assessable under the Act accrued to it. As the claims were rejected by the Commissioner of Income-tax (Appeals), the assessee filed an appeal before the Tribunal. The Tribunal held that there was transfer of shares by the assessee to his wife but no gain accrued which could be added in the income of the assessee as capital gain under section 45 of the Act.

The Indore Bench of the Tribunal-the order which gave rise to the appeal filed by the Revenue as seen above- categorically observed that "the question of a family settlement comes in when there is a dispute between admitted co-sharers or persons claiming a share in the properties although their rights may be disputed by the other co-sharers. In the present case, the wife was not claiming any right of sharing the assessee's properties as a co-sharer. Her claim was for maintenance and it was in lieu of maintenance that the properties in question were transferred by the assessee to her. The right of a wife for maintenance is an incident of the status or estate of matrimony and a Hindu is under a legal obligation to maintain his wife. The obligation to maintain the wife is personal in character and arises from the very existence of the relations between two parties. Therefore, when certain property is transferred to the wife in settlement of a claim for maintenance, it cannot, amount to a family settlement because there is no dispute between the co-shares and the other persons are not interested in the dispute."- refer H.H. Maharani Manekaraje Pawar v. ITO [1986] 15 ITD 545 (Indore)

The High Court endorsed the views of the Tribunal and held as under-

"The property was given to wife in connection with an agreement to live apart. Such an act is permissible under section 64(1)(iv) of the Act. The giving of property was not as a consideration but was in connection with an agreement to live apart.

According to section 125(4) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898, the wife is disentitled to receive any allowance from her husband if 'they are living separately by mutual consent' (in this case living apart is through court decree). The assessee in the instant case gave the property in connection with an agreement to live apart and thus created a case of living separately by mutual consent. There was no question of any capital gain in terms of section 45 of the Act. Therefore, the Tribunal was right in law in holding that no capital gain arose to the assessee under section 45 of the Act.

As to whether, the transaction amounted to transfer, it was found that the assessee extinguished his right on the above said property and as such the act was covered by section 2(47) of the Act and was clearly transfer in terms of the provisions of the Act. The spouse became the owner of the property given to her in connection with the agreement to live apart. It was clearly a case of transfer of capital asset in favour of the wife, though in pursuance of the consent decree and in connection with the agreement to live apart in terms of section 45 of the Act.

Therefore, the Tribunal was right in holding that there was a transfer of shares by the assessee but no capital gain arose to the assessee within the meaning of section 45 of the Act.".

NAME IN WHICH BONDS SHOULD BE PURCHASED

A question arises as to whether deduction under section 54EC be available where assessee invests in REC/NHAI bonds is-sued under section 54EC and name of spouse/son appears as co-holder? The answer appears to be "Yes" in view of ITAT's decision in ITO v. Smt. Sarawsati Ramanathan [2009] 116 ITD 234 (Delhi) (SMC) wherein it was held that the word 'invested' in section 54EC cannot be interpreted to mean 'invested in the assessee's name' as such an interpretation adds words into the section and also ignores the purpose which the section is intended to serve. There is no requirement in section 54EC that the investment should be in the name of the assessee. The requirement, having regard to the object of the section to exempt capital gains if the sale proceeds find their way into certain specified assets, is that the sale proceeds of the capital asset must be invested in certain specified assets such as bonds of the NABARD, the National Highways Authority of India; the Rural Electrification Corporation Ltd.; National Housing Bank, etc. These are corporations established by the Government of India for development of infrastructure in the country and to muster funds for the purpose an incentive to invest in these corporations carrying out infrastructure development activities was given in the form of exemption from capital gains tax if the sale proceeds were invested in the bonds issued by these corporations. If development of infrastructure is the object, it would hardly matter whether the investment is made in the name of the assessee exclusively or in the joint names of the assessee and somebody else. The only condition is that the funds used for the investment must be traceable to the sale proceeds of the capital asset.

The requirement of section 54EC is that "the assessee has, at any time within the period of six months after the date of such transfer, invested the whole or any part of capital gains in the long-term specified asset.....". So what is relevant for claiming exemption under section 54EC is that the whole or any part of the capital gain should be invested in the long-term specified assets. If the amount of capital gain is invested by the assessee, the requirement of the section is fulfilled. It is wholly extraneous that the name of another person is also introduced as co-holder- Dr. (Mrs.) Sudha S.Trivedi v. ITO [2009] 31 SOT 38 (Mum. - Trib.).

Deduction will be available where assessee is a co-holder even though name of the spouse appears first in the REC bonds -Asstt. CIT v. Vijay S. Shirodkar [2011] 14 taxmann.com 70/48 SOT 8 (Mum. - Trib.)

Points to note: In Dr. (Mrs.) Sudha S. Trivedi (supra), the Bonds appeared in assessee's balance sheet. In Asstt. CIT v.Vijay. S. Shirodkar (supra), the assessee furnished a letter from REC confirming that the maturity proceeds of bonds will be credited to assessee's account.

Deposit in names of partners: In ITO v. Jifri & Kareem [1988] 24 ITD 288 (Co-chin - Trib.) the Cochin Bench of the Tribunal held that a firm is entitled to benefit under section 54E even though it has deposited the consideration received on sale of certain capital assets in names of its partners. Although this decision was delivered in relation to section 54E it should be applicable to section 54EC also.

Proprietary firm whether qualifies for appointment as auditor in firm name

The Chartered Accountants Act,1949 as amended by the Amendment Act, 2011 recognises sole proprietorship firm of CA registered with ICAI as a 'firm'. The following points are noteworthy:

According to new clause (ca) of section 2(1) of the 1949 Act, the term "firm" inter alia includes "sole proprietorship" registered with ICAI.

New clause (haa) defines "sole proprietorship" to mean an individual who engages himself in the practice of accountancy or offers to perform services referred to in clauses (ii) to (iv) of sub-section (2).

However, it appears that proprietorship firm cannot be appointed as auditor in firm name in view of the following:

Explanation to section 139(4) of the 2013 Act provides that for the purposes of Chapter XX, "firm" shall include Limited Liability Partnership incorporated under the LLP Act, 2008.

The definition of "firm" in Explanation to section 139(4) of the 2013 Act is silent on whether sole proprietorship CA firm which is recognized as "firm" in CA Act, 1949 is also covered in definition of firm.

Though definition of "firm" in Explanation is an inclusive one, it appears that proviso to section 141(1) of the 2013 Act clinches the issue. The said proviso provides that a firm of chartered accountants may be appointed by its firm name to be auditor of a company, "if majority of its partners practising in India are qualified for appointment as aforesaid". Obviously, there is no question of "majority of partners" in a sole proprietorship CA firm.

Thus, it follows that a company must appoint the proprietor of the so called firm by his name in his individual capacity as its auditor and the auditor's report will have to be signed by the proprietor himself in his own name. - MCA's Circular : No. 8/229/56 PR, dated 20-3-1957.

14.7-7 If authorized by the articles, a company may be a member of another company, but according to section 42 a body corporate cannot be a member of a company which is its holding company and any allotment or transfer of shares in a company to its subsidiary shall be void, except in the case where the subsidiary is concerned as the legal representative of a deceased member of the holding company or where the subsidiary is concerned as a trustee without itself or its holding company being beneficially interested under the trust or interested only by way of security for any money lent if money-lending is its ordinary business. Short of becoming a subsidiary in any way, it would appear that mutual cross holding of shares between two companies is not prohibited under the Act. But, the moment the subsidiary and holding company relationship comes into existence not only the subsidiary company is forbidden to be a member of its holding company, which means that it should immediately divest its holdings, and also it is deprived of its right to vote at meetings of the holding company or of any class of members thereof if it does not divest, and this deprivation cannot be avoided by bringing in a nominee for the subsidiary. These restrictions extend to a holding company even when it is a company limited by guarantee or an unlimited company, the reference to shares held by the subsidiary being construed as including a reference to the interest of its members, whatever the form of that interest, section 42 of the Act. 12.1 Permanent account number [Section 139A]

Section 139A of the Act provides that persons specified therein, who is not allotted permanent account number (PAN), should apply to Assessing Officer for allotment thereof.

In the Memorandum, reasons for amendment are explained as follows:

"In order to use PAN as Unique Entity Number (UEN) for non-individual entities, it is proposed that every person, not being an individual, which enters into a financial transaction of an amount aggregating to two lakh and fifty thousand rupees or more in a financial year shall be required to apply to the Assessing Officer for allotment of PAN.

In order to link the financial transactions with the natural persons, it is also proposed that the managing director, director, partner, trustee, author, founder, karta, chief executive officer, principal officer or office bearer or any person competent to act on behalf of such entities shall also apply to the Assessing Officer for allotment of PAN".

To achieve the above purpose, clauses (v) and (vi) are inserted in section 139A(1) of the Act, by Finance Act, 2018, with effect from April 1, 2018, which read as follows:

"139A(1) Every person,-

(i) to (iv) …; or

(v) being a resident, other than an individual, which enters into a financial transaction of an amount aggregating to two lakh fifty thousand rupees or more in a financial year; or

(vi) who is managing director, director, partner, trustee, author, founder, karta, chief executive officer, principal officer or office bearer of the person referred to in clause (v) or any person competent to act on behalf of the person referred to in clause (v),

and who has not been allotted a permanent account number shall, within such time, as may be prescribed, apply to the Assessing Officer for the allotment of a permanent account number".

Pursuant to amendment, any person (being a resident) other than individual (the entity), who:

enters into a financial transaction of Rs. 2,50,000 or more in the financial year; and

does not possess PAN,

should apply to Assessing Officer for obtaining PAN.

Further, in terms of the amendment, if any person who is a managing director or director or partner or trustee or author or founder or karta or chief executive officer or principal officer or office bearer, of the entity referred above, should also apply to Assessing Officer for obtaining PAN, if he does not have one.

In case of person holding such positions and not having PAN, the requirement would apply only if the entity, in which he is holding the position, enters into a financial transaction in excess of the specified amount during the financial year.

100. (1) Where an offence under this Regulation or the rules has been committed by a company, every person who, at the time the offence was committed, was in charge of, and was responsible to the company for the conduct of the business of the company, as well as the company shall be deemed to be guilty of the offence and shall be liable to be proceeded against and punished accordingly:

Provided that nothing contained in this sub-section shall render any such person liable to any punishment provided in this Regulation if he proves that the offence was committed without his knowledge or that he exercised all due diligence to prevent the commission of such offence.

(2) Notwithstanding anything contained in sub-section (1), where an offence under this Regulation has been committed by a company and it is proved that the offence has been committed with the consent or connivance of, or is attributable to any neglect on the part of any director, manager, secretary or other officer of the company, such director, manager, secretary or other officer shall also be deemed to be guilty of that offence and shall be liable to be proceeded against and punished accordingly.

(3) Where an offence under this Regulation has been committed by a Hindu undivided family, the Karta thereof shall be deemed to be guilty of the offence and shall be liable to be proceeded against and punished accordingly:

Provided that nothing contained in this sub-section shall render the Karta liable to any punishment if he proves that the offence was committed without his knowledge or that he had exercised all due diligence to prevent the commission of such offence:

Provided further that where an offence under this Regulation has been committed by a Hindu undivided family and it is proved that the offence has been committed with the consent or connivance of or is attributable to any neglect on the part of any adult member of the Hindu Undivided Family, such member shall also be deemed to be guilty of that offence and shall be liable to be proceeded against and punished accordingly.

(1) The Chairperson, the whole time members, or any officer as may be nominated by Chairperson by designation or otherwise are hereby severally authorized for and on behalf of the Authority to endorse and transfer negotiable instruments, stock-receipts, stock, debentures, shares, securities, and documents of title to movable and immovable properties standing in the name of or held by the Authority, and to draw, accept and endorse bills of exchange and other instruments in the current and authorized business of the Authority and to sign all other accounts, receipts and documents connected with such business.

(2) Plaints, written statements, complaints, affidavits, petitions and all other documents connected with legal proceedings may be signed and verified on behalf of the authority by any officer authorized by the Chairperson to sign such documents for and on behalf of the authority.

Joint trial of several accused persons

15[41. (1) Any anumber of accused persons may be charged jointly and tried together for an offence averred to have been committed by them collectively.

(2) Any number of accused persons, whether charged, jointly or not, may be tried together for an offence averred to have been committed by one or more of them and to he been abetted by the other or others.

(3) Where the accused persons are so charged under sub-rule (1) or (2) any one or more of them may at the same time be charged with and tried for any other offence averred to have been committed individually or collectively:

Provided that all the said offences are based on the same facts, or form, or are part of, a series of offences of the same or similar character.

(4) In the cases mentioned above, notice of the intention to try the accused persons together shall be given to each of the accused person at the time of his being informed of the charge, and any accused persom may claim, either by notice to the authority covening the court or when arraigned before the court, by notice to the court, that he or some other accused person be tried separately on one or more of the charges included in the charge-sheet, on the ground that the evidence of one or more of the other accused proposed to be tried togheter with him will be material to his defence, or that otherwise he would be prejudiced or embarrassed in his defence, the convening authority or court, if satisfied that the evidence will be material or that the accussed person may be prejudiced or embarrassed in his defence as aforesaid, and if the nature of the charge admits of this, shall allow the calim, and such accussed person, or, as the case may be, the other accussed person or persons whose separate trial has been claimed, shall be tried separately.

(5) Where any such claim as is referred to in sub-rule (4) has been made and disallowed by the authority convening the court, or by the court, the disallowance of such claim shall not be a ground for refusing confirmation of the fining or sentence unless, in the opinion of the confirming authority, substantial miscarriage of justice has occurred by reason of the disallowance of such claim.

(6) Where the proceedings of any court-material in respect of any charge against an accused person are not confirmed on the graound stated in sub-rule (5) such accused person may be tried again on that charge.]

Joint charges

55. (1) Any number of accused may be charged jointly and tried together for an offence averred to have been committed jointly by them.

(2) Any number of accused though not charged jointly may also be tried together for an offence averred to have been committed by one or more of them and abetted by other or others.

(3) Where the accused are so charged under sub-rule (1) or sub-rule (2), any one or more of them may be charged with, and tried for, any other offence with which they could have been charged under sub-rule (1) of rule 53.

that the cheque is drawn by a person and on an account maintained by him with a banker;

(ii)

for the payment of any amount of money to another person from out of that account for the discharge, in whole or in part, of any debt or other liability; and

the said cheque is returned by the bank unpaid, either because of the amount of money standing to the credit of that account is insufficient to honour the cheque or that it exceeds the amount arranged to be paid from that account.

Therefore, a person who is the signatory to the cheque and the cheque is drawn by that person on an account maintained by him and the cheque has been issued for the discharge, in whole or in part, of any debt or other liability and the said cheque has been returned by the bank unpaid, such person can be said to have committed an offence. He submits that in terms of Section 141 of the NI Act, it is only where the offence is committed by a company or a firm or other association of individuals, that the person, who is in-charge of or responsible for the company, is additionally made liable to face prosecution under Section 138 of the NI Act. He submits that as the accused no.1 is only a proprietorship concern, and in terms of Section 138 of the NI Act, only its proprietor and the signatory of the cheque, that is, the accused no.2, can face the prosecution.

He submits that the petitioner had represented herself to be the authorized signatory on behalf of the accused no.1.

6. I have considered the submissions made by the learned counsels for the parties.

7. Section 138 of the NI Act reads as under:

"138. Dishonour of cheque for insufficiency, etc., of funds in the account.— Where any cheque drawn by a person on an account maintained by him with a banker for payment of any amount of money to another person from out of that account for the discharge, in whole or in part, of any debt or other liability, is returned by the bank unpaid, either because of the amount of money standing to the credit of that account is insufficient to honour the cheque or that it exceeds the amount arranged to be paid from that account by an agreement made with that bank, such person shall be deemed to have committed an offence and shall, without prejudice to any other provision of this Act, be punished with imprisonment for a term which may be extended to two years, or with fine which may extend to twice the amount of the cheque, or with both:

Provided that nothing contained in this section shall apply unless--

(a)

the cheque has been presented to the bank within a period of six months from the date on which it is drawn or within the period of its validity, whichever is earlier;

(b)

the payee or the holder in due course of the cheque, as the case may be, makes a demand for the payment of the said amount of money by giving a notice; in writing, to the drawer of the cheque, within thirty days of the receipt of information by him from the bank regarding the return of the cheque as unpaid; and

(c)

the drawer of such cheque fails to make the payment of the said amount of money to the payee or, as the case may be, to the holder in due course of the cheque, within fifteen days of the receipt of the said notice.

Explanation.— For the purposes of this section, "debt of other liability" means a legally enforceable debt or other liability. "

(Emphasis supplied)

Since, this expression has not been defined, the same has to be interpreted ejusdem generis having regard to the purpose of the principle of vicarious liability incorporated in section 141. The terms "complaint", "persons" "association of persons" "company" and "directors" have been explained by this Court in Raghu Lakshminarayanan v. Fine Tubes, (2007) 5 SCC 103." 11. If the cheque in question is returned unpaid on account of the conditions mentioned under section 138 of the Act, such person alone is liable to be prosecuted for the offence under section 138 of the Act. The same is apparent from the phraseology '…such person shall be deemed to have committed the offence…' used in section 138 of the Act. Proceedings and prosecution can only continue against the drawer of the cheque as the penal provisions have to be strictly construed as they are. It is, thus, that nobody barring the drawer of the cheque can be held criminally liable otherwise. It is trite law that penal provisions should be construed strictly and the emphasis is on the words, 'such person' which relates to the person, who has drawn the cheque in favour of the payee.

12. Reliance in this regard be placed upon Alka Khandu Avhad v. Amar Syamprasad Mishra [2021] 128 taxmann.com 252/167 SCL 134 (SC)/4 SCC 675, wherein the Hon'ble Supreme Court, after dealing with similar facts, held as under:-

"9. On a fair reading of section 138 of the NI Act, before a person can be prosecuted, the following conditions are required to be satisfied: 9.1. That the cheque in drawn by a person and on an account maintained by him with a banker.

9.2 For the payment of any amount of money to another person from out of that account for the discharge, in whole or in part, of any debt or other liability.

9.3 The said cheque is returned by the bank unpaid, either because of the amount of money standing to the credit of that account is insufficient to honour the cheque or that it exceeds the amount arranged to be paid from that accused.

10. Therefore, a person who is the signatory to the cheque and the cheque is drawn by that person on an account maintained by him and the cheque has been issued for the discharge, in whole or in part, of any debt or other liability and the said cheque has been returned by the bank unpaid, such person can be said to have committed an offence. Section 138 of the NI Act does not speak about the joint liability. Even in case of a joint liability, in case of individual persons, a person other than a person who has drawn the cheque on an account maintained by him, cannot be prosecuted for the offence under section 138 of the NI Act. A person might have been jointly liable to pay the debt, but if such a person who might have been liable to pay the debt jointly, cannot be prosecuted unless the bank account is jointly maintained and that he was a signatory to the cheque."

13. In view of the aforesaid, the present petition is allowed and the Complaint Case No. 4061/2020, CC NI ACT 118/2021 dated 11-12-2020 titled "Ajay Chanana (supra).", filed by the respondent/complainant against the petitioner and the other accused under section 138 of the Act, pending before the learned Metropolitan Magistrate (NI Act), Rohini Courts, Delhi, is quashed qua the accused no. 2 therein i.e. the petitioner herein.

14. Accordingly, the present petition alongwith the application, if any, is disposed of in the above terms.
