The Supreme Court held that, since Axis Bank had realised substantial sale proceeds and was now impleaded before the Court, it was necessary for the High Court to first examine the inter se priority of charges between EPFO and the secured creditors in accordance with section 11(2) of the PF Act and section 35 of the SARFAESI Act. Accordingly, the impugned order was set aside and the matter was remanded to the High Court for fresh adjudication after impleading Axis Bank and affording due opportunity of hearing to all parties.

9. Notice issued to partners is deemed notice to firm and partners are jointly and severally liable u/s 138 of NI Act

Dhanasingh Prabhu v. Chandrasekar [2025] 176 taxmann.com 443 (SC)

In the present case, the Supreme Court examined whether a complaint under section 138 read with section 141 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881, is maintainable against partners of a partnership firm when the statutory notice was issued only to the partners and not separately to the firm, and the firm itself was not initially named as an accused. The appellant-complainant had advanced a loan to the respondents, who were partners of a firm, and a cheque issued from the firm's account towards discharge of the debt was dishonoured. The High Court had quashed the complaint on the ground that the partnership firm was neither served with statutory notice nor made a party to the proceedings, and therefore the requirements of section 141 were not satisfied. Reversing the High Court's view, the Supreme Court held that a partnership firm is not a separate juristic entity distinct from its partners but only a compendious name for the partners, who are jointly and severally liable for the acts of the firm. It was observed that, unlike a company where liability of directors is vicarious, the liability of partners is direct and joint. The Court further held that even in the absence of the firm being named as an accused, proceedings against the partners are maintainable, and any such defect is curable by permitting the firm to be **impleaded** at a later stage. Accordingly, the Supreme Court set aside the impugned order of the High Court and restored the complaint.

5.22D-7h MENS REA AND VICARIOUS AND STRICT LIABILITY - It is well-settled that the strict criminal liability of companies, partnership firms, or legal persons is in a class by itself and poses problems peculiar to them. Since a legal person is a fiction of the law and does not exist in actuality, the issue of vicarious liability of the office bearers through whom a company or a partnership firm or association of persons must necessarily act, comes to the fore.1 Strict vicarious liability is somewhat an exception to the general rule of direct personal culpability and is a modern development through statutory provisions. That there can be such vicarious criminal liability by legislative mandate is no longer in dispute. Nevertheless steeped as we are in the basic principles of criminal jurisprudence that mens rea must be an ingredient of an offence and both the act and intent must concur to constitute a crime, it requires some effort to accept whole-heartedly the legislative mandate of vicarious criminality even in the absence of either of the aforesaid ingredients.

Vicarious liability ‘is a necessary doctrine for the proper enforcement of much modern legislation—but it is not one to be extended.1 Whether one person will be held responsible for the acts of another is a matter of construction in each case. Regard must be had to the object of the statute, the words used, the nature of the duty laid down, the person upon whom it is imposed, the person by whom it would in ordinary circumstances be performed and the person upon whom the penalty is imposed.2

If the doctrine of vicarious liability is held to apply, a person subject to a statutory duty to which a penal sanction is attached who chooses to delegate the performance of that duty to another person (usually but not necessarily an employee), will nevertheless be himself liable for breaches of that duty by his delegate. In many cases his delegate’s ‘knowledge’ will be imputed to him.3

That there can be such vicarious criminal liability by legislative mandate is no longer in dispute. Nevertheless steeped as we are in the basic principles of criminal jurisprudence that mens rea must be an ingredient of an offence and both the act and intent must concur to constitute a crime, it requires some effort to accept whole-heartedly the legislative mandate of vicarious criminality even in the absence of either of the aforesaid ingredients.

CONCEPT OF 'ARTIFICIAL PERSON' Every human being is a person in the eye of law. When a person is ordinarily understood to be a natural person, it only means a human being. But a person is also artificially created and recognised in law as such. Such persons are called in different names, such as "juristic person", "juridical person", "legal entity" etc., In some countries, even human beings were not treated as persons in law, for example, in Roman Law, a slave was not a person and he had no right to a family. In other words, he was treated like an animal. In French colonies also, before the slavery was abolished, the slaves were not treated as the legal persons. They were given legal status of person only through a statute during the later period. With the development of Society, co-operation among various sections of people became absolutely necessary for the well being of the humanity. Therefore, it became a natural necessity for the formation of institutions like the corporations and companies, etc. These institutions like corporations, companies etc., were given legal status of a person. By virtue of the statutory recognition, these artificial persons came to own property and enjoy various statutory rights and even some constitutional rights. As the society started growing more and more, there came more number of fictional personalities viz., juristic persons in different names enjoying different kinds of rights and liabilities as recognized under the various laws. [Para 20]

The term 'person' employed in section 138 of the N.I. Act has not been defined in the Act. [Para 23]

Section 3(42) of the General Clauses Act, 1897, is precisely in pari materia to section 11 of IPC. The definition of the term 'person' made both in section 3(42) of the General Clauses Act and section 11 of IPC is not exhaustive. It is hardly a definition. It is undoubtedly inclusive. The indication of the intention of the Legislature is to give wider sense so as to mean not only natural persons but to include artificial or juridical persons also, provided, such artificial or juridical person is a legal entity. For instance, an idol is a juridical person capable of owning property and is, therefore, a "person". But, a proprietary concern is not a legal entity and so, it is not a person in terms of section 11 of IPC. Similarly, a Hindu Undivided Family is a legal entity capable of owning property and, therefore, undoubtedly, such a HUF is a person as defined in section 3(42) of the General Clauses Act and section 11 of IPC. Therefore, for an offence committed by a HUF punishable under section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, the HUF can be prosecuted and punished, but, at the same time, since, the HUF is an artificial person, sentence of imprisonment can not be imposed on the HUF. For an offence committed by an artificial /juridical person, unless it is specifically provided in the statute, every individual who is a component of the artificial or juridical person cannot be held vicariously liable for punishment; it is only the artificial or juridical person who is liable for punishment. Complainant/Payee has no onus to prove the financial capacity at the threshold.

In proceedings under Section 138 of the NI Act, the Complainant is not required to establish their financial capacity at the initial stage. Once the drawer admits to signing the cheque, the statutory presumption under Sections 118 and 139 of the NI Act operates in favour of the Complainant, presuming the existence of a legally enforceable debt. The onus is not on the Complainant at the threshold to prove their financial wherewithal to make the payment in discharge of which the cheque was allegedly issued. Only if an objection is specifically raised in the reply notice or any pleading that the Complainant lacked the financial position to advance the claimed loan amount, would the Complainant be required to bring cogent material indicating financial capacity and actual advancement of the loan.

Recently, in Ashok Singh v. State of Uttar Pradesh25, the Appellant/Complainant had advanced a loan to the Accused, who in discharge of the debt, issued a cheque. When presented, the cheque was dishonoured with the endorsement "payment stopped by drawer." A legal notice was sent within, but the Accused neither replied nor made payment. The Trial Court and Appellate Court convicted the Accused under Section 138 of the NI Act after finding the debt legally enforceable. However, the High Court reversed this decision, holding that the Complainant failed to prove his case because he did not disclose bank account details, the date of withdrawal, or the specific date when the cheque was obtained. The Supreme Court found this approach fundamentally erroneous. The Accused had admitted signing the cheque but claimed it was lost, though the intimation about the lost cheque was suspiciously sent to the police only a year after the cheque was presented. Further, the Accused had not raised the defence of the Complainant's lack of financial capacity in his reply notice. In fact, no reply was given to the statutory notice at all.

The primary liability under Section 138 is on the drawer, who must ensure that there are adequate funds in the account at the time the cheque is presented. Additionally, the offence under Section 138 is not complete until a demand notice is served on the drawer, emphasizing the drawer's responsibility. The drawer is considered the principal offender if the cheque is returned unpaid, subject to the fulfilment of the necessary conditions before and after the cheque is dishonoured.

15.2. General Rule of Criminal Liability The High Court noted the general rule against vicarious liability in criminal cases, where individuals are typically not held criminally liable for acts committed by others. However, this principle is subject to exceptions created by specific statutory provisions extending liability to additional parties. Section 141, NI Act is one such provision that extends criminal liability for dishonour of a cheque committed by a company to its officers. The Court emphasized that liability under Section 141 arises from the conduct, act, or omission of the person involved, not merely their position in the company. The provision establishes vicarious liability for officers of the company, such as signatories of the cheque, managing directors, or those in charge of its affairs, by legal fiction. Thus, while the drawer of the cheque remains primarily liable, Section 141 broadens liability to include others associated with the company's management, ensuring accountability beyond the drawer alone.

15.3. Authorised signatory cannot be equated to the company

Further, the High Court delved into the distinction between legal entities and individuals acting as authorized signatories within the framework of the NI Act. The Court observed that while individuals may sign cheques as authorized representatives of companies, they do not assume legal identity of the company itself. It clarified that a legal entity, such as a corporation or company, is an artificial creation of the law endowed with rights, duties, and the capacity to sue and be sued independently of the individuals who manage or represent it. The Court emphasized that an authorized signatory, despite acting on behalf of a company, remains distinct as an individual under the law. This distinction is crucial as it clarifies that the actions and obligations undertaken by an authorized signatory are attributable to the company they represent, but do not merge their legal status with that of the company itself. Thus, while an authorized signatory may bind the company through their actions, they do not transform into a legal entity in the eyes of law.

15.4. Interpretation of the Section 143-A and the legislative intent

Moreover, the High Court highlighted the principle of statutory interpretation, particularly in relation to Sections 143A and 148 of the NI Act, which are under consideration. It discussed the dichotomy between interpreting statutes based on their plain language versus applying purposive construction. According to the Court, when the statutory language is clear and unambiguous, it speaks for itself, and there is no need for further interpretation. The natural and ordinary meaning of words should prevail unless the legal context necessitates a different interpretation to align with the legislative intent or to avoid absurd outcomes.

15.4.1. The Court further elucidated that legislative intent should guide the interpretation of statutes, with all parts of a statute considered together to discern the overall purpose. It stressed that words and phrases within a statute must be construed in context, taking into account the legislative objectives and the broader framework of the law. This holistic approach ensures that statutory interpretation remains faithful to the lawmakers' intentions and avoids inconsistencies or injustices that may arise from a literal reading of isolated provisions.

15.4.2. The High Court emphasized that Section 143A should be interpreted plainly, without resorting to other rules of interpretation. It asserted that the term 'drawer' in Section 143A has a clear and unambiguous meaning, referring specifically to the person who issues the cheque. Referring to the Statement of Objects and Purposes of the Negotiable Instruments (Amendment) Act, 2018, the High Court noted that the purpose of Section 143A is to provide interim relief to payees of dishonoured cheques by imposing liability on the drawer. This, according to the High Court, aligns with the legislative intent to curb frivolous litigations and expedite resolution of cheque dishonour cases.

15.4.3. The High Court rejected the inclusion of authorized signatories within the definition of 'drawer'. It pointed out that the legislature's choice of words in Section 143A specifically targets the drawer of the cheque, whether an individual or a company, and does not extend liability to authorized signatories. Drawing from established legal precedents, the High Court underscored that the term 'drawer' carries a specific legal meaning within the NI Act. It highlighted the cases where Courts consistently interpreted 'drawer' to refer strictly to the issuer of the cheque, reinforcing its decision to uphold this interpretation. 1. Introduction

The decision of the Hon’ble Supreme Court in Saroj Pandey v. Govt. Of Nct Of Delhi [2026] 185 taxmann.com 280 (SC) is a significant pronouncement on the nuanced issue of liability of directors under fiscal and penal laws. At a time when regulatory enforcement is becoming increasingly stringent, the judgment provides much-needed clarity on the extent to which individuals occupying managerial positions can be fastened with liability for acts of a company.

The judgment lays down the boundaries to the extent to which directors are liable and more specifically when they are not liable for the act of the Company being a separate legal entity. Though rendered in the context of Section 138 and 141 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 (“N.I. Act”), commonly associated with cheque dishonour cases, the underlying reasoning transcends the statute. The principles articulated by the Court are of wider relevance and have direct bearing on fiscal statutes, including the CGST Act, where similar provisions impose vicarious liability.

2. Concept of Separate Legal Entity and Role of Directors

The doctrine of separate legal entity, firmly embedded in company law jurisprudence since the landmark decision of the House of Lords in Salomon v. Salomon (1897) A.C. 22) followed by the Indian Supreme Court in a plethora of judgements including in the famous Vodafone International Holdings B.V. v. Union of India [2012] 17 taxmann.com 202 (SC)/[2012] 204 Taxman 408 (SC)/[2012] 341 ITR 1 (SC), recognises a company as a juristic person distinct from its shareholders and directors. This principle has significant implications in fiscal jurisprudence as well, where the company is treated as an independent taxable entity, capable of owning property, incurring liabilities, and being assessed in its own name. Consequently, tax obligations—whether under direct or indirect tax regimes—are ordinarily fastened upon the company itself, and not upon those who manage its affairs. The sanctity of this principle ensures commercial certainty and facilitates risk-taking by insulating individuals from personal exposure arising out of corporate operations.

However, the role of directors introduces a nuanced dimension to this doctrine. While directors act as the “directing mind and will” of the company, their liability in tax matters is not automatic but arises only in specific statutory or exceptional circumstances. Tax statutes, including provisions under the Income-tax Act and GST laws, carve out limited situations where directors may be held personally liable—typically where there is evidence of fraud, wilful default, misfeasance, or where statutory dues cannot be recovered from the company. Even in such cases, the law requires strict compliance with conditions precedent before piercing the corporate veil, thereby maintaining a careful balance between accountability and the foundational principle of separate legal personality.

Judicial trends have consistently underscored that lifting the corporate veil is an exception rather than the rule, to be invoked sparingly and only where the corporate form is abused to evade tax or perpetrate illegality. Courts have cautioned against a routine attribution of liability to directors merely on account of their position, emphasising that vicarious liability must be expressly provided by statute and cannot be inferred. Thus, while directors play a central role in corporate governance and decision-making, their personal exposure in tax matters remains circumscribed, reinforcing that the company—being a separate legal entity—continues to bear primary responsibility for its fiscal obligations.

3. Factual Background

Coming to the case in hand, the appellant was one of the directors of the accused company which had issued cheques towards payment for supply of goods. The cheques were dishonoured upon presentation, following which statutory notice was issued and criminal proceedings were initiated. The director was arrayed as an accused primarily on the ground that she had signed a Board Resolution, which, according to the complainant, demonstrated her involvement in the affairs of the company. This reasoning found favour both with the Magistrate and the High Court, leading to the continuation of proceedings against her.

4. Provision Relating to Prosecution of Director

Section 141 of the N.I. Act, provides the statutory framework for fastening vicarious liability upon directors and officers of a company. The provision makes it clear that liability is not automatic but conditional upon the person being “in charge of” and “responsible to” the company for the conduct of its business at the relevant time. The provisos further carve out safeguards, including absence of knowledge and exercise of due diligence.

A striking feature of the present discussion is the similarity between Section 141 of the N.I. Act and Section 137 of the CGST Act. Both provisions employ nearly identical language in attributing liability to persons in charge of and responsible for the conduct of business, while also recognising defences based on lack of knowledge and due diligence.

Obligation of the Drawer of the Cheque

The High Court observed that under section 7 of the NI Act, the maker of a bill of exchange or cheque is termed the drawer, and the person directed to pay is called the drawee. The drawer is the individual who issues the cheque. sections 138, 143A, and 148 of the NI Act fall under Chapter XVII, which pertains to penalties for the dishonour of certain cheques due to insufficient funds. A plain reading of section 138 highlights that the drawer must have an account with sufficient funds to cover the cheque. The primary liability under section 138 is on the drawer, who must ensure that there are adequate funds in the account at the time the cheque is presented. Additionally, the offence under section 138 is not complete until a demand notice is served on the drawer, emphasizing the drawer's responsibility. The drawer is considered the principal offender if the cheque is returned unpaid, subject to the fulfilment of the necessary conditions before and after the cheque is dishonoured. [Para 15.1]

General Rule of Criminal Liability

The High Court noted the general rule against vicarious liability in criminal cases, where individuals are typically not held criminally liable for acts committed by others. However, this principle is subject to exceptions created by specific statutory provisions extending liability to additional parties. Section 141, NI Act is one such provision that extends criminal liability for dishonour of a cheque committed by a company to its officers. The Court emphasized that liability under section 141 arises from the conduct, act, or omission of the person involved, not merely their position in the company. The provision establishes vicarious liability for officers of the company, such as signatories of the cheque, managing directors, or those in charge of its affairs, by legal fiction. Thus, while the drawer of the cheque remains primarily liable, section 141 broadens liability to include others associated with the company's management, ensuring accountability beyond the drawer alone. [Para 15.2]

Authorised signatory cannot be equated to the company

Further, the High Court delved into the distinction between legal entities and individuals acting as authorized signatories within the framework of the NI Act. The Court observed that while individuals may sign cheques as authorized representatives of companies, they do not assume legal identity of the company itself. It clarified that a legal entity, such as a corporation or company, is an artificial creation of the law endowed with rights, duties, and the capacity to sue and be sued independently of the individuals who manage or represent it. The Court emphasized that an authorized signatory, despite acting on behalf of a company, remains distinct as an individual under the law. This distinction is crucial as it clarifies that the actions and obligations undertaken by an authorized signatory are attributable to the company they represent, but do not merge their legal status with that of the company itself. Thus, while an authorized signatory may bind the company through their actions, they do not transform into a legal entity in the eyes of law. [Para 15.3]

Interpretation of the section 143A and the legislative intent

Moreover, the High Court highlighted the principle of statutory interpretation, particularly in relation to sections 143A and 148 of the NI Act, which are under consideration. It discussed the dichotomy between interpreting statutes based on their plain language versus applying purposive construction. According to the Court, when the statutory language is clear and unambiguous, it speaks for itself, and there is no need for further interpretation. The natural and ordinary meaning of words should prevail unless the legal context necessitates a different interpretation to align with the legislative intent or to avoid absurd outcomes. [Para 15.4]

The Court further elucidated that legislative intent should guide the interpretation of statutes, with all parts of a statute considered together to discern the overall purpose. It stressed that words and phrases within a statute must be construed in context, taking into account the legislative objectives and the broader framework of the law. This holistic approach ensures that statutory interpretation remains faithful to the lawmakers' intentions and avoids inconsistencies or injustices that may arise from a literal reading of isolated provisions. [Para 15.4.1]

The High Court emphasized that section 143A should be interpreted plainly, without resorting to other rules of interpretation. It asserted that the term 'drawer' in section 143A has a clear and unambiguous meaning, referring specifically to the person who issues the cheque. Referring to the Statement of Objects and Purposes of the Negotiable Instruments (Amendment) Act, 2018, the High Court noted that the purpose of section 143A is to provide interim relief to payees of dishonoured cheques by imposing liability on the drawer. This, according to the High Court, aligns with the legislative intent to curb frivolous litigations and expedite resolution of cheque dishonour cases. [Para 15.4.2]

For this purpose, seniority shall be determined by the order in which the names stand in the register of members.

u Reg. 92. Any one of two or more joint holders of a share may give effectual receipts for any dividends, bonuses or other moneys payable in respect of such share.

14.7-6a Act provisions on joint-holding of shares - Section 169(8) provides that where two or more persons hold any share or interest in a company jointly, a requisition, or a notice calling a (general) meeting, signed by one or some only of them shall have the same force and effect as if it had been signed by all of them. Similarly, section 399(2) provides that joint-holders count as one member. As regards payment of dividends, section 205(5)(b) provides that in the case of joint shareholders it may be paid to that one of the shareholders first named in the register of members or to such person and to such address as the joint shareholders may in writing direct.

Company as a member [Section 42]

14.7-7 If authorized by the articles, a company may be a member of another company, but according to section 42 a body corporate cannot be a member of a company which is its holding company and any allotment or transfer of shares in a company to its subsidiary shall be void, except in the case where the subsidiary is concerned as the legal representative of a deceased member of the holding company or where the subsidiary is concerned as a trustee without itself or its holding company being beneficially interested under the trust or interested only by way of security for any money lent if money-lending is its ordinary business. Short of becoming a subsidiary in any way, it would appear that mutual cross holding of shares between two companies is not prohibited under the Act. But, the moment the subsidiary and holding company relationship comes into existence not only the subsidiary company is forbidden to be a member of its holding company, which means that it should immediately divest its holdings, and also it is deprived of its right to vote at meetings of the holding company or of any class of members thereof if it does not divest, and this deprivation cannot be avoided by bringing in a nominee for the subsidiary. These restrictions extend to a holding company even when it is a company limited by guarantee or an unlimited company, the reference to shares held by the subsidiary being construed as including a reference to the interest of its members, whatever the form of that interest, section 42 of the Act. However, in the case of amalgamation, section 42 has no application, Himachal Telematics v. Himachal Futuristic Communications Ltd. [1996] 8 SCL 172 (Delhi).

Foreign company or body corporate as a member

14.7-8 The eligibility and extent of holding capital by such bodies in Indian companies is controlled by the RBI/Ministry of Finance Schemes announced from time to time known as ‘caps’ under various sectoral or other programmes of foreign investment in India forming the Government Policy. The voting rights of such bodies are ordinarily governed by the Act provisions, but those may be substantially modified by the rules of the Schemes and ‘caps’: CDS Financial Services (Mauritius) Ltd. v. BPL Communications Ltd. [2004] Comp. Cas. 374/56 SCL 665 (Bom.).

JOINT OWNERSHIP

Jointly owned property is any property held in the names of two or more parties. The PBPT Act, 1988 does not cover all types of joint ownership as exception to benami transaction. The section 2(9)(A)(iv) refers to specified transactions between two or more parties as exception to benami transaction. There is a rider in section 2(9)(A)(iv) to claim exclusion from benami transaction. This is only in respect of property jointly held by a person in the names of his brother, sister or lineal ascendant and lineal descendants. In order to come out of the ambit of benami transaction, the individual must be a joint owner in the document evidencing the transaction of the property along with others specified persons mentioned in this section and the consideration must flow out of the known sources of the individual. If the property is not in joint ownership as specified in the Benami Act, then it would fall within the definition of benami Transaction and all consequences would follow. Joint ownership must be evidenced by a document. Mere oral claim would not suffice.

As per Financial dictionary (www.thefreedictionary.com/account) account could mean:

"Account

An agreement between an institution and a person, or another institution, whereby the first institution agrees to hold money and/or other assets on behalf of the second. What the holder may do with those assets depends upon the nature of the account. In a checking account and a savings account, a bank holds money for the client and pays it (them or he/she) a certain percentage in interest. This payment gives the bank the right to lend the money to other clients or invest it within the confines of law and banking regulation. However, the client has the right to withdraw the total amount of money on demand. In a brokerage account, a broker holds money and securities for the client and makes transactions with them at the client's request. In exchange, the broker charges commissions for the transactions."

As per legal dictionary (www.thefreedictionary.com) account could mean "a written list of transactions, noting money owed and money paid; a detailed statement of mutual demands arising out of contract or a fiduciary relationship".

In view of the above, it appears, account, in the context, means an agreement between a financial institution or bank and the holder of an account where the institution or bank agrees to hold money or other asset (say, dematerialised account for shares, commodities, gold, silver, etc.) on behalf of account holder. Its location can be determined on the basis of circulars, etc., discussed (see para 10.1.1c).

Signing authority in any account implies that, pursuant to a contract or otherwise, a person is empowered to operate the account under his signature.

Thus, any person pursuant to the contract or otherwise who has a power to operate any account, as explained above, being a signing authority, would be obliged to file return of income, if he is not otherwise required to furnish return under section 139(1). WHETHER DEDUCTION IS AVAILABLE IF NEW HOUSE PURCHASED IN JOINT NAMES OF ASSESSEE AND HIS WIFE?

In CIT v. Ravinder Kumar Arora [2011] 15 taxmann.com 307/203 Taxman 289 (Delhi - Trib.), it was held that while section 54F mandates that the house should be purchased by the assessee, it does not stipulate that the house should be purchased in the name of the assessee only. Therefore, deduction can neither by denied nor restricted to 50% where assessee purchases new house jointly in the name of his wife. Merely because he has included the name of his wife and the property purchased in the joint names would not make any difference. Such a conduct has to be, rather, encouraged which gives empowerment to women. There are various schemes floated by the Government itself permitting joint ownership with wife.

35.5

Evidence by documents

Provisions regarding documentary evidence are as follows.

Presumption regarding Documents seized from a person - Any document seized from a person shall be presumed to be true about the contents therein. Signature and other part of hand written document on such seized document, purporting to have been of a person or reasonably assumed to be of that person shall be presumed to be of that person. If such person claims that the document is not true or not signed by him, the burden of proof is on him [section 139(i) of Customs Act].

Presumption regarding documents received from place outside India - If any document is received from a place out of India in the course of investigation, it will be presumed that signature and other part of hand written document on such seized document, purporting to have been of a person or reasonably assumed to be of that person shall be presumed to be of that person. However, in case of such documents, there is no presumption that the contents are true. In other words, in case of documents obtained from abroad, prosecution has to prove that the contents are true, though they don't have to prove that the signature or hand-writing is of that person only, who is purported to have signed it or written it [section 139(ii) & (c) of Customs Act].

Meaning of 'document' for section 139 of Customs Act - Section 139 of Customs Act provides for presumptions of documents in certain cases. For purposes of section 139, 'document' includes inventories, photographs and lists certified by Magistrate under section 110(1C) or by Commissioner (Appeals) under section 110(1D) of Customs Act - Explanation to section 139 of Customs Act [The words in italics inserted w.e.f. 28-3-2021].

Other documents admissible - (a) A document which is required by law to be stamped, will be admissible as evidence even if it is not duly stamped. [Section 139(b) of Customs Act] (b) Micro film or Photostat/Xerox copy of document or reproduction of image is admissible, without further proof of original [Section 138C(1) of Customs Act].

In Kirpal Castings v. CCE 1999(108) ELT 552 (CEGAT), it was held that once photostat copies are made available to appellant, giving of original is not required.

Charge of under-valuation on basis of unsigned Xerox copies of documents is not sustainable - CC v. Bussa Overseas (2007) 216 ELT 659 (SC).

Fax letters are deemed to be 'documents' without proof of evidence, particularly when genuineness is acknowledged and corroborated by other evidence - Dungarmal Pruthviraj v. CC (2011) 272 ELT 606 (CESTAT).

Computer printouts - Statement printed by Computer is admissible if (a) Computer printout was produced during the period when the computer was used for storing and processing the information (b) the information contained in the statement was regularly supplied to computer during the period (c) computer was operating properly during the period or breakdowns were not significant to affect accuracy of documents (d) the print out is reproduced in ordinary course of activities. [Section 138C(2) of Customs Act].

The computer print outs will be allowed as evidence even if multiple computers or different computers or different combinations of computers were used. A statement or a certificate given by a responsible person to the best of his knowledge and belief identifying the statement or describing its contents or giving particulars of computers used in production of documents shall be evidence of any matter contained in the certificate.

39.1

Signing of audit reports

Section 145 of the 2013 Act makes the following provisions signing of audit report are as under:—

Only the person appointed as an auditor of the company shall sign the auditor's report or sign or certify any other document of the company in accordance with the provisions of section 141(2). [Section 145, first limb]

If a firm including a LLP is appointed as an auditor of a company, only the partners who are Chartered Accountants in practice shall be authorised to act and sign on behalf of the firm. [Section 141(2)]

39.1-1 Signing auditors' report in firms name Whether legally valid

As section 229 of the 1956 Act [corresponding to section 141(2) of the 2013 Act] clearly provides that if a firm of chartered accountants is appointed as auditor, only a partner in the firm [who is a CA] may sign the auditor's report or sign or authenticate any other document required by law to be signed or authenticated by the auditor, the practice of merely affixing the "firm name" on the audit report or such other document is not correct in the eye of law. The partner concerned should invariably sign in his own hand for and on behalf of the firm appointed to audit a company's accounts. - MCA's Circular Letter : No. 26/72 [F. No. 14/12/72 CL-V], dated 29-7-1972.

Possession involves animus

Possession involves animus and corpus. If there is animus, it is immaterial whether the possession is actual or constructive or physical or mediate or immediate or direct or indirect or exclusive, joint or concurrent (see Narendra Nath Mozumdar v. State AIR 1951 Cal. 140). When a property is in the possession of a person’s wife, clerk or servant of that person, it is in the person’s possession (section 27 of the Indian Penal Code)

12.1 Permanent account number [Section 139A]

Section 139A of the Act provides that persons specified therein, who is not allotted permanent account number (PAN), should apply to Assessing Officer for allotment thereof.

In the Memorandum, reasons for amendment are explained as follows:

"In order to use PAN as Unique Entity Number (UEN) for non-individual entities, it is proposed that every person, not being an individual, which enters into a financial transaction of an amount aggregating to two lakh and fifty thousand rupees or more in a financial year shall be required to apply to the Assessing Officer for allotment of PAN.

In order to link the financial transactions with the natural persons, it is also proposed that the managing director, director, partner, trustee, author, founder, karta, chief executive officer, principal officer or office bearer or any person competent to act on behalf of such entities shall also apply to the Assessing Officer for allotment of PAN".

To achieve the above purpose, clauses (v) and (vi) are inserted in section 139A(1) of the Act, by Finance Act, 2018, with effect from April 1, 2018, which read as follows:

"139A(1) Every person,-

(i) to (iv) …; or

(v) being a resident, other than an individual, which enters into a financial transaction of an amount aggregating to two lakh fifty thousand rupees or more in a financial year; or

(vi) who is managing director, director, partner, trustee, author, founder, karta, chief executive officer, principal officer or office bearer of the person referred to in clause (v) or any person competent to act on behalf of the person referred to in clause (v),

and who has not been allotted a permanent account number shall, within such time, as may be prescribed, apply to the Assessing Officer for the allotment of a permanent account number".

Pursuant to amendment, any person (being a resident) other than individual (the entity), who:

enters into a financial transaction of Rs. 2,50,000 or more in the financial year; and

does not possess PAN,

should apply to Assessing Officer for obtaining PAN.

Further, in terms of the amendment, if any person who is a managing director or director or partner or trustee or author or founder or karta or chief executive officer or principal officer or office bearer, of the entity referred above, should also apply to Assessing Officer for obtaining PAN, if he does not have one.

In case of person holding such positions and not having PAN, the requirement would apply only if the entity, in which he is holding the position, enters into a financial transaction in excess of the specified amount during the financial year.

18.17-3 Directors etc. liable only if offense committed with their connivance or due to their negligence

As per clause (2) of the section (as contained in many of the Acts), in case of other directors, manager and Secretary, they are held guilty only when it is proved that the offence was committed with their consent/connivance or is attributable to their negligence, i.e. the burden of proof is on prosecution (complainant) to allege and prove that the offence was committed with their consent/connivance or negligence.

In SMS Pharmaceuticals Ltd. v. Neeta Bhalla (2005) 8 SCC 89 = 148 Taxman 128 = 63 SCL 93 (SC 3 member bench), it has been held that simply being a director in a company, one is not supposed to be in-charge of affairs of the company. A director may not know anything about day-to-day functioning of a company. As a director, he may be attending meetings of Board where usually they decide policy matters and guide the course of business of a company. One or two directors may be made responsible for day-to-day functions of the company by a resolution. - - However, in case of MD or JMD, by virtue of the office they hold as Managing Director or Joint Managing Director, these persons are in charge of and responsible for the conduct of business of the company. In order to escape liability, they have to prove that when the offense was committed, they had no knowledge of the offense or that they exercised all due diligence to prevent commission of the offense [decision in case of bouncing of cheque under Negotiable Instruments Act, but principle should apply in all cases].

It is trite law that wherever a legal fiction of the principle of vicarious liability is attracted, and a person otherwise not personally involved in the commission of an offense is made liable for the same, it has to be specifically provided in the statute concerned - Maharashtra State Electricity Board v. Datar Switchgear Ltd. (2010) 10 SCC 479 = 105 SCL 253 = 8 taxmann.com 223 = 159 Comp Cas 545 (SC).

In State of Haryana v. Brij Lal Mittal (1998) 93 Comp Cas 329 (SC) = (1998) 5 SCC 343 = AIR 1998 SC 2327 = 1998 AIR SCW 2240, (matter under Drugs & Cosmetics Act), it was held that vicarious liability of a person for an offence of company arises only if at the material time he was in charge of and was also responsible to the company for conduct of its business. Simply because a person is a director does not mean that both these requirements are fulfilled. If there is not even allegation that the director was in charge and responsible to the company, he cannot be prosecuted. - following Delhi Municipal Corporation v. Ram Kishan Rothgi (1983) 1 SCC 1 = AIR 1983 SC 67. - same view in Shyam Sunder v. State of Haryana AIR 1989 SC 1982 = (1989) 4 SCC 630 = 67 Comp Cas 1 (SC), where it was held that all directors cannot be held responsible. - followed in D G Jhaver v. State of Punjab (1997) 24 CLA 133 (P&H), where in a case under Insecticides Act, it was held that complaint should state that the director was in charge and responsible to company - same view in Pepsico India Holdings P Ltd. v. Food Inspector (2011) 1 SCC 176 (SC 3 member bench).

In Sunil Bharti Mittal v. Central Bureau of Investigation (2015) 4 SCC 609 (SC 3 member bench), it has been held that director can be held vicariously liable only if (a) there is sufficient incriminating evidence against him coupled with criminal intent or (b) statutory regime attracts doctrine of vicarious liability.

15.31

Money belongs to Pvt. Co. of which assessee and husband the only directors

Where assessee was a director along with her husband of a private limited company and money found in a search at her premises was claimed to have been accounted for in the books of account of above company, explanation of assessee was reasonable and said amount could not be treated as her income. It was not abnormal in the case of a private limited company where the only directors happen to be husband and wife and carrying on the business as was done by them at the relevant period, i.e., that of sending persons abroad, to have cash of the private limited company with the individual directors. This was perfectly normal and stood to reason. Thus, the money in question belonged to a private limited company and not to the assessee-individual. - Mrs. K.S. Mohammed v. ITO [1989] 33 TTJ (Bom.) 468

Thus, a joint holder is also a member. He has his own rights as a member - e.g. he can inspect register of members, attend general meeting, sign for a requisition meeting, apply for winding up, apply to NCLT for oppression and mismanagement. A joint holder is jointly and severally liable for calls. [Regulation 15 of Table F]. Joint holder can be considered for purpose of quorum - As per section 103(1) of Companies Act, 2013 [Corresponding to section 174 of the 1956 Act], quorum at general meeting consists of members personally present. Thus, if first named member as well as joint holder attends the meeting, both are members and hence can be considered for purpose of quorum.

When joint holder counted as single member - Joint holders are treated as single member in following cases - (a) for counting number of members of a private company - section 2(68) of Companies Act, 2013 [parallel proviso to section 3(1)(iii) of the 1956 Act]. (b) In case of application to NCLT in respect of oppression and mismanagement, any one joint holder can sign the application. However, for counting number of members required to sign the application, joint shareholders will be counted as 'one member' - section 244(1) of Companies Act, 2013 [Corresponding to section 399(2) of the 1956 Act].

This is a legal fiction and cannot be extended beyond its limited scope. The sections 2(68) and 244(1) themselves state that this is only for the purpose of those sections.

Who can be punished

Any person who commits an offence as prescribed is punishable.

Offences in case of company or firm - In case of Company or partnership firm, every person who was in-charge of or was responsible to affairs of the Company/firm is deemed to be guilty. Normally, a Managing Director (partner in case of firm) or other person specially authorised is deemed to be in-charge. However, such person can prove that offence was committed without his knowledge or he had taken due care to prevent the offence [section 140(1) of Customs Act].

In addition, if it is proved that the offence in relation to Company is committed with consent or connivance of, or due to neglect on part of any director, manager or Secretary or other officer of Company or partnership firm, such person shall be deemed to be guilty [section 140(2) of Customs Act].

Difference between provisions of section 140(1) and section 140(2) of Customs Act is that in former case, the person in charge is deemed to be guilty and burden of proof is on him to prove that he had no knowledge; while in later case, burden of proof is on prosecution to prove that offence was committed with knowledge or connivance of the director, manager, secretary or other officer.

In Sunil Bharti Mittal v. Central Bureau of Investigation (2015) 4 SCC 609 (SC 3 member bench), it has been held that director can be held vicariously liable only if (a) there is sufficient incriminating evidence against him coupled with criminal intent or (b) statutory regime attracts doctrine of vicarious liability.

In Girdhari Lal Gupta v. D N Mehta AIR 1972 SC 2162, it was held that the first part of definition is applicable to the one who is in overall control of the company. In Municipal Corporation of Delhi v. Ram Kishan Rohtagi AIR 1983 SC 67, it was held that there should be averment that director was responsible to the conduct of business of the company. Otherwise, he cannot be prosecuted. If there is no evidence that they were responsible for conduct of business of the company, they cannot be prosecuted - followed in D K Jhaver v. State of Punjab (1997) 24 CLA 133 (P&H).

A director/partner as well as the Company/firm can be prosecuted. Of course, Company/firm can only be fined, while the guilty officers/partners can be imprisoned and personal fine also can be imposed. In some cases, it has been held that a director can be prosecuted even if company itself is not prosecuted.

Company includes firm and AOP - As per Explanation to section 140(2) of Customs Act, 'company' means any body corporate and includes a firm or other association of individuals, and 'director' in relation to firm means a partner of the firm.

33.3-1 Company can be prosecuted even if law provides for compulsory imprisonment

There was controversy whether a company can be prosecuted in respect of offences which provide for compulsory imprisonment. Some sections of various laws provide for compulsory imprisonment. It was argued that a company cannot be punished under these sections as a company, being an artificial person, cannot be imprisoned. Finally, the controversy has been resolved, and it has been held in Standard Chartered Bank v. Directorate of Enforcement (2005) 4 SCC 530 = 145 Taxman 154 = 275 ITR 81 = 60 SCL 217 = AIR 2005 SC 2622 (SC 5 member bench majority decision) that company can be prosecuted even in respect of offences which provide for compulsory imprisonment - followed in Madhumilan Syntex v. UOI (2007) 160 Taxman 71 = 210 ELT 484 (SC) [Earlier contrary decision in Assistant Commissioner v. Velliappa Textiles (2003) 11 SCC 405 = 132 Taxman 165 = 157 ELT 369 = 263 ITR 550 = AIR 2004 SC 86 = 2003 AIR SCW 5647 = 46 SCL 808 (SC 3 member bench 2 v. 1 order) is now overruled].

4.19-8 Other interesting cases In the case which arose before the Madhya Pradesh High Court in CIT v. H.H. Maharani Manekaraje Pawar [1996] 86 Taxman 449 (MP) the facts were as under-

In pursuance of a consent decree to live apart obtained from competent court, the assessee gave some equity shares to his wife along with cash and other properties. The Assessing Officer held that the assessee transferred the shares and other assets and he added the capital gain to the income of the assessee. The assessee filed an appeal claiming that there was no transfer of capital asset and no capital gain assessable under the Act accrued to it. As the claims were rejected by the Commissioner of Income-tax (Appeals), the assessee filed an appeal before the Tribunal. The Tribunal held that there was transfer of shares by the assessee to his wife but no gain accrued which could be added in the income of the assessee as capital gain under section 45 of the Act.

The Indore Bench of the Tribunal-the order which gave rise to the appeal filed by the Revenue as seen above- categorically observed that "the question of a family settlement comes in when there is a dispute between admitted co-sharers or persons claiming a share in the properties although their rights may be disputed by the other co-sharers. In the present case, the wife was not claiming any right of sharing the assessee's properties as a co-sharer. Her claim was for maintenance and it was in lieu of maintenance that the properties in question were transferred by the assessee to her. The right of a wife for maintenance is an incident of the status or estate of matrimony and a Hindu is under a legal obligation to maintain his wife. The obligation to maintain the wife is personal in character and arises from the very existence of the relations between two parties. Therefore, when certain property is transferred to the wife in settlement of a claim for maintenance, it cannot, amount to a family settlement because there is no dispute between the co-shares and the other persons are not interested in the dispute."- refer H.H. Maharani Manekaraje Pawar v. ITO [1986] 15 ITD 545 (Indore)

The High Court endorsed the views of the Tribunal and held as under-

"The property was given to wife in connection with an agreement to live apart. Such an act is permissible under section 64(1)(iv) of the Act. The giving of property was not as a consideration but was in connection with an agreement to live apart.

According to section 125(4) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898, the wife is disentitled to receive any allowance from her husband if 'they are living separately by mutual consent' (in this case living apart is through court decree). The assessee in the instant case gave the property in connection with an agreement to live apart and thus created a case of living separately by mutual consent. There was no question of any capital gain in terms of section 45 of the Act. Therefore, the Tribunal was right in law in holding that no capital gain arose to the assessee under section 45 of the Act.

As to whether, the transaction amounted to transfer, it was found that the assessee extinguished his right on the above said property and as such the act was covered by section 2(47) of the Act and was clearly transfer in terms of the provisions of the Act. The spouse became the owner of the property given to her in connection with the agreement to live apart. It was clearly a case of transfer of capital asset in favour of the wife, though in pursuance of the consent decree and in connection with the agreement to live apart in terms of section 45 of the Act.

Therefore, the Tribunal was right in holding that there was a transfer of shares by the assessee but no capital gain arose to the assessee within the meaning of section 45 of the Act.".

Sarawsati Ramanathan [2009] 116 ITD 234 (Delhi) (SMC) wherein it was held that the word 'invested' in section 54EC cannot be interpreted to mean 'invested in the assessee's name' as such an interpretation adds words into the section and also ignores the purpose which the section is intended to serve. There is no requirement in section 54EC that the investment should be in the name of the assessee. The requirement, having regard to the object of the section to exempt capital gains if the sale proceeds find their way into certain specified assets, is that the sale proceeds of the capital asset must be invested in certain specified assets such as bonds of the NABARD, the National Highways Authority of India; the Rural Electrification Corporation Ltd.; National Housing Bank, etc. These are corporations established by the Government of India for development of infrastructure in the country and to muster funds for the purpose an incentive to invest in these corporations carrying out infrastructure development activities was given in the form of exemption from capital gains tax if the sale proceeds were invested in the bonds issued by these corporations. If development of infrastructure is the object, it would hardly matter whether the investment is made in the name of the assessee exclusively or in the joint names of the assessee and somebody else. The only condition is that the funds used for the investment must be traceable to the sale proceeds of the capital asset.

The requirement of section 54EC is that "the assessee has, at any time within the period of six months after the date of such transfer, invested the whole or any part of capital gains in the long-term specified asset.....". So what is relevant for claiming exemption under section 54EC is that the whole or any part of the capital gain should be invested in the long-term specified assets. If the amount of capital gain is invested by the assessee, the requirement of the section is fulfilled. It is wholly extraneous that the name of another person is also introduced as co-holder- Dr. (Mrs.) Sudha S.Trivedi v. ITO [2009] 31 SOT 38 (Mum. - Trib.).

Deduction will be available where assessee is a co-holder even though name of the spouse appears first in the REC bonds -Asstt. CIT v. Vijay S. Shirodkar [2011] 14 taxmann.com 70/48 SOT 8 (Mum. - Trib.)

Points to note: In Dr. (Mrs.) Sudha S. Trivedi (supra), the Bonds appeared in assessee's balance sheet. In Asstt. CIT v.Vijay. S. Shirodkar (supra), the assessee furnished a letter from REC confirming that the maturity proceeds of bonds will be credited to assessee's account.

Deposit in names of partners: In ITO v. Jifri & Kareem [1988] 24 ITD 288 (Co-chin - Trib.) the Cochin Bench of the Tribunal held that a firm is entitled to benefit under section 54E even though it has deposited the consideration received on sale of certain capital assets in names of its partners. Although this decision was delivered in relation to section 54E it should be applicable to section 54EC also.

23.4

Proprietary firm whether qualifies for appointment as auditor in firm name

The Chartered Accountants Act,1949 as amended by the Amendment Act, 2011 recognises sole proprietorship firm of CA registered with ICAI as a 'firm'. The following points are noteworthy:

According to new clause (ca) of section 2(1) of the 1949 Act, the term "firm" inter alia includes "sole proprietorship" registered with ICAI.

New clause (haa) defines "sole proprietorship" to mean an individual who engages himself in the practice of accountancy or offers to perform services referred to in clauses (ii) to (iv) of sub-section (2).

However, it appears that proprietorship firm cannot be appointed as auditor in firm name in view of the following:

Explanation to section 139(4) of the 2013 Act provides that for the purposes of Chapter XX, "firm" shall include Limited Liability Partnership incorporated under the LLP Act, 2008.

The definition of "firm" in Explanation to section 139(4) of the 2013 Act is silent on whether sole proprietorship CA firm which is recognized as "firm" in CA Act, 1949 is also covered in definition of firm.

Though definition of "firm" in Explanation is an inclusive one, it appears that proviso to section 141(1) of the 2013 Act clinches the issue. The said proviso provides that a firm of chartered accountants may be appointed by its firm name to be auditor of a company, "if majority of its partners practising in India are qualified for appointment as aforesaid". Obviously, there is no question of "majority of partners" in a sole proprietorship CA firm.

Thus, it follows that a company must appoint the proprietor of the so called firm by his name in his individual capacity as its auditor and the auditor's report will have to be signed by the proprietor himself in his own name. - MCA's Circular : No. 8/229/56 PR, dated 20-3-1957.

ITO [2017] 79 taxmann.com 156 (Chennai - Trib.) held that "where the assessee-HUF used its capital gain from sale of diamonds to purchase a property, even though it was registered in the individual name of Karta, property would belong to HUF; HUF would be eligible for exemption under section 54F of the Act."

The Chennai Bench agreed with the submissions made on behalf of the assessee that "the Bangalore Bench of this Tri-bunal in ITO v. Ramesh Kumar (HUF) in IT Appeal No. 628 (Bang.) of 2010-order dated 29th October,2010- examined this issue and found that a Karta of HUF or a coparcener of HUF can hold a property on behalf of the HUF."

The Chennai Bench also placed its reliance on the decision of the Karnataka High Court in the case of DIT (International Taxation) v. Mrs. Jennifer Bhide [2011] 15 taxmann.com 82/203 Taxman 208 (Kar.) wherein the Karnataka High Court held that there was no requirement that the investment should be in the name of the assessee only. In the case before the Karnataka High Court, the assessee sold the property and purchased another property in the joint names of herself and her husband. The Karnataka High Court found that merely because in the sale deed, the assessee's husband name was also mentioned, the benefit of deduction cannot be denied on that ground. These decisions, cited before the Bench, enabled the Tribunal to decide that "merely because the property was registered in the name of the Karta of HUF, the Assessing Officer cannot disallow the claim of deduction under Section 54Fof the Act."

11.9

INSTRUMENT OF TRANSFER OF SECURITY

A company shall not register transfer unless proper instrument of transfer duly stamped and executed by transferor and transferee specifying name, address and occupation of transferee is delivered to company along with original share/debenture certificate or letter of allotment of shares/debentures. These requirements are mandatory and transfer cannot be registered if transfer deed does not fulfil these requirements. Hence, a company (public or private) can decline transfer in following situations.

The share transfer deed should be in prescribed form. If it is not in prescribed form, the transfer cannot be said to be as per law. The transfer deed must be lodged within its validity period.

Execution of transfer deed by transferor and transferee - The transfer deed should be duly executed by transferor and transferee or by a person authorised on their behalf. Name, occupation and address of transferee should be specified. If the deed is not properly executed, transfer can be declined. In case of joint holding, all joint holders must sign and their signatures should be witnessed. If signatures are not witnessed, transfer can be declined.

Original share certificates to be enclosed - Shares cannot be transferred unless the original share certificates are attached to the share transfer deed. If company has not issued share certificate, original letter of allotment should be attached. This is the specific requirement.

If share certificate has been lost, first duplicate will have to be obtained.

11.9-1 Witnessing of signature of transferor/s.

The signature of transferor/s has to be witnessed. Otherwise, transfer is required to be rejected. Note that attestation is not compulsory, but 'witness' is essential.

11.9-2 Transfer of security where signature of transferor does not tally

Normally, share transfer should be declined if signature of share transferor/s does not tally with the specimen signature available with the company. This is because, if the signature of transferor does not tally, the instrument of transfer cannot be said to be properly executed by or on behalf of transferor.

Attestation of signature - There is a provision in share transfer form that in case of signature difference, the signature of transferor can be attested by * Magistrate * Notary Public * manager of transferor's bank * member of a stock exchange.

If the signature does not tally and the variation is major, transfer can be declined even if signature is attested, on the ground that transfer deed is not properly executed. This is because transfer cannot be recorded unless 'duly executed' document is submitted to the company. If the signature of transferor does not tally, the document cannot be termed as 'duly executed'.

If the signature is attested, and company records the transfer even if signature does not tally, there is no legal protection to the company, if it later turns out that the signature was forged. It may be noted that forgery is nullity at law and forged document can never pass on a good title.

Normally, if the signature is attested, minor variations may be ignored. However, if the variation is major, the company is indeed in a difficult position, if the signature is attested. This is because there is no provision in law that the company will be indemnified if company registers the transfer based on the basis of attested signatures. Some unscrupulous transferors deliberately make wrong signatures, so that transfer is delayed and they can enjoy benefit of shares like dividend, bonus, rights etc. even after they sell the shares and get the money.

If signature is attested by notary under his seal and required stamps has been affixed, there is a legal presumption that the official acts are properly done. Hence, company may act upon such attestation. However, the legal presumption is rebuttable.

Protection to company if it acts in good faith - In Bhuwaneshwar Nath Nigam v. Hindustan Lever (2002) 38 SCL 124 = 111 Comp Cas 590 (CLB), company issued a warning to transferor in respect of 200 shares as there was minor signature difference. Since company did not receive any objection, the shares were transferred. In respect of some shares, there was no signature difference and signature was attested by Bank and hence company effected the transfer. Later, shareholder filed petition that his signature was forged and attestation was fraudulent. It was held that the transfers made by company were valid and company is not liable. It was also held that all persons to whom shares were subsequently transferred should have been impleaded.

Company can apply for rectification of register if signature does not tally - In difficulty, Company can apply for rectification of register in case of difference in signature under section 53 of the 2011 Act.

11.1-4 Blank transfer deed Practice of dating of stamp by ROC was introduced to stop problems created due to blank transfer deeds.

Blank transfers is an accepted practice in share market. Blank transfer can be held invalid only in case of fraud or forgery or when transfer is without consideration. Validity of blank transfers has been upheld in Howrah Trading Co. Ltd. v. CIT (1959) 29 Comp Cas 282 (SC) = (1959) Supp 2 SCR 448 = AIR 1959 SC 775 and relying on Vasudev Ramchandra Shelat v. Pranlal Jayanand Thaker AIR 1974 SC 1728 = 45 Comp Cas 43 (SC). In S Anuratha v. AKMN Cylinders P Ltd. (1999) 19 SCL 1 (CLB), it was held that blank transfers are valid.

Companies Act, 2013 does not contain any provision relating to dating of share transfer form. There is no provision in Rules also.

Probable reason is that after wide spread use of demat shares on stock exchange, the provision has lost its usefulness.

11.1-5 Time limit for submission of transfer deed is not mandatory

Share certificate with transfer deed should be lodged within 60 days as per section 56 of Companies Act, 2013.

In Dove Investments v. Gujarat Industrial Inv. Corpn (2006) 66 SCL 89 = 129 Comp Cas 929 (SC 2 member bench), it was held that time limit for submission of transfer deed, specified in section 108 of the 1956 Act is directory. The company cannot refuse transfer even if application for transfer is submitted late, unless the company shows that prejudice is caused to it (due to late submission).

In Gujarat Industrial Investment Corpn v. Sterling Holiday Resorts (2005) 57 SCL 88 = 124 Comp Cas 390 (CLB), it has been held that the two month limit prescribed in section 108(1C) of the 1956 Act are directory and not mandatory. Transfer is required to be registered even if documents are lodged beyond a period of two months. In this case, actually, the transfer deeds were date stamped by authority as prescribed under section 108(1A) of the 1956 Act. Even then, it was held that section 108(1A) of the 1956 Act does not apply to transfer deeds lodged with bank/Financial Institution and transfer is required to be registered even if transfer deed is filed beyond two months - view confirmed in Dove Investments v. Gujarat Industrial Investment Corpn. Ltd. (2005) 60 SCL 604 (Mad HC DB) - order confirmed in Dove Investments v. Gujarat Industrial Inv. Corpn (2006) 66 SCL 89 = 129 Comp Cas 929 (SC 2 member bench).

11.1-6 Signing of transfer deed for shares

The transfer deed should be signed by the transferor.

Signature in case of joint holding - In case of joint holding, all joint holders must sign the transfer deed. - Hemalata Saha v. Stadmed P Ltd. AIR 1965 Cal 436.

If transfer deed is signed by only three out of four joint holders, transfer cannot be registered - Smt Claude-Lila Parulekar v. Sakal Papers P Ltd. (2005) 11 SCC 73 = 59 SCL 414 (SC).

Signature by power of attorney holder - Transfer deed can be signed by holder of power of attorney on behalf of transferor/s. Such power of attorney should be registered with company beforehand or certified copy should be furnished along with the transfer deed. If power of attorney was already registered with company by submitting certified copy, its registration number and date of registration with the company shall be given on reverse of transfer deed. However, a power of attorney holder cannot appoint a nominee. Similarly, a power of attorney holder cannot be appointed as a nominee.

Signature by holder of probate or letter of administration - Transfer by legal representative of deceased member is specifically permitted under section 56(5) of Companies Act, 2013 [parallel section 109 of the 1956 Act]
